stem: A records office runs a server-side web portal that keeps its client secret in a server vault. Each employee signs in to Docusign interactively and sends envelopes as themselves. Which OAuth flow best fits?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant
Implicit Grant
Confidential Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: A server that can protect a client secret plus an individual user who signs in interactively is the textbook case for Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE is for SPAs and native apps that cannot hold a secret; this portal has a server vault, so the confidential variant applies.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is for unattended service integrations that impersonate a consented user, not for employees signing in interactively.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant is a legacy browser flow that Docusign does not recommend; a server that can hold a secret should never use it.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Secret stored on a server plus an interactive user sign-in means Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the portal can keep a secret and each employee is present to sign in. The trap is A: PKCE-based Public Auth Code also signs users in, but it is meant for clients that cannot store a secret, which is not the case here. B needs no user at all, and C is the legacy browser flow Docusign no longer recommends.

stem: A developer promotes an integration key from the developer environment to production. Which configuration must be added again on the production version of the key?

options.text: Redirect URIs and secret keys
A new integration key GUID, because the demo GUID is invalid in production
The integration type chosen under How will you use this integration?
The Account Base URI value shown on the Apps and Keys page

answerText: Redirect URIs and secret keys
explanation: Go-Live duplicates the integration key into production, but configuration parameters such as secrets and redirect URIs are not copied and must be added in production.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Secrets and redirect URIs are not copied during Go-Live and must be added to the production key.
optionExplanations.B: The production key has the same value as the demo key; it is duplicated, not regenerated.
optionExplanations.C: The integration type is selected when the key is set up, before Go-Live; it is not re-entered in production.
optionExplanations.D: The Account Base URI is displayed by Docusign for the account (and returned by userinfo); you read it, you do not recreate it.

whyNotOthers: A is right because secrets and redirect URIs are not duplicated with the key. The trap is B: the production key is a separate copy, but it keeps the same key value, so no new GUID is needed. C is chosen before Go-Live, not recreated afterwards, and D is a read-only value Docusign displays for the account, not something you configure.

stem: One high-value envelope sent through the eSignature REST API must post its status events to a different listener URL than the account's Connect configuration. No other envelope should use that URL. What should the developer do?

options.text: Create a second account-level Connect configuration filtered to the sending user
Create an organization-level Connect configuration for the account
Set the envelope's notification object (reminders and expiration)
Add an eventNotification object to the Envelopes:create request

answerText: Add an eventNotification object to the Envelopes:create request
explanation: Envelope-level Connect is configured with the eventNotification property on Envelopes:create, so the custom listener URL applies only to that one envelope. The clue is that no other envelope may use the URL.

optionExplanations.A: An account-level configuration filtered by user still covers all envelopes that user sends or receives, not one envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Organization-level Connect covers envelopes for all or selected accounts in the org, far wider than one envelope.
optionExplanations.C: The envelope notification object sets reminders and expiration for signers; it does not define a webhook.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. eventNotification on Envelopes:create defines an envelope-level webhook URL and events for that envelope only.

whyNotOthers: D is right because eventNotification scopes the webhook to the single envelope being created. The trap is A: an account-level configuration filtered to one user would also fire for every other envelope that user sends. B is broader still (accounts across the org), and C confuses the notification object, which controls reminders and expiration, with eventNotification.

stem: An integration calls Envelopes:create and the recipients must receive the envelope as soon as the call succeeds. Which value should the request's status property have?

options.text: created
voided
completed
sent

answerText: sent
explanation: Setting status to sent in the Envelopes:create request sends the envelope immediately. The clue is that recipients must receive it as soon as the call succeeds.

optionExplanations.A: created saves the envelope as a draft; nothing is delivered until the status is later changed to sent.
optionExplanations.B: voided is used to cancel an envelope that is already in process; it cannot be used to deliver a new one.
optionExplanations.C: completed is reached by Docusign after every recipient finishes; an integration does not set it on create.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. status sent tells Envelopes:create to send the envelope to recipients immediately.

whyNotOthers: D is right because sent is the only status that delivers the envelope on creation. The trap is A: created is a valid value for the same request, but it only saves a draft. B and C are not set on create: voided cancels an in-process envelope and completed is set by Docusign when all recipients finish.

stem: A custom website must show a Docusign web form inline on its own page. The app has already called Instances:createInstance with a clientUserId and received the instance URL. Which client-side component renders that URL in the page?

options.text: An embedded signing URL from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
A remote instance created with sendOption and recipients[]
Brand destination URLs on the account brand
Docusign JS client SDK

answerText: Docusign JS client SDK
explanation: The app already holds the instance URL from createInstance with a clientUserId, which is the embedded pattern; Docusign JS is the client-side SDK that renders that URL inline.

optionExplanations.A: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient returns a signing view for an existing envelope recipient; an embedded web form instance has no envelope until the first submit, and it already has its own instance URL.
optionExplanations.B: A remote instance emails participants a link; it does not render anything inline on the custom website.
optionExplanations.C: Destination URLs only redirect remote signers after events such as signing complete; they do not render a form.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign JS is the JavaScript client SDK Docusign provides to embed a web form instance URL inside a host web page.

whyNotOthers: D is right because Docusign JS is the documented way to embed a web form instance URL in a host page. The trap is A: embedded signing does use a recipient view URL, but that is for an envelope, and an embedded web form instance has its own URL and no envelope yet. B and C fail because a remote instance sends email links and destination URLs only redirect after signing.

stem: An ERP sync job already stores the agreementId of a signed supply contract. It must copy that agreement's AI-extracted parties and provisions into the ERP. Which call should it make?

options.text: Agreements:getAgreementsList
eSignature Envelopes:get on the source envelope
Agreements:getAgreement
Agreements:createAgreementSummary

answerText: Agreements:getAgreement
explanation: Agreements:getAgreement returns the full structured record (type, category, parties, provisions) for one agreement. The job already has the agreementId, so a direct single-record call is the right fit.

optionExplanations.A: Lists agreements for the account; useful when the ID is unknown, but the job already has the agreementId.
optionExplanations.B: Returns envelope metadata (status, recipients, dates), not the AI-extracted parties and provisions stored in Agreement Manager.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Returns one agreement's structured, AI-extracted data, which is exactly what the ERP sync needs.
optionExplanations.D: Generates an AI-written summary of the agreement document, not structured field values to map into an ERP.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the ID is known and the job needs one agreement's extracted fields. The trap is B: the contract was signed in an eSignature envelope, but Envelopes:get returns envelope status and recipients, not Iris-extracted parties and provisions. A lists many agreements (a search step that is unnecessary here) and D produces an AI prose summary rather than structured fields.

stem: A loan intake workflow must capture applicant details on a form and use those values to fill the agreement the applicant then signs. Which step order should the workflow use?

options.text: Collect Data with Web Forms, then Prepare eSignature Template, then Send Documents for Signature
Send Documents for Signature, then Collect Data with Web Forms
Prepare eSignature Template, then Collect Data with Web Forms, then Send Documents for Signature
Collect Data with Web Forms, then a Send an Email step with the form attached

answerText: Collect Data with Web Forms, then Prepare eSignature Template, then Send Documents for Signature
explanation: The form values must exist before the template step can map them into the document, and the Prepare step is followed by Send Documents for Signature. Step order must match the business process: collect, prepare, sign.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Collect the data, prepare the template with the collected values, then send it for signature.
optionExplanations.B: Signing first means the agreement cannot contain the applicant's form values.
optionExplanations.C: The Prepare eSignature Template step runs before the form, so the variables it should map are still empty.
optionExplanations.D: An email step only notifies; it does not produce a signed agreement.

whyNotOthers: A is right because data is collected first, mapped into the template, then sent for signature. The trap is C: it uses the right steps, but preparing the template before the form runs means there are no applicant values to map yet. B sends for signature before any data exists, and D never requests a signature at all.

stem: A customer wants Docusign to call its external service (for example, to verify entered data or store completed files) during an agreement process, packaged so account admins can simply install it. What does an extension app provide?

options.text: A way for an external app to call eSignature APIs with an integration key
A Connect webhook that pushes envelope events to an external listener
A branded signing page hosted on the customer's own website
A packaged way to connect third-party service functionality into Docusign

answerText: A packaged way to connect third-party service functionality into Docusign
explanation: Extension apps connect third-party services into Docusign: Docusign calls the external service through the app's actions, and admins install the app from the App Center. The clue is that Docusign must call out to the service and admins install it.

optionExplanations.A: An integration key lets an external app call Docusign APIs; here Docusign must call the external service, which is the reverse direction.
optionExplanations.B: Connect pushes event notifications outward; it does not let Docusign invoke an external service as part of the process.
optionExplanations.C: Branding or embedding the signing page changes the UI, not which external functionality Docusign can invoke.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. An extension app packages external functionality (verify, read/write data, store files) that Docusign invokes and admins install.

whyNotOthers: D is right because an extension app plugs external functionality into Docusign and is installed from the App Center. The trap is A: an integration key lets your app call Docusign, which is the opposite direction. B (Connect) only notifies a listener of events, and C is a signing-UI customization, neither of which is an installable package of external functionality.

stem: A financial-aid office builds a browser-only single-page application with no backend. It cannot protect a client secret, and each individual user must sign in. Which flow should the team keep?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: A browser-only SPA is a public client that cannot keep a secret, and users sign in, so Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE is the recommended flow.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant requires a protected client secret, which a browser-only SPA cannot keep.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is for unattended service integrations and needs a protected RSA private key; it does not sign in individual users.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. SPA, no secret, interactive user: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant used to be the SPA answer but is legacy and not recommended; Public Auth Code with PKCE replaces it.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the clues are no backend, no secret, and an interactive user. The trap is D: Implicit Grant was historically used for SPAs, but it is legacy and Docusign recommends Public Auth Code with PKCE instead. A needs a secret the SPA cannot protect, and B has no user sign-in.

stem: A software vendor is building an app that many Docusign customers will use with their own Docusign accounts, authorizing the app to connect to their accounts. Which integration type should the vendor choose?

options.text: Private custom integration
Third-party integration key
Embedded integration
Public integration

answerText: Public integration
explanation: An app built for multiple Docusign customers who connect it to their own Docusign accounts is a Public integration (it requires joining the Docusign Partner Program).

optionExplanations.A: Private custom integration is for apps directly used by your own employees or your customers' employees, not a multi-customer partner app.
optionExplanations.B: Third-party integration key is chosen by a customer who must supply its own key to a partner integration, not by the vendor.
optionExplanations.C: Embedded integration is for vendors whose customers use Docusign features through the vendor's own account, without their own Docusign accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A public integration serves many Docusign customers who authorize it against their own accounts.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the deciding clue is that customers use their own Docusign accounts and authorize the app. The trap is C: Embedded integration is also for vendors, but there the customers do not have their own Docusign accounts and use the vendor's account. A is for apps used by your own employees or your customers' employees, and B is for a customer who must supply its own key to a partner product.

stem: A system must learn as soon as recipients complete signing, without making excessive API calls. Which option should be used?

options.text: Poll Envelopes:get for every open envelope every minute
Poll each envelope once every 15 minutes as the primary status method
Subscribe to Connect events
Rely on the completion email sent to the envelope sender

answerText: Subscribe to Connect events
explanation: Connect pushes a message only when something changes, so the system learns of completions immediately and spends no API calls checking.

optionExplanations.A: Polling every minute violates the once-per-15-minutes-per-envelope limit and can fail Go-Live review.
optionExplanations.B: Compliant polling still uses API calls for unchanged envelopes and adds up to 15 minutes of delay.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect pushes events when they occur, with no polling calls.
optionExplanations.D: Completion emails go to people, not systems, and are not an integration mechanism.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a webhook delivers the event when it happens and does not consume API calls. The trap is B: polling every 15 minutes per envelope respects the polling limit, but it still burns calls and can be up to 15 minutes late. A violates the polling limit outright, and D relies on a human-facing email that a system cannot use reliably.

stem: A developer wants to create an envelope now and send it later, after an internal reviewer approves it. Which status value should the Envelopes:create request use?

options.text: sent
draft
created
completed

answerText: created
explanation: status created builds the envelope without sending it, leaving a draft that can be sent later. The clue is 'create now, send later'.

optionExplanations.A: sent delivers the envelope immediately, before the reviewer can approve it.
optionExplanations.B: draft describes the result, but it is not the status value; the API expects created.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. status created saves the envelope as a draft so it can be sent later.
optionExplanations.D: completed is a terminal status set by Docusign after all recipients finish.

whyNotOthers: C is right because created is the API value for a draft envelope. The trap is B: the envelope is called a draft, but draft is not a valid status value. A would send immediately and D is set by Docusign after all recipients finish.

stem: An app creates one embedded web form instance per customer record and must map each instance back to that record. Which createInstance value carries your system's own user identifier?

options.text: The formId of the web form configuration
The envelopeId of the generated envelope
clientUserId
The instance URL

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: clientUserId is the value your app supplies to tie the embedded instance to its own user or record.

optionExplanations.A: The formId identifies the configuration that every instance is created from, so it is the same for all customers and cannot identify one record.
optionExplanations.B: For an embedded instance the envelope is only created when the first user submits, so there is no envelopeId at creation time (and standalone forms never have one).
optionExplanations.C: Correct. clientUserId is a value you choose to identify the user in your system (max 100 characters), and it is required for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.D: The instance URL is what Docusign JS renders; it is generated by Docusign, not a value you supply from your records.

whyNotOthers: C is right because clientUserId is your own identifier, supplied on createInstance. The trap is A: it is a real Web Forms ID, but it identifies the shared form configuration, not an individual customer. B and D fail because the envelope does not exist yet when an embedded instance is created and the instance URL is a Docusign-generated rendering URL.

stem: A renewals app must find all NDAs expiring this quarter, then show the full extracted data for the one the user selects. The app does not know any agreementId in advance. Which approach fits?

options.text: Call Agreements:getAgreement with the expiration criteria as parameters
Call Agreements:getAgreementsList to find matches, then Agreements:getAgreement for the selected one
Call eSignature Envelopes:listStatusChanges filtered by completed date
Call Agreements:createAgreementSummary on every agreement in the account

answerText: Call Agreements:getAgreementsList to find matches, then Agreements:getAgreement for the selected one
explanation: The app has criteria but no agreementId, so it first lists or searches agreements with getAgreementsList and then calls getAgreement for the chosen record.

optionExplanations.A: getAgreement requires a specific agreementId; it is not a search operation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. List or search agreements first, then retrieve the detailed record for the selected agreement.
optionExplanations.C: Returns envelope status changes; it does not filter on AI-extracted agreement fields such as expiration date.
optionExplanations.D: Produces AI summaries one agreement at a time; it neither filters nor returns structured fields.

whyNotOthers: B is right because search comes first when the ID is unknown, then the detail call. The trap is A: getAgreement does return the full extracted data, but it needs a specific agreementId in the path and does not search by criteria. C finds completed envelopes, not agreements with extracted expiration dates, and D creates AI summaries rather than filtering agreements.

stem: In a US new-hire workflow, the new hire has already submitted a web form. Next, the new hire must be invited to complete identity verification themselves. Which step sequence matches the Workflow Builder onboarding pattern?

options.text: Verify Someone's Identity, then Set Up Invite
Send an Email step, then Send Documents for Signature
Show a Confirmation Screen, then Verify Someone's Identity
Set Up Invite, then Verify Someone's Identity

answerText: Set Up Invite, then Verify Someone's Identity
explanation: In the course onboarding example, a Set Up Invite step invites the new hire, and the Verify Someone's Identity step follows it. The invite must come first so the participant can reach the verification step.

optionExplanations.A: Reversed order: the participant cannot complete verification before being invited to it.
optionExplanations.B: An email notification followed by signing skips the required identity verification.
optionExplanations.C: A confirmation screen displays a message; it does not invite a participant to act.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Set Up Invite routes the new hire to the workflow, then Verify Someone's Identity runs.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the participant is invited first and then completes the identity step. The trap is A: it uses the same two steps but in reverse, so the verification would run before the new hire was invited to it. B skips verification entirely, and C only shows a screen; it does not invite the participant.

stem: An extension app will be used only by one organization's own Docusign production accounts and must not be installable by other customers. Which distribution is appropriate?

options.text: Public app with publicationRegions limited to the organization's region
Leave the approved app in the developer account
Private extension app shared with the organization's production accounts
Public app installed only by admins who know its App ID

answerText: Private extension app shared with the organization's production accounts
explanation: Private distribution limits installation to a specific list of production accounts, which matches an app meant for one organization only.

optionExplanations.A: publicationRegions limits regions, not organizations; any customer in the region could install a public app.
optionExplanations.B: Before publishing, an app is usable only in the developer account in demo, not in the organization's production accounts.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Private distribution lets only the listed production accounts install the app.
optionExplanations.D: Public apps are available to all App Center users; knowing an App ID is not an access restriction.

whyNotOthers: C is right because private distribution restricts installation to listed production accounts. The trap is A: publicationRegions restricts geography for public apps, so any customer in that region could still install it. B keeps the app in the demo developer account only, and D is not a real access control because public apps are available to all App Center users.

stem: A partner vendor's scheduled service runs nightly on a secure server, sending envelopes from a dedicated system sender account. No person is present to sign in. Which option is correct?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: JSON Web Token Grant
explanation: No user is present, so JWT Grant is the fit: the service signs an assertion with its RSA private key and impersonates the consented system user.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant fits servers that store a secret, but it still requires an interactive user sign-in.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Unattended service using a system user after consent is JWT Grant.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE is an interactive flow for clients without a secret, not an unattended job.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a legacy interactive browser flow and cannot run unattended.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the deciding clue is that nobody is present to sign in. The trap is A: the secure server could store a secret, but Confidential Auth Code still needs a user to sign in through a browser. C and D are also interactive browser flows.

stem: After Go-Live, an eSignature app authenticates in production but its API calls still go to https://demo.docusign.net/restapi and fail. What must be changed?

options.text: Keep the demo host but send the production access token with each call
Hardcode https://www.docusign.net/restapi for every production account
Call the account's production base URI (from userinfo) instead of the demo host
Generate a new integration key so that calls are routed to production

answerText: Call the account's production base URI (from userinfo) instead of the demo host
explanation: Production API calls must use the account's base URI, which you obtain from the userinfo endpoint (for example https://{server}.docusign.net/restapi), instead of demo.docusign.net.

optionExplanations.A: A production token is not valid against the demo host; the host itself must change.
optionExplanations.B: Production accounts sit on different servers, so a single hardcoded host fails for many accounts; use the base_uri from userinfo.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The production base URI comes from the userinfo response (or the Account Base URI on Apps and Keys).
optionExplanations.D: The production key has the same value as the demo key; the routing problem is the host, not the key.

whyNotOthers: C is right because production accounts live on a specific server whose base URI comes from userinfo. The trap is B: it does use a production host, but hardcoding one server breaks accounts that live on other data centers (NA2, EU, CA and so on). A mixes a production token with the demo host, and D is unnecessary because the key keeps the same value in production.

stem: A company wants one webhook configuration that receives events for envelopes across all accounts in its Docusign organization. What should the Connect configuration be?

options.text: An account-level Connect configuration in each account
Organization-level Connect
eventNotification on every envelope
An account-level configuration in the primary account only

answerText: Organization-level Connect
explanation: Organization-level Connect covers envelopes sent or received by all or selected accounts in the organization from a single configuration.

optionExplanations.A: Works, but requires a separate configuration in every account instead of one org-wide configuration.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Organization-level Connect covers all or selected accounts in the organization.
optionExplanations.C: eventNotification covers only API-sent envelopes, one envelope at a time.
optionExplanations.D: An account-level configuration sees only its own account's envelopes.

whyNotOthers: B is right because only an org-level configuration spans multiple accounts at once. The trap is A: one account-level configuration per account would deliver the events, but it is several configurations to maintain, not the single webhook requested. C only covers API-sent envelopes and must be repeated on each one, and D misses every other account.

stem: A sent envelope contains a fatal error and no one should sign it. The integration must cancel it permanently. Which status should it set?

options.text: created
voided
declined
deleted

answerText: voided
explanation: Voiding (status voided with a voidedReason) permanently cancels an in-process envelope and stops signing. The clue is a sent envelope that must be canceled permanently.

optionExplanations.A: created describes a draft; it does not cancel an envelope that is already sent.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. status voided permanently cancels the in-process envelope so no one can sign it.
optionExplanations.C: declined is recorded when a recipient refuses to sign; the sender does not set it to cancel.
optionExplanations.D: deleted is not the documented cancel action for an in-process envelope; voiding is.

whyNotOthers: B is right because voided is the documented way to cancel an envelope that is in process. The trap is D: deleting sounds permanent, but it is not how the sender cancels an in-process envelope. A only applies to drafts and C is an action a recipient takes, not one the sender sets.

stem: A public-sector records office requires signers to prove their identity with a government-issued photo ID before they can sign. What must be added to each signer in the Envelopes:create request?

options.text: authenticationMethod on the EnvelopeViews:createRecipient call
An identityVerification object with the account's IDV workflowId
An accessCode on the recipient
A clientUserId on the recipient

answerText: An identityVerification object with the account's IDV workflowId
explanation: A government photo ID check before signing is ID verification, configured with identityVerification.workflowId on the recipient.

optionExplanations.A: authenticationMethod only records on the certificate how your app authenticated the user; it does not enforce any identity check.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. ID verification is enforced by adding identityVerification.workflowId (from IdentityVerifications:list, REST v2.1) to the recipient.
optionExplanations.C: An access code is a shared secret entered by the recipient; it does not check a government photo ID.
optionExplanations.D: clientUserId makes the recipient an embedded signer; it adds no identity verification.

whyNotOthers: B is right because IDV is enforced per recipient with identityVerification.workflowId. The trap is A: it is identity-related and appears on the certificate, but it only records your app's own authentication and enforces nothing. C and D fail because an access code checks a shared secret, not an ID, and clientUserId only controls embedded signing.

stem: A real-estate company has thousands of signed leases that were never sent through Docusign. It wants them in Agreement Manager with AI-extracted data like any other agreement. Which capability fits?

options.text: Bulk import the legacy agreements into Agreement Manager
Re-send each lease as a new eSignature envelope
Agreements:getAgreementsList
Store key lease terms as envelope custom fields

answerText: Bulk import the legacy agreements into Agreement Manager
explanation: Agreement Manager supports bulk import of existing, non-Docusign agreements, and AI extraction runs on imported agreements just as on completed envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bulk import adds legacy agreements to Agreement Manager so AI extraction can run on them.
optionExplanations.B: Already-signed leases do not need to be re-signed; import is the intended path for legacy contracts.
optionExplanations.C: Reads agreements already in Agreement Manager; it cannot add the legacy leases.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope custom fields are eSignature metadata and do not create agreement records.

whyNotOthers: A is right because import brings the existing files into the repository where Iris extracts their data. The trap is B: completed envelopes do flow into Agreement Manager, but re-sending already-signed leases is unnecessary and creates new signing events. C only reads agreements already in the repository, and D stores data on envelopes, not in Agreement Manager.

stem: After the signing step, a contracts workflow must save the completed agreement to the company's Box account. The Box extension app is already installed. Which step should be added?

options.text: A Send an Email step that mails the document to a shared inbox
A Read step from an extension app
A Store Files extension app step placed after Send Documents for Signature
A Store Files extension app step placed before Send Documents for Signature

answerText: A Store Files extension app step placed after Send Documents for Signature
explanation: Store Files app steps automate storage of completed agreements in services such as Box or Google Drive. It must come after the signing step so the stored file is the completed agreement.

optionExplanations.A: Emailing a document is not archiving it in Box.
optionExplanations.B: Read steps import data into the workflow; they do not save files externally.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A Store Files step after signing saves the completed agreement to Box.
optionExplanations.D: Placed before signing, it would save a document that has not been signed yet.

whyNotOthers: C is right because Store Files is the app-step category for saving documents, and it runs after signing. The trap is D: correct step type, wrong position, so it would store the unsigned document. A only emails the file, and B imports data from an external system rather than saving files to it.

stem: Within the actions object of the manifest, what is the primary purpose of the connectionsReference property?

options.text: It specifies the OAuth scopes required by the external API
It indicates whether the app is PUBLIC or PRIVATE
It defines the endpoint URL for the external API call
It links the action to authentication defined in the connections object

answerText: It links the action to authentication defined in the connections object
explanation: connectionsReference points an action to a named connection, so the action uses that connection's authentication.

optionExplanations.A: Scopes are part of the connection's auth configuration, not the reference.
optionExplanations.B: PUBLIC or PRIVATE is set by the distribution property.
optionExplanations.C: The endpoint is defined by the action; connectionsReference only points to auth.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. It links the action to the authentication declared in a named connection.

whyNotOthers: D is right because connectionsReference ties an action to a connection's auth settings. The trap is A: scopes are configured in the connection itself, not in the reference. B is the distribution property, and C is part of the action's own endpoint definition.

stem: A JWT integration's token request fails with consent_required. The impersonated user has never granted consent for the requested scopes. What must be obtained before token requests succeed?

options.text: Individual or admin consent for the integration key and requested scopes
A newly generated RSA key pair for the integration key
A client secret added to the JWT token request
Production approval (Go-Live) for the integration key

answerText: Individual or admin consent for the integration key and requested scopes
explanation: JWT Grant only issues tokens after the impersonated user, or an admin on their behalf, has consented to the integration key and its scopes; consent_required means that step is missing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. JWT needs individual or admin consent for the integration key and scopes before tokens are issued.
optionExplanations.B: A new RSA key pair fixes signing problems, but the user would still not have consented.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant authenticates with an RSA-signed assertion; a client secret is not used and does not grant consent.
optionExplanations.D: Go-Live promotes the key to production; it does not record consent from the impersonated user.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the error and the stem both point to missing consent. The trap is B: key problems also break JWT requests, but a new RSA key pair does not grant consent. C is not part of JWT Grant, and D is about promoting the key to production, not about consent.

stem: After Go-Live, an app that creates envelopes from a server template fails in production with a template-not-found error. It still sends the templateId it used in the developer account. What is the fix?

options.text: Wait for the Go-Live review to finish copying the developer templates
Create the template in the production account and use its production templateId
Keep the same templateId and only switch the base URI to production
Switch the app to composite templates, because server templates are demo-only

answerText: Create the template in the production account and use its production templateId
explanation: Production account data is separate from the developer account, so templates must be created in production, and they get new production template IDs.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live duplicates only the integration key; templates are never copied by the review.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Recreate or migrate the template in production and reference its new production templateId.
optionExplanations.C: The base URI change is needed, but the demo templateId does not exist in the production account.
optionExplanations.D: Server templates are fully supported in production; there is no need to change the request model.

whyNotOthers: B is right because templates are not migrated by Go-Live and production templates have their own IDs. The trap is C: switching the base URI is also required after Go-Live, but the demo templateId still does not exist in the production account. A is wrong because Go-Live only duplicates the integration key, and D is wrong because server templates work in production.

stem: A listener must receive Connected Fields verification results, which Docusign delivers through the extension-executed event. Which Connect message format must the configuration use?

options.text: JSON SIM (Connect 2.0) format
Legacy XML SIM format
XML aggregate mode
SOAP messages using the eSignature SOAP object model

answerText: JSON SIM (Connect 2.0) format
explanation: The extension-executed event, which carries Connected Fields verification results, is available only with the JSON SIM format.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. extension-executed is available only with JSON SIM.
optionExplanations.B: Legacy XML SIM sends individual messages but does not provide the extension-executed event.
optionExplanations.C: Aggregate mode is a legacy XML option and does not deliver extension-executed.
optionExplanations.D: SOAP-style XML messages are the legacy format; the event is JSON SIM only.

whyNotOthers: A is right because extension-executed is a JSON SIM-only event. The trap is B: XML SIM also sends individual messages, but it is the legacy format and does not offer this event. C and D are other legacy XML options that are envelope-focused and also lack the event.

stem: A network retry might submit the same create-envelope request twice. Which sender-supplied value on the envelope helps the app avoid creating a duplicate?

options.text: transactionId
recipientId
batchId
envelopeId

answerText: transactionId
explanation: transactionId is a sender-generated value on the envelope definition that lets the app recognize whether an earlier create request already produced the envelope. The clue is 'sender-supplied'.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A sender-generated transactionId lets the app detect a create request that already succeeded.
optionExplanations.B: recipientId identifies a recipient within one envelope; it says nothing about duplicate envelopes.
optionExplanations.C: batchId is returned when a bulk send is initiated; it tracks a batch, not a single create retry.
optionExplanations.D: envelopeId is generated by Docusign and returned only after success, so the client cannot supply it for a retry.

whyNotOthers: A is right because transactionId is the value the sender generates to identify the create attempt. The trap is D: envelopeId identifies the envelope, but Docusign generates it and only returns it after a successful create. B identifies a recipient within an envelope and C identifies a bulk send batch.

stem: A university financial-aid office wants Docusign to send each signer a one-time code by text message, which the signer must enter before opening the envelope. Which recipient authentication method fits?

options.text: Phone authentication (code by SMS or voice call)
Access code
Knowledge-based authentication (KBA)
authenticationMethod recorded on createRecipient

answerText: Phone authentication (code by SMS or voice call)
explanation: The clue is a one-time code that Docusign sends by text message, which is phone authentication.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Phone authentication sends the recipient a code by SMS or call that must be entered before access; it is configured with an identityVerification workflowId.
optionExplanations.B: An access code is chosen by the sender and shared out of band; Docusign does not generate and text it as a one-time code.
optionExplanations.C: KBA asks public-record questions (US only); it does not send a code.
optionExplanations.D: This only records your app's own authentication on the certificate and enforces nothing.

whyNotOthers: A is right because phone authentication delivers a code by SMS or voice before the recipient can access the envelope. The trap is B: it is also a code the signer types, but the sender sets it and shares it out of band. C and D fail because KBA uses public-record questions and authenticationMethod only records authentication.

stem: A pull request syncs agreements to a records system that must keep a copy of each agreement file, not only its extracted fields. The code calls only Agreements:getAgreement. What should the plan add?

options.text: Nothing; Agreements:getAgreement already returns the document file content
A call to Agreements:getAgreementsList for the same agreement
A call to Agreements:createAgreementSummary to produce the stored copy
A separate document download step for the agreement file

answerText: A separate document download step for the agreement file
explanation: getAgreement returns structured JSON (type, parties, provisions), not the document file. A records system that needs the file itself needs a separate document download step.

optionExplanations.A: getAgreement returns structured metadata and extracted values, not the agreement file itself.
optionExplanations.B: The list call returns agreement records for many agreements, not the document file.
optionExplanations.C: An AI summary is generated text, not a copy of the signed agreement.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The file must be retrieved with a separate document download, in addition to the extracted data.

whyNotOthers: D is right because extracted data and the document file are different things. The trap is A: getAgreement does return the full agreement record, but that record is metadata and extracted values, not the PDF. B returns list-level agreement data, and C returns an AI-written summary, which is not a copy of the agreement.

stem: On a web form, applicants choose 'Individual' or 'Business'. A separate eSignature template already exists for each type. What should follow the form step?

options.text: Two Collect Data with Web Forms steps in sequence
A Branching Rule step on the applicant-type field, with its own Prepare and Send steps on each path
One Prepare eSignature Template step that always uses the Individual template
A Show a Confirmation Screen step asking the applicant which agreement to sign

answerText: A Branching Rule step on the applicant-type field, with its own Prepare and Send steps on each path
explanation: Branching rules route the workflow down different paths based on a condition, here the form field. Each path then prepares and sends its own template.

optionExplanations.A: A second form collects more data but does not route to a different agreement.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The branching rule evaluates the form value and routes each applicant type to its own template.
optionExplanations.C: A single fixed template ignores the applicant type, so business applicants get the wrong agreement.
optionExplanations.D: A confirmation screen displays information; it cannot branch the workflow.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the form answer decides which template is used, and that is what a branching rule does. The trap is C: Prepare eSignature Template is meant for one template used by every instance, which does not fit two applicant types. A only collects more data, and D shows a message; neither routes the process.

stem: A partner wants Docusign customers broadly to discover and install its app. Which distribution should it choose?

options.text: Private extension app
Public extension app published to the Docusign App Center
Private app shared with every customer's account ID
Send customers the manifest file to upload into their own accounts

answerText: Public extension app published to the Docusign App Center
explanation: Public distribution makes the app available to all App Center users, which is what broad discovery and installation require.

optionExplanations.A: Private apps are limited to specific accounts, so customers cannot broadly discover them.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A public app in the App Center can be discovered and installed by all customers.
optionExplanations.C: Private sharing uses a limited list of production accounts; it is not a broad distribution model.
optionExplanations.D: Manifests are uploaded by the developer in the Developer Console; customers install from the App Center.

whyNotOthers: B is right because public apps are listed for all customers in the App Center. The trap is C: private sharing works from a predefined list of production accounts and cannot realistically cover every customer. A restricts installation, and D does not work because customers install apps from the App Center, not by uploading a manifest.

stem: A web app uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant (users sign in) and only needs to send eSignature envelopes and read the user's account information. Which scopes should it request at consent?

options.text: signature impersonation
Every available scope, to avoid re-consent later
No scopes; Docusign infers permissions from the API calls
Only the minimum needed for those calls, such as signature

answerText: Only the minimum needed for those calls, such as signature
explanation: Least privilege: request only the scopes the API calls need; signature covers most eSignature actions for a signed-in user.

optionExplanations.A: impersonation is for JWT Grant acting as a user; a signed-in Auth Code user does not need it.
optionExplanations.B: Requesting every scope breaks least privilege and makes the consent screen broader than needed.
optionExplanations.C: Docusign does not infer permissions; scopes must be listed on the consent request.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Request only the scopes the operations need, here signature.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the app's calls only need eSignature access for a signed-in user. The trap is A: signature impersonation is the standard JWT consent, but impersonation is unnecessary when the user signs in directly. B over-requests, and C fails because scopes must be requested explicitly.

stem: An integration key that uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant has just gone live. Which settings must the developer add to the production version of the key?

options.text: Secret key and redirect URIs
An RSA key pair only
A new integration key GUID
Nothing, because the developer key's settings apply in production

answerText: Secret key and redirect URIs
explanation: For Authorization Code Grant apps, the After Go-Live guidance says to add redirect URIs and secrets on the production key, because they are not copied from the developer environment.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Authorization Code Grant needs a secret key and redirect URIs, which must be added in production.
optionExplanations.B: RSA key pairs are the JWT Grant credential; a Confidential Authorization Code Grant app needs a secret.
optionExplanations.C: The production key keeps the same value as the demo key.
optionExplanations.D: Production OAuth settings are separate from the developer account's settings; nothing carries over.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the clue is Confidential Authorization Code Grant, which needs a secret and redirect URIs. The trap is B: an RSA key pair is what JWT Grant apps add in production, not Authorization Code Grant apps. C is wrong because the key keeps its value, and D is wrong because production OAuth settings are separate from developer settings.

stem: A listener must verify that each incoming webhook message really came from Docusign and was not altered in transit. Which control does this?

options.text: Check that the payload's envelopeId exists in the account
Rely on the listener's HTTPS certificate alone
Use a long, unguessable listener URL path
Validate the HMAC signature in the X-DocuSign-Signature-1 header

answerText: Validate the HMAC signature in the X-DocuSign-Signature-1 header
explanation: With HMAC security, Docusign hashes the message body with a shared secret key and sends it in X-DocuSign-Signature headers, proving both authenticity and integrity.

optionExplanations.A: Anyone who knows an envelope ID can put it in a forged payload.
optionExplanations.B: HTTPS encrypts traffic and authenticates the listener, not the sender.
optionExplanations.C: A hidden URL is obscurity, not authentication; it can leak.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Recomputing the HMAC with the shared key verifies authenticity and integrity.

whyNotOthers: D is right because only the HMAC check proves the sender knew the shared key and the body is unchanged. The trap is B: HTTPS is required and encrypts the traffic, but the listener's certificate proves the listener's identity, not that the caller is Docusign. A and C rely on values an attacker could obtain or guess.

stem: An envelope request uses a server template already stored in Docusign (template reference model). Which value identifies that template?

options.text: compositeTemplates with an inlineTemplate
anchorString with offsets
roleName in templateRoles
templateId

answerText: templateId
explanation: In the template reference model, templateId identifies the saved template and templateRoles map recipients into its roles.

optionExplanations.A: compositeTemplates is a different envelope model; an inlineTemplate supplies runtime data, not a stored template ID.
optionExplanations.B: anchorString with offsets positions tabs relative to text; it does not reference a template.
optionExplanations.C: roleName in templateRoles matches a recipient to a template role; it does not say which template to use.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. templateId references the template stored in Docusign.

whyNotOthers: D is right because templateId is the reference to the stored template. The trap is C: roleName is part of the same request, but it maps recipients to roles and does not identify the template. A is a different envelope model and B places tabs relative to document text.

stem: Maya's partner app sends envelopes for remote signing (signers open them from email). After finishing, signers must land on the vendor's own page. Which feature controls this?

options.text: returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
Docusign JS sessionEnd event handler
A Connect webhook
Brand destination URLs

answerText: Brand destination URLs
explanation: The clue is remote signing; post-signing redirects for remote signers are set with brand destination URLs.

optionExplanations.A: returnUrl sets the post-session redirect for embedded signing only; remote signers opening email links never go through createRecipient.
optionExplanations.B: This event handler runs in your page during embedded signing; it does not apply to remote signers.
optionExplanations.C: Connect notifies your server of events; it cannot redirect the signer's browser.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A brand's destination URLs set where remote signers are redirected after events such as signing complete.

whyNotOthers: D is right because destination URLs on a brand control where remote signers go after signing. The trap is A: it is the redirect setting for embedded signing, which does not apply to remote signers. B and C fail because the sessionEnd handler only exists in an embedded session and Connect is server-to-server.

stem: An app displays the legal provisions in use across the organization's agreements and reads its data from the Agreement Manager API. What is the key advantage over the eSignature REST API for this purpose?

options.text: The Agreement Manager API is exempt from API rate limits
eSignature form data holds the same provisions; Agreement Manager is just faster
It returns structured, AI-extracted data such as parties and provisions
It uses a separate token type unrelated to eSignature OAuth

answerText: It returns structured, AI-extracted data such as parties and provisions
explanation: Agreement Manager (Iris) extracts parties, dates and provisions from agreements and the API exposes them as structured data. The eSignature API exposes envelopes and tab values, not extracted provisions.

optionExplanations.A: False; Agreement Manager calls are still subject to API limits.
optionExplanations.B: Form data contains tab values entered during signing, not provisions extracted from the agreement text.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The API returns AI-extracted structured data such as parties and provisions.
optionExplanations.D: False; the same OAuth tokens are used, with Agreement Manager scopes such as adm_store_unified_repo_read requested.

whyNotOthers: C is right because AI-extracted provisions are what the app displays. The trap is B: eSignature form data does return values signers typed into tabs, but those are not the clause-level provisions Iris extracts from the document text. A is false because API rate limits still apply, and D is false because Agreement Manager uses the same OAuth tokens as eSignature, with Agreement Manager scopes added.

stem: A marketing website has no server-side code. Site visitors, who have no Docusign accounts, must be able to start a client intake workflow themselves by clicking a button. Which start method fits?

options.text: From a link
Manually in Docusign (Run Workflow)
From an API call
Triggered from a CLM workflow

answerText: From a link
explanation: From a link gives a URL that starts the workflow when opened. It can be embedded in a website and is recommended for self-service intake initiated by a participant.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The workflow link can be embedded in the site so participants start it themselves.
optionExplanations.B: Run Workflow is used by internal users with Workflows: Prepare permission, not by anonymous visitors.
optionExplanations.C: An API trigger needs backend code holding an access token; the site has no server side.
optionExplanations.D: A CLM-triggered start runs from within Docusign CLM, not from a public website.

whyNotOthers: A is right because a visitor opening the link starts the workflow, with no backend involved. The trap is C: From an API call also starts workflows from outside Docusign, but it requires server code with an OAuth token, which this site does not have. B needs an internal user with Workflows: Prepare permission, and D is started from inside Docusign CLM.

stem: An extension app action must call an external API endpoint. Where in the manifest is that endpoint described?

options.text: In an action definition in the manifest's actions object
In the extensions object's actionReferences list
In the App Center listing description
In the connections object, next to the OAuth settings

answerText: In an action definition in the manifest's actions object
explanation: Each action in the actions object describes an external operation, including the endpoint Docusign calls.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The action definition describes the external endpoint Docusign calls.
optionExplanations.B: actionReferences only points to actions by name; it does not define endpoints.
optionExplanations.C: Listing text is marketing content shown in the App Center, not configuration for calls.
optionExplanations.D: Connections define how to authenticate (OAuth URLs, credentials), not the operation endpoint.

whyNotOthers: A is right because actions hold the callable operations and their endpoints. The trap is D: connections hold authentication details (such as token and authorization URLs), not the operation's endpoint. B only lists action names for an extension, and C is listing text for the App Center.

stem: After receiving an access token, the app must find which account ID and base URI to use for API calls. Which endpoint returns that account context?

options.text: /oauth/token
eSignature Accounts:get (/restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId})
/oauth/userinfo
The sub claim of the JWT assertion

answerText: /oauth/userinfo
explanation: /oauth/userinfo returns the user's accounts; the app uses the account with is_default=true and takes its account_id and base_uri for every API URL.

optionExplanations.A: /oauth/token returns the access token and its lifetime, not the account list or base URIs.
optionExplanations.B: Accounts:get needs the account ID and base URI in its URL, so it cannot be how you discover them.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. /oauth/userinfo returns accounts with account_id, base_uri, and is_default.
optionExplanations.D: sub is the user ID the app puts in the JWT; it identifies the user, not the account or base URI.

whyNotOthers: C is right because userinfo is the discovery step after any OAuth flow. The trap is B: Accounts:get returns account details, but you already need the account ID and base URI to call it. A returns the token itself, and D is the user ID the app supplies in a JWT, not account context.

stem: An integration checks envelope status by polling each envelope every few seconds. Which change best follows Docusign API usage guidelines?

options.text: Poll each envelope every 60 seconds instead
Ask Docusign to raise the account's hourly API limit
Spread the polling across several integration keys
Use Connect webhooks to receive status changes

answerText: Use Connect webhooks to receive status changes
explanation: Docusign recommends Connect so status changes are pushed to the app instead of polled; polling a single envelope is limited to once every 15 minutes.

optionExplanations.A: Every 60 seconds still exceeds the limit of one status poll per envelope every 15 minutes.
optionExplanations.B: A higher limit does not fix inefficient polling, and limit increases require efficient apps.
optionExplanations.C: The hourly limit is per account and shared by all keys, so more keys add no capacity.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Connect pushes envelope events, which avoids excessive status polling.

whyNotOthers: D is right because Connect removes the need to poll. The trap is A: it reduces the call rate, but polling every minute still breaks the rule of at most one status request per envelope every 15 minutes. B treats the symptom instead of the inefficient pattern, and C does not help because the hourly limit is shared by all integrations on the account.

stem: A Connect listener is down for 20 minutes during maintenance while envelopes are completing. What happens to the events Docusign tried to send?

options.text: They are lost; the app must poll to recover them
Docusign holds the envelopes until the listener is back
Docusign treats each delivery as failed and retries it later
Docusign switches to emailing the events to the account admin

answerText: Docusign treats each delivery as failed and retries it later
explanation: Failed Connect deliveries are retried with exponential back-off, so events sent during a short outage are delivered once the listener responds again.

optionExplanations.A: Events are retried, not discarded; polling is only a fallback for catch-up.
optionExplanations.B: Envelope signing is not paused because a listener is down.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect retries failed deliveries using exponential back-off.
optionExplanations.D: Connect does not reroute events to email when the listener fails.

whyNotOthers: C is right because Connect has a built-in retry process for failed deliveries. The trap is A: polling with listStatusChanges is a valid catch-up tool, but events are not simply lost, because Connect retries them. B and D describe behavior Connect does not have; envelope processing continues regardless of the listener.

stem: An agreement was sent with the eSignature REST API. Before anyone signs, legal finds a fatal error and the agreement must be canceled permanently. Which status should the integration set in an Envelopes:update request?

options.text: voided
created
purged
deleted

answerText: voided
explanation: Setting status to voided (with a voidedReason) in Envelopes:update cancels the in-process envelope, stops signing and notifies recipients.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. status voided with a voidedReason permanently cancels the in-process envelope.
optionExplanations.B: created is the draft status; it does not cancel an envelope that has been sent.
optionExplanations.C: Purging removes document content from completed envelopes; it does not stop an in-process envelope.
optionExplanations.D: deleted is not the documented cancel action for an in-process envelope; voiding is.

whyNotOthers: A is right because voided is the cancel action for an envelope in process. The trap is D: deleted sounds like cancellation, but it is not the documented way to cancel a sent envelope. B is the draft status and C refers to removing documents after completion, not stopping signing.

stem: Robin is integrating a financial aid web form into a university website and wants the form to appear directly inside the site's UI. Which component must Robin use alongside the Web Forms API call to render the instance URL within the custom page?

options.text: The eSignature REST API EnvelopeViews:createRecipient endpoint
The Docusign JS client SDK
The Responsive Signing feature
A Workflow Builder 'From a link' start URL

answerText: The Docusign JS client SDK
explanation: Docusign provides the Docusign JS client SDK alongside the Web Forms API specifically to embed a web form instance in a website.

optionExplanations.A: This returns an embedded signing URL for an envelope recipient; it is not used to render a web form instance URL.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The Web Forms API returns the instance URL and Docusign JS renders it inline in the host page.
optionExplanations.C: Responsive signing adapts document layout for mobile devices; it does not embed a web form instance.
optionExplanations.D: A From a link URL starts a Maestro workflow; it is not the component that renders a web form instance URL from the Web Forms API.

whyNotOthers: B is right because Docusign JS takes the instance URL from the Web Forms API and renders it in the page. The trap is A: it is the embedded-signing endpoint for envelopes, so it sounds right for 'embedding', but web form instances are rendered from their own instance URL. C and D fail because responsive signing is a document display feature and a workflow start link launches a Maestro workflow rather than rendering this instance.

stem: A reporting service needs the extracted expiration date and total agreement value of one signed and stored agreement whose agreementId it already has. Which call returns these values?

options.text: The Connect envelope-completed webhook payload
eSignature EnvelopeFormData:get on the source envelope
Agreements:getAgreement
Agreements:createAgreementSummary

answerText: Agreements:getAgreement
explanation: getAgreement returns the provisions object for one agreement, which includes extracted values such as expiration_date and total_agreement_value.

optionExplanations.A: Connect reports envelope events; it does not deliver Agreement Manager extracted provisions.
optionExplanations.B: Returns signer-entered tab values, not the AI-extracted provisions of the agreement.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. getAgreement returns the agreement's provisions, including expiration date and total value.
optionExplanations.D: Creates an AI-written summary; it does not return discrete fields for reporting.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the values are AI-extracted provisions of a known agreement. The trap is B: form data returns what signers typed into tabs, which only matches if someone happened to place a tab for each value, and it is not the extracted provision. A notifies about envelope events and does not carry Agreement Manager extractions, and D returns prose rather than discrete field values.

stem: A backend service must start a published Maestro workflow and pass customer values from its database. Which call sequence is correct?

options.text: Envelopes:create, then TriggerWorkflow with the envelope ID
TriggerWorkflow first, then GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements to validate the inputs
GetWorkflowsList, then cancelWorkflowInstance
Get a token with aow_manage, call GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements, then TriggerWorkflow with trigger_inputs

answerText: Get a token with aow_manage, call GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements, then TriggerWorkflow with trigger_inputs
explanation: The API trigger flow is: get a token that includes aow_manage, call GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements for the trigger URL and input schema, then call TriggerWorkflow with the required inputs.

optionExplanations.A: A workflow is not triggered from an envelope ID; the workflow creates its own signing steps.
optionExplanations.B: Requirements must be read first; triggering blind risks missing required inputs.
optionExplanations.C: cancelWorkflowInstance stops a running instance; it does not start one.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Token with aow_manage, then trigger requirements, then TriggerWorkflow with the inputs.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the trigger requirements tell the app where to send the request and which inputs are required. The trap is B: it uses the right two calls in the wrong order, so the app would trigger before it knows the URL and schema. A creates an eSignature envelope the workflow does not need, and C cancels an instance instead of starting one.

stem: How do extension apps help a developer expand a solution's visibility and reach?

options.text: They let customers call the developer's API using their own integration keys
They are published to the Docusign App Center, reaching Docusign's customer base
They add custom endpoints to the Docusign eSignature REST API
They are installed automatically in every Docusign account after review

answerText: They are published to the Docusign App Center, reaching Docusign's customer base
explanation: Publishing to the Docusign App Center puts the app in front of Docusign's large customer base, which is the visibility and reach benefit.

optionExplanations.A: Integration keys are for apps calling Docusign APIs; they do not make an extension app discoverable.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Publishing to the App Center exposes the app to Docusign customers.
optionExplanations.C: Extension apps do not change Docusign's API surface; Docusign calls the developer's endpoints.
optionExplanations.D: Admins install apps from the App Center; nothing is installed automatically in every account.

whyNotOthers: B is right because App Center publication is the reach mechanism. The trap is C: extension apps make Docusign call your endpoints; they do not add new endpoints to Docusign's APIs. A confuses integration keys with extension apps, and D is wrong because admins choose to install apps.

stem: A native desktop app cannot store a client secret securely. Each individual user signs in to send envelopes. Which OAuth grant type should the team configure?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
Implicit Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: A native app is a public client: it cannot keep a secret, and users sign in, so Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE is the grant to configure.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant needs a client secret, which a native app cannot store securely.
optionExplanations.B: Implicit Grant avoids a secret but is legacy; Docusign recommends Public Auth Code with PKCE.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Native app, no secret, interactive user: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant is for unattended services after consent, not an app where each user signs in.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the app cannot keep a secret and users are present. The trap is B: Implicit Grant also avoids a secret, but it is legacy and Docusign recommends the PKCE code flow instead. A needs a secret the app cannot protect, and D is for services with no user present.

stem: A developer promotes an integration key to production during Go-Live. The integration uses Confidential Authorization Code Grant with a secret key and a redirect URI configured in Apps and Keys. What is the state of these OAuth parameters in production right after the key is duplicated?

options.text: They are not copied over and must be set up manually in production
Only the redirect URIs are copied; the secret key must be regenerated in production
Production generates placeholder secrets and redirect URIs that must not be modified
The key, secrets and redirect URIs are all duplicated, so the app works immediately

answerText: They are not copied over and must be set up manually in production
explanation: Go-Live duplicates the integration key (same value) into production, but configuration parameters such as secrets and redirect URIs are not duplicated and must be added in production.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Secrets and redirect URIs are not duplicated; add them to the production key.
optionExplanations.B: Redirect URIs are not copied either; both must be added in production.
optionExplanations.C: Docusign does not create placeholder values; you add the real secrets and redirect URIs yourself.
optionExplanations.D: Only the key value is duplicated; its secrets and redirect URIs are not.

whyNotOthers: A is right because neither secrets nor redirect URIs are copied. The trap is B: it correctly says a new secret is needed, but redirect URIs are not copied either. C invents placeholder values, and D is the common assumption that everything carries over, which leaves the production app unable to authenticate.

stem: A listener sometimes receives the same Connect message twice, and the downstream system creates duplicate records. Which option should be used?

options.text: Return HTTP 409 for duplicates so Docusign stops sending them
Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
Delete and recreate the Connect configuration
Switch the configuration to XML aggregate mode

answerText: Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
explanation: Connect can deliver the same event more than once (for example after retries), so the listener must recognize and safely skip events it has already processed.

optionExplanations.A: A non-2xx response is treated as a failure and triggers more retries.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Track processed events or check envelope state so repeats do no harm.
optionExplanations.C: Recreating the configuration does not prevent duplicate deliveries.
optionExplanations.D: Aggregate mode merges related events in legacy XML; it does not prevent retried duplicates.

whyNotOthers: B is right because idempotent processing makes duplicate deliveries harmless. The trap is A: rejecting the duplicate looks logical, but any non-2xx response is a failure that makes Connect retry, producing even more deliveries. C does not change delivery semantics, and D only combines related events in legacy XML; it does not stop redeliveries.

stem: An envelope must combine two saved server templates plus runtime recipient data in one API call. Which envelope model supports this?

options.text: Template reference model (templateId plus templateRoles)
Direct documents model (documents plus recipients)
Composite templates model (compositeTemplates array)
Two separate envelopes linked by a custom field

answerText: Composite templates model (compositeTemplates array)
explanation: Only composite templates can apply multiple server templates in a single envelope per API call and add runtime data with inline templates. The clue is 'two saved server templates'.

optionExplanations.A: The template reference model (templateId plus templateRoles) uses a single template and cannot combine multiple templates.
optionExplanations.B: The direct documents model supplies documents directly and does not apply saved templates.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Composite templates can combine multiple server templates and inline runtime data in one envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Two envelopes would split the agreement; the requirement is one envelope built from both templates.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the compositeTemplates array can mix several server templates with inline templates. The trap is A: templateId is the simple way to use a saved template, but it cannot combine multiple templates. B uses no saved templates and D produces two envelopes instead of one.

stem: A value the signer types into a field must be checked against an external system of record during signing. Which feature supports this?

options.text: A Data IO extension
A public App Center listing
Connected Fields (data verification extension)
The Connect extension-executed event

answerText: Connected Fields (data verification extension)
explanation: Real-time verification of a signer-entered value during signing is the Connected Fields use case.

optionExplanations.A: Data IO extensions read from and write to a system of record from Maestro workflows; they do not verify fields during eSignature signing.
optionExplanations.B: A listing is a distribution choice for an extension app; it is not the feature that validates a field.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connected Fields bind tabs to an extension that verifies the entered data against an external system during signing.
optionExplanations.D: This event reports verification results after they happen; it does not perform the check.

whyNotOthers: C is right because Connected Fields verify signer data against an external source during signing. The trap is A: it also talks to a system of record, but its extension point is Maestro workflows, not eSignature signing. B and D fail because App Center listing is about distribution and the Connect event only reports results.

stem: A developer must look up agreements by counterparty and then open one of them in full. Which pair of Agreement Manager requests is correct?

options.text: GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId} with a party filter
GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements, then GET .../agreements/{agreementId}
GET /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes, then GET .../envelopes/{envelopeId}
POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize

answerText: GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements, then GET .../agreements/{agreementId}
explanation: The list endpoint GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements finds matching agreements; GET .../agreements/{agreementId} then retrieves one in full.

optionExplanations.A: The single-agreement path needs an agreementId, which the developer does not have before searching.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. List agreements first, then get the selected agreement by ID.
optionExplanations.C: These are eSignature envelope endpoints, not Agreement Manager agreement endpoints.
optionExplanations.D: This creates an AI summary of a known agreement; it does not search by counterparty.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the lookup needs the list endpoint before the single-agreement endpoint. The trap is C: it has the same list-then-get shape, but it targets eSignature envelopes, not Agreement Manager agreements and their extracted parties. A needs an agreementId the developer does not have yet, and D summarizes one known agreement.

stem: A TriggerWorkflow call returns 400 because the request lacks a value the workflow requires at start. Authentication succeeds. What should the developer inspect?

options.text: The event list in the Connect configuration
The scopes on the access token
The trigger_input_schema from GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements and how trigger_inputs are mapped
Whether the workflow's new instances are paused

answerText: The trigger_input_schema from GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements and how trigger_inputs are mapped
explanation: TriggerWorkflow validates the input data against the workflow's trigger input schema. A missing required starting value points to the schema and the mapping of trigger_inputs.

optionExplanations.A: Connect only delivers events; it has no effect on trigger input validation.
optionExplanations.B: Authentication already succeeds, so the token's scopes are not the cause.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Compare the request's trigger_inputs with the required fields in trigger_input_schema.
optionExplanations.D: Pausing blocks new instances regardless of the inputs; it does not produce a missing-field error.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the clue is a missing required value while authentication succeeds. The trap is B: scope problems are a common runtime error, but they cause authorization failures, not a missing-input rejection. A affects event delivery only, and D concerns whether new instances can start at all, not input validation.

stem: An extension action must call an external API with OAuth credentials, and the developer wants those auth details defined once in the manifest. Which object holds them?

options.text: extensions
publisher
actions, with each action storing its own client secret
connections

answerText: connections
explanation: The connections object defines reusable authentication configuration that actions reference.

optionExplanations.A: extensions declare extension types and reference actions; they do not hold credentials.
optionExplanations.B: publisher contains organization contact information only.
optionExplanations.C: Actions point to a connection via connectionsReference instead of storing credentials themselves.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. connections defines the authentication used by actions.

whyNotOthers: D is right because connections hold the OAuth configuration. The trap is C: actions reference a connection through connectionsReference rather than storing credentials themselves. A lists extension types and their actions, and B holds publisher details.
