stem: A banking application runs a daily automated process that generates compliance reports and voids expired agreements, using a system sender account with no user login. Which OAuth 2.0 flow is recommended?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
Implicit Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant

answerText: JSON Web Token Grant
explanation: JWT Grant is the service-integration flow: it uses an RSA key pair and prior consent to get a token with no interactive login, which suits scheduled processes.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant needs an interactive user to sign in, and nobody is present for this process.
optionExplanations.B: Implicit Grant is a legacy, interactive browser flow.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant is interactive and meant for clients that cannot keep a secret, not for unattended automation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. JWT Grant is the unattended service-integration flow using an RSA key pair and prior consent.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the process runs with no user login. The trap is A: a bank backend can store a secret, but Confidential Auth Code still needs someone to sign in through a browser. B and C are also interactive flows.

stem: A developer clicks Start Go live, logs in to the production account, and sees an error message instead of a list of accounts to select. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The app has not yet made 20 eSignature API calls in the developer account
The integration key has no secret key configured
The integration type selected for the key does not match the account type
The Go-Live request is in Pending approval for up to 48 hours

answerText: The integration type selected for the key does not match the account type
explanation: The course states that an error instead of a list of accounts means the integration type specified for the key does not match the type of the account you logged into.

optionExplanations.A: The 20 API call requirement was removed; Go-Live can start right after the key is set up.
optionExplanations.B: A missing secret does not stop the account list from appearing during Start Go live.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An integration type that does not match the account type produces this error.
optionExplanations.D: Pending approval is a status shown after you select the account, not an error in place of the list.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the account list is filtered by the integration type chosen for the key. The trap is A: the old 20 API call requirement no longer exists, so you can start Go-Live right after creating the key. B is unrelated to account selection, and D is a status shown after submission, not an error during account selection.

stem: A team wants smaller Connect messages and will query full envelope details through the API only when needed. What should the Connect configuration do?

options.text: Use JSON SIM and include only the event data the listener needs
Include documents and the full envelope summary in every message
Switch to legacy XML, which sends smaller messages
Enable aggregate mode to shrink each message

answerText: Use JSON SIM and include only the event data the listener needs
explanation: JSON SIM messages are event-focused and customizable, so the configuration can include only the data needed and leave documents out.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. JSON SIM messages can be limited to the data the listener needs.
optionExplanations.B: Including documents and full summaries makes every message larger.
optionExplanations.C: Legacy XML messages are envelope-focused and larger than JSON SIM messages.
optionExplanations.D: Aggregate mode combines events into fewer messages; it does not shrink payloads.

whyNotOthers: A is right because JSON SIM lets you choose what each message carries. The trap is C: legacy XML is envelope-focused and its messages are larger, not smaller. B is the opposite of the goal, and D reduces the number of messages, not the size of each one.

stem: A document can vary in page length, but the signature field must appear next to a specific text string. Which tab placement method is best?

options.text: xPosition and yPosition on a fixed page
Anchor tagging with anchorString and offsets
templateId with templateRoles
tabLabel matching the text string

answerText: Anchor tagging with anchorString and offsets
explanation: Anchor tabs place fields relative to text in the document, so they follow the text when page length changes. The clue is 'next to a specific text string'.

optionExplanations.A: Fixed x and y coordinates on a page do not move when the text shifts to another place or page.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anchor tagging finds the text and places the tab relative to it using offsets.
optionExplanations.C: templateId references a saved template; it does not decide where a tab is placed in a variable document.
optionExplanations.D: tabLabel identifies a tab, for example to share or map values; it does not position the tab.

whyNotOthers: B is right because anchorString plus offsets ties the tab to the text. The trap is A: fixed positioning is valid tab placement, but it uses page coordinates that break when content moves. C references a template rather than placing tabs, and tabLabel names a tab for data mapping without positioning it.

stem: A records office must retrieve the ID images and personal details retained from a signer's completed ID Verification event. Which API is relevant?

options.text: IdentityVerifications:list
ID Evidence API
The certificate of completion
The Agreement Manager API

answerText: ID Evidence API
explanation: Retained data from a completed IDV event is retrieved with the ID Evidence API.

optionExplanations.A: This lists the account's IDV workflows so you can set workflowId on a recipient; it returns no evidence from completed verifications.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The ID Evidence API retrieves the ID verification data your administrator has configured the account to retain.
optionExplanations.C: The certificate records events and authentication methods; it does not contain the retained ID images.
optionExplanations.D: Agreement Manager returns agreements and AI-extracted agreement data, not ID verification evidence.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the ID Evidence API returns retained evidence from ID verification events. The trap is A: it is the IDV API you use when sending, but it lists configurations rather than results. C and D fail because the certificate does not hold ID images and Agreement Manager covers agreement data.

stem: An operations group wants contracts signed on paper years ago to appear in Agreement Manager reports with extracted dates and parties. Which capability matters?

options.text: Bulk import the legacy contracts into Agreement Manager
Call Agreements:getAgreement on each paper contract's scanned file
Attach the scans to new envelopes as supplemental documents
Record the key dates as eSignature envelope custom fields

answerText: Bulk import the legacy contracts into Agreement Manager
explanation: Importing legacy agreements adds them to Agreement Manager, where AI extraction surfaces dates and parties for reporting.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bulk import brings the legacy contracts into Agreement Manager so their data is extracted.
optionExplanations.B: getAgreement reads existing agreement records by ID; it cannot take a scanned file as input.
optionExplanations.C: Supplemental documents ride along with a new envelope; they do not import the old contracts as agreements.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope custom fields do not create agreements or feed Agreement Manager reports.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the contracts must first exist in the repository before any data can be read. The trap is C: it puts the files into Docusign, but as envelope attachments, which neither imports the old contracts as agreements nor extracts their terms. B only reads agreements that already exist in Agreement Manager, and D stores values on envelopes rather than creating agreement records.

stem: A custom web app triggers a workflow and wants users to complete it inside the app's own page, without leaving the app. What should the app do with the TriggerWorkflow response?

options.text: Redirect the browser to the returned workflow instance URL
Load the returned workflow instance URL in an iframe
Call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient with the workflow ID
Poll getWorkflowInstance and rebuild each step in custom UI

answerText: Load the returned workflow instance URL in an iframe
explanation: TriggerWorkflow returns an instance URL. Embedding it in an iframe keeps the app's UI visible while the user completes the workflow.

optionExplanations.A: Supported, but the user is routed to Docusign and does not return to the app when done.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Embedding the instance URL in an iframe keeps the workflow inside the app.
optionExplanations.C: createRecipient creates an envelope signing view; it does not open a workflow instance.
optionExplanations.D: getWorkflowInstance returns status details; the app cannot run workflow steps itself.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the requirement is to stay inside the app, which the iframe option provides. The trap is A: redirecting to the instance URL is also supported, but the user leaves the app and stays on Docusign when finished. C is the eSignature embedded signing call and does not take a workflow ID, and D only reads status; it cannot render steps.

stem: An action must use a named connection defined in the manifest. Which property links the action to that connection?

options.text: actionReferences
distribution
connectionsReference
publicationRegions

answerText: connectionsReference
explanation: connectionsReference on the action names the connection whose authentication it uses.

optionExplanations.A: actionReferences links extensions to actions, not actions to connections.
optionExplanations.B: distribution sets PUBLIC or PRIVATE.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. connectionsReference ties the action to a named connection.
optionExplanations.D: publicationRegions sets installable regions for public apps.

whyNotOthers: C is right because connectionsReference links an action to a connection. The trap is A: actionReferences links an extension to its actions, one level up. B and D are distribution settings.

stem: A REST API request returns 401 Unauthorized even though /oauth/token returned an access token. Where should the access token be supplied on API calls?

options.text: In the Authorization header as Bearer <access_token>
In the Authorization header as Basic base64(integrationKey:secretKey)
As an access_token query string parameter
In the JSON request body next to the envelope definition

answerText: In the Authorization header as Bearer <access_token>
explanation: Docusign REST calls authenticate with the header Authorization: Bearer followed by the access token.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Send Authorization: Bearer <access_token> on every API request.
optionExplanations.B: The Basic header is used at /oauth/token in the confidential flow, not on REST API calls.
optionExplanations.C: Docusign APIs read the token from the Authorization header, not the query string.
optionExplanations.D: The request body holds the envelope definition; the token belongs in the Authorization header.

whyNotOthers: A is right because API requests carry the access token in a Bearer Authorization header. The trap is B: a Basic header with the integration key and secret is correct for the /oauth/token code exchange, but not for API calls. C and D are not where Docusign reads the token.

stem: A developer is setting up a new integration key in the developer account. Which step must be completed on the key before the Go-Live process can be completed?

options.text: Make 20 successful eSignature API calls with the key
Select an option under How will you use this integration?
Generate an RSA key pair for the production environment
Open a Docusign Support case asking for the key to be promoted

answerText: Select an option under How will you use this integration?
explanation: The course notes that you must select an option in the How will you use this integration? section before you can complete Go-Live.

optionExplanations.A: The 20 API call requirement was removed; you can submit right after creating the key.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The How will you use this integration? choice must be made before Go-Live can be completed.
optionExplanations.C: Production credentials are added on the production key after Go-Live, not generated beforehand.
optionExplanations.D: eSignature Go-Live is started from Apps and Keys with Actions > Start Go live, not by a support case.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the integration type (classification) is required for Go-Live. The trap is A: older guidance required 20 API calls, but that requirement no longer exists. C is wrong because production credentials are added after Go-Live on the production key, and D describes the support-case route some other APIs use, not eSignature Go-Live from Apps and Keys.

stem: Developer guidance must explain how a partner app attaches its own webhook URL and event list to each envelope it sends, without touching the customer's eSignature Admin settings. What should the guidance recommend?

options.text: Add the listener in eSignature Admin > Connect for the customer's account
Call the ConnectConfigurations API to create a configuration with urlToPublishTo
Store the listener URL in an envelope custom field
Include an eventNotification object (URL and events) in each Envelopes:create request

answerText: Include an eventNotification object (URL and events) in each Envelopes:create request
explanation: Envelope-level Connect is set through the eventNotification property when the envelope is created by API, so the app controls its webhook per envelope without changing account settings.

optionExplanations.A: eSignature Admin > Connect creates an account-level configuration, which changes the customer's account settings.
optionExplanations.B: ConnectConfigurations with urlToPublishTo creates an account-level configuration, not a per-envelope webhook.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope custom fields hold metadata; Connect does not read a listener URL from them.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. eventNotification in Envelopes:create defines a per-envelope webhook controlled entirely by the sending app.

whyNotOthers: D is right because eventNotification travels with each envelope request and needs no admin configuration. The trap is B: the ConnectConfigurations API with urlToPublishTo creates an account-level configuration, which is exactly the account setting the app must not change. A is the same account-level setup done in the UI, and C stores data on the envelope but never causes Connect to send anything.

stem: A recipient must sign inside the host app instead of through an email link. Which property on the signer in the envelope definition marks embedded signing?

options.text: clientUserId
recipientId
returnUrl
EnvelopeViews:createRecipient

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: Setting clientUserId on the signer when the envelope is created marks the recipient as embedded. The clue is a property on the signer in the envelope definition.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Setting clientUserId on the signer marks the recipient as embedded (captive).
optionExplanations.B: recipientId identifies the recipient within the envelope; every recipient has one, embedded or not.
optionExplanations.C: returnUrl is sent in the createRecipient request to say where to redirect after signing; it is not a recipient property.
optionExplanations.D: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient is the endpoint that returns the signing URL, not a recipient property.

whyNotOthers: A is right because clientUserId is the recipient property that makes the signer embedded. The trap is D: createRecipient is required for embedded signing, but it is the later API call that returns the signing URL, not a recipient property. B exists for every recipient and C belongs to the createRecipient request.

stem: A financial-aid portal must show a template-based web form inline, so the student fills it in without leaving the portal. Which combination delivers this?

options.text: Create an embedded instance with clientUserId, then render its URL with Docusign JS
Create a remote instance with sendOption and recipients[], then render it with Docusign JS
Create a standalone configuration and call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
Send an envelope with clientUserId and email the signing URL to the student

answerText: Create an embedded instance with clientUserId, then render its URL with Docusign JS
explanation: Inline display inside the portal means an embedded instance: createInstance with clientUserId, then Docusign JS to render the URL.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Embedded instances require clientUserId on Instances:createInstance, and Docusign JS renders the returned instance URL in the portal.
optionExplanations.B: Remote instances are delivered to participants by email (sendOption with recipients by roleName); they are not the embedded pattern.
optionExplanations.C: A standalone configuration never creates an envelope, so there is no envelope recipient view to request.
optionExplanations.D: This is embedded signing of an envelope, not a web form, and emailing a short-lived signing URL is not an inline experience.

whyNotOthers: A is right because embedded instances are identified by clientUserId and rendered with Docusign JS. The trap is B: Docusign JS is the right renderer, but a remote instance is the email-delivered mode, so the student would leave the portal. C and D fail because a standalone form has no envelope to view and an emailed envelope signing URL is not a web form embedded in the page.

stem: A document-management system has an agreementId and has already stored the agreement's extracted metadata. It now needs the actual agreement file for its archive. What should the plan include?

options.text: A document download step for the agreement file
Calling Agreements:getAgreement again, since the file is inside the provisions object
Calling Agreements:createAgreementSummary to obtain the archived copy
Calling Agreements:getAgreementsList filtered by the agreementId

answerText: A document download step for the agreement file
explanation: Extracted metadata and the agreement file are separate; the archive needs a document download step for the file itself.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The agreement file is retrieved through a document download, separate from the metadata.
optionExplanations.B: The provisions object contains extracted values, not the document content.
optionExplanations.C: A summary is AI-generated text, not the archived agreement.
optionExplanations.D: The list call returns agreement records, not document files.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the metadata is already stored and only the file is missing. The trap is B: getAgreement is the right call for the extracted record, but the provisions object holds values like dates and amounts, not the document. C returns AI-written text, and D returns list-level agreement records, neither of which is the file.

stem: A workflow designer cannot find the Salesforce writeback step in Workflow Builder. Which prerequisite is most likely missing?

options.text: An administrator has not installed and authorized the Salesforce extension app from App Center
The Salesforce endpoint is not listed in a Connect configuration
Connected fields are not enabled on the workflow
The integration key lacks the extended scope

answerText: An administrator has not installed and authorized the Salesforce extension app from App Center
explanation: Workflow Builder app steps come from extension apps that an administrator has installed from Docusign App Center and authorized for the account. Without that, the step is not available.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The extension app must be installed from App Center and authorized before its steps appear.
optionExplanations.B: Connect sends event notifications; it does not add steps to Workflow Builder.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.D: The extended scope extends refresh token life; it does not enable extension app steps.

whyNotOthers: A is right because extension app steps only appear once the app is installed and authorized in the account. The trap is C: connected fields are an extension feature, but they work in eSignature and are not supported in Maestro workflows. B is for outbound event notifications, and D concerns refresh tokens, not workflow steps.

stem: A sales team uses Maestro to generate contracts. A workflow must retrieve a client's pricing tier and contract duration from the internal ERP to pre-fill documents. Which extension type performs this read inside the workflow?

options.text: File IO extension app
Connected Fields extension app
Data IO extension app
Docusign Connect webhook listener

answerText: Data IO extension app
explanation: Data IO extension apps read (and write) structured data in external systems from Maestro workflows, which is what pulling pricing data from the ERP needs.

optionExplanations.A: File IO moves documents to storage; it does not read field data.
optionExplanations.B: Connected fields verify eSignature fields and are not supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Data IO reads structured data from the ERP in the workflow.
optionExplanations.D: A Connect listener receives events; it cannot be a workflow read step.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the workflow needs to read structured ERP data. The trap is B: connected fields also use a system of record, but they verify eSignature field values and are not supported in Maestro. A handles files, and D only receives event notifications.

stem: A legal operations portal has a secured backend that stores the client secret. Each employee must sign in with their own Docusign credentials so every envelope is attributed to the person who sent it. Which OAuth flow fits?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JWT Grant impersonating each employee after consent
Implicit Grant
Confidential Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Employees are present and must sign in with their own credentials, and the backend can protect a secret, so Confidential Authorization Code Grant is the fit.

optionExplanations.A: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE is meant for clients without a safe place for a secret; this backend has one.
optionExplanations.B: JWT impersonation skips user sign-in entirely and is intended for unattended service integrations, not employees who must log in themselves.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant is a legacy flow that returns tokens to the browser and is not recommended by Docusign.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Interactive per-user sign-in on a backend that can protect a secret is Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the requirement is an interactive sign-in by each employee on a backend that can keep a secret. The trap is B: JWT can impersonate users after consent, but it involves no sign-in at all and is designed for services with no user present. A is for clients that cannot store a secret, and C is the legacy browser flow.

stem: A company buys a partner product that asks each customer to supply its own Docusign integration key. When the company creates that key, which integration type should it choose?

options.text: Third-party integration key
Private custom integration
Public integration
Embedded integration

answerText: Third-party integration key
explanation: When you use a Docusign partner integration for your business need and it requires you to provide your own integration key, the classification is Third-party integration key.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A partner integration that needs the customer's own key uses the Third-party integration key type.
optionExplanations.B: Private custom integration is for an app the company builds for direct use by its employees or its customers' employees.
optionExplanations.C: Public integration is chosen by the vendor publishing an app for many Docusign customers, not by a customer.
optionExplanations.D: Embedded integration is for vendors offering Docusign features through their own account, with an ISV Embed license.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the clue is a partner product that requires the customer's own key. The trap is B: the key lives in the company's account and its employees use it, but the app was built by a partner, not as a custom integration. C is for the vendor that builds a multi-customer app, and D is for a vendor embedding Docusign features through its own account.

stem: A custom integration needs real-time updates for one specific envelope it creates with the eSignature REST API, independent of the account-level Connect configuration. How must the developer configure this webhook?

options.text: Include the eventNotification object in the envelope creation request body
Use the Maestro API to start a workflow instance holding the listener URL
Register a listener for the Envelope ID in Docusign Admin Connect settings
Base the envelope on a web form that has Connect enabled

answerText: Include the eventNotification object in the envelope creation request body
explanation: Adding eventNotification to the Envelopes:create payload sets up an envelope-level webhook for that envelope, separate from any account-level configuration.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. eventNotification in the Envelopes:create body defines a per-envelope Connect webhook.
optionExplanations.B: Maestro orchestrates multi-step workflows; it is not how an eSignature envelope gets its own webhook.
optionExplanations.C: Admin Connect settings create account-level configurations; there is no per-Envelope-ID listener there.
optionExplanations.D: Web forms are a different sending model and do not provide a per-envelope webhook.

whyNotOthers: A is right because envelope-level Connect is configured only through eventNotification in the API request. The trap is C: Docusign Admin does host Connect settings, but they are account-level and cannot target one Envelope ID. B uses Maestro, which orchestrates workflows rather than attaching a webhook to an eSignature envelope, and D is a different sending model with no per-envelope webhook.

stem: An app has created and sent an envelope for an embedded recipient. What must the app request before the recipient can sign in the host application?

options.text: A sender view URL from EnvelopeViews:createSender
The signing link from the recipient's email invitation
The envelope details from Envelopes:get
A recipient view URL from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient

answerText: A recipient view URL from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
explanation: Embedded signing requires requesting a short-lived recipient view URL from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient and redirecting the user to it.

optionExplanations.A: createSender returns a sender view for preparing and sending, not a signing session.
optionExplanations.B: Embedded (clientUserId) recipients are not sent an email invitation to sign.
optionExplanations.C: Envelopes:get returns envelope information; it does not return a signing URL.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. EnvelopeViews:createRecipient returns the short-lived URL for the embedded signing session.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the recipient view is the signing ceremony URL. The trap is A: createSender is also an embedded view, but it opens the sending and tagging experience, not signing. B fails because embedded recipients do not get an email invitation and C returns envelope data, not a signing session.

stem: Sofia's partner app creates one embedded web form instance per customer and needs a value it controls to link each instance to the customer record. Which value should it supply?

options.text: The web form configuration formId
A brandId
The returnUrl
clientUserId

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: The stem asks for a value the app controls per customer, which is clientUserId.

optionExplanations.A: formId selects which configuration to instantiate; all customers share it, so it cannot link an instance to one record.
optionExplanations.B: brandId applies branding to an envelope; it carries no customer identity.
optionExplanations.C: returnUrl is where the participant is sent after finishing; it is not an identifier for the instance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. clientUserId identifies the user in your system and is required on Instances:createInstance for embedded instances.

whyNotOthers: D is right because clientUserId is the per-user value your app supplies on createInstance. The trap is A: it appears in the same request path, but it is the same for every instance of that form. B and C fail because branding and redirect settings do not identify a customer.

stem: A renewal is identified by querying the Agreement Manager API for upcoming expiration dates. That should start an automated multi-step renewal process (prefill new documents, collect signatures). Which service is recommended for programmatically starting that process?

options.text: Workflow Builder (Maestro) API
Web Forms API
eSignature REST API
Connected Fields API

answerText: Workflow Builder (Maestro) API
explanation: The Workflow Builder (Maestro) API triggers a published multi-step workflow, which can prefill documents and route them for signature.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The Workflow Builder API triggers a multi-step workflow from an integration.
optionExplanations.B: Web Forms creates form instances for data collection, not a full orchestrated renewal process.
optionExplanations.C: Sends envelopes, which covers only the signing step, not the orchestration of the whole renewal.
optionExplanations.D: Connected Fields verifies data in fields against external sources; it does not start workflows.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the requirement is to launch an orchestrated multi-step process. The trap is C: the eSignature REST API can send the renewal envelope, but it does not orchestrate the surrounding steps, so the integration would have to build them itself. B collects data in a form instance and D verifies field data against external systems; neither starts a multi-step workflow.

stem: A workflow must automatically archive the final signed agreement to Google Drive after all recipients complete signing. Which type of step must the designer add?

options.text: An extension app step (Store Files) using the Google Drive app
A second Send Documents for Signature step
A Branching Rule step
A Collect Data with Web Forms step

answerText: An extension app step (Store Files) using the Google Drive app
explanation: Apps steps call installed extension apps; Store Files steps automate storage of completed agreements in services such as Google Drive.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A Store Files app step with the Google Drive extension archives the completed agreement.
optionExplanations.B: Another signing step sends a document again; it does not archive anything.
optionExplanations.C: A branch can check that the envelope is completed, but it cannot save the file itself.
optionExplanations.D: Web forms collect participant data; they do not store documents externally.

whyNotOthers: A is right because only an extension app step can write the file to Google Drive. The trap is C: the course example uses a Branching Rule on envelope status before storing, but the branch only decides the path; it does not store anything. B sends another envelope, and D collects data.

stem: An extension action must call a third-party API whose request and response format does not conform to the Docusign action schema. What should the developer add?

options.text: A Connect configuration using a custom XML format
An API proxy that translates requests and responses
Extra OAuth scopes on the connection
Concerto type definitions declared in the manifest

answerText: An API proxy that translates requests and responses
explanation: If external endpoints do not conform to the Docusign action schema, an API proxy translates the requests and responses into the format Docusign expects.

optionExplanations.A: Connect sends event notifications; it does not translate extension action calls.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. An API proxy translates between Docusign's action schema and the third-party format.
optionExplanations.C: Scopes control what the token can access, not the payload format.
optionExplanations.D: Concerto models data types; it does not convert a non-conforming API's requests and responses.

whyNotOthers: B is right because a proxy reshapes payloads between Docusign and the API. The trap is D: Concerto describes the data model for Data IO and connected fields, but it does not convert an incompatible API's payloads. A is an event webhook and C only changes authorization.

stem: A single-page app is served from a CDN and has no backend server. Each user must sign in with their own Docusign account. The security reviewer notes that authorization code flows are safer than token-in-URL flows. Which flow should the developer choose?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: An authorization code flow is preferred, and because the SPA has no backend to hold a secret, the right code flow is the public one with PKCE.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant is a code flow too, but its secret would be exposed in the browser because there is no backend.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is a service-to-service flow with no user sign-in and needs a protected private key.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A code flow for a client that cannot hold a secret is Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant returns the token in the redirect URL, which is the legacy pattern the reviewer wants to avoid.

whyNotOthers: C is right because it is an authorization code flow that works without a secret. The trap is A: it is also an authorization code flow, but it requires a client secret that a CDN-served SPA has nowhere safe to store. B does not sign users in, and D is the token-in-URL legacy flow the reviewer wants to avoid.

stem: After Go-Live, a production app still sends users to account-d.docusign.com to sign in. Which authentication host must it use in production?

options.text: account-d.docusign.com
demo.docusign.net
The account's base URI, such as https://na2.docusign.net
account.docusign.com

answerText: account.docusign.com
explanation: The After Go-Live guidance says to change the OAuth authentication host from https://account-d.docusign.com to https://account.docusign.com.

optionExplanations.A: account-d.docusign.com is the developer environment authentication host.
optionExplanations.B: demo.docusign.net is the demo eSignature API host, not an authentication host.
optionExplanations.C: The base URI is used for eSignature API calls, not for OAuth authentication.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Production OAuth uses https://account.docusign.com.

whyNotOthers: D is right because account.docusign.com is the production authentication service. The trap is C: the base URI is the production host for API calls, not for OAuth sign-in. A is the developer environment authentication host, and B is the demo API host.

stem: An architect must justify replacing a polling loop with webhooks. The account is close to its hourly API limit. Which statement is the strongest justification?

options.text: Polling status calls are exempt from hourly API limits
Ask Docusign to raise the account's hourly API limit
Use Connect; pushed messages do not count against API limits
Use Connect, although each delivered message counts as one API call

answerText: Use Connect; pushed messages do not count against API limits
explanation: Connect messages are pushed by Docusign and do not count against the account's API limits, which directly addresses the near-limit problem in the stem.

optionExplanations.A: Status polling calls count against API limits and are also restricted to once per 15 minutes per envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Raising limits does not fix wasteful polling and is not the recommended design.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect pushes messages that do not count against API limits and arrive only when something changes.
optionExplanations.D: Connect messages do not count as API calls; this misstates the key advantage.

whyNotOthers: C is right because webhook deliveries are not API calls made by the app. The trap is D: it picks the right feature but attaches a false cost, since Connect messages do not consume API quota. A is false because status calls do count and polling is also limited per envelope, and B treats the symptom instead of removing the polling.

stem: An app generates embedded signing URLs when envelopes are created, often hours before users open the page. What is the risk?

options.text: The envelope is voided automatically
Recipients receive duplicate email invitations
The short-lived, single-use URL may expire before use
Nothing; the URL stays valid until the envelope expires

answerText: The short-lived, single-use URL may expire before use
explanation: Recipient view URLs are short-lived (about 5 minutes) and single-use, so they should be requested only when the user is ready to sign.

optionExplanations.A: An expired signing URL does not void the envelope; the app can request a new URL.
optionExplanations.B: Embedded signers are not emailed, and generating a URL does not send invitations.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Signing URLs expire within minutes and work once, so early generation leads to expired links.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope expiration is separate; the signing URL itself expires within minutes.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a URL generated hours earlier will have expired. The trap is D: the envelope itself stays valid for a long time, but the signing URL does not. A and B describe effects that unused signing URLs do not cause.

stem: A developer must require ID verification (government photo ID) for a signer. How does the developer obtain and apply the right configuration?

options.text: AccountSignatureProviders:list, then recipientSignatureProviders on the signer
Set idCheckConfigurationName to 'ID Check $'
IdentityVerifications:list (REST v2.1), then identityVerification.workflowId on the recipient
TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, then tab extensionData

answerText: IdentityVerifications:list (REST v2.1), then identityVerification.workflowId on the recipient
explanation: The workflowId for IDV comes from IdentityVerifications:list and is applied in the recipient's identityVerification object.

optionExplanations.A: These configure EU standards-based signatures (AES/QES signature providers), not the ID verification workflow for a government photo ID check.
optionExplanations.B: That configures knowledge-based authentication, which asks public-record questions (US only); it does not check a photo ID.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. IdentityVerifications:list returns the account's IDV workflow IDs, and the chosen workflowId goes in the recipient's identityVerification object.
optionExplanations.D: This is the Connected Fields send flow, which verifies field values against an external system, not the signer's identity document.

whyNotOthers: C is right because IDV workflow IDs come from IdentityVerifications:list and are set as identityVerification.workflowId. The trap is A: it is a parallel 'list then apply to signer' pattern, but it selects a signature provider for SBS, not an IDV workflow. B and D fail because ID Check is KBA and Connected Fields verifies data in tabs.

stem: An internal service must return the extracted provisions of one agreement whose agreementId it receives. Which Agreement Manager request should it send?

options.text: GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements
GET /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/form_data
GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}
POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}/ai/actions/summarize

answerText: GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/agreements/{agreementId}
explanation: GET .../agreements/{agreementId} (Agreements:getAgreement) returns one agreement's full record, including its provisions. The service already receives the agreementId.

optionExplanations.A: The list endpoint is used for searching; the service already has the agreementId.
optionExplanations.B: An eSignature envelope endpoint for tab values, not Agreement Manager provisions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. getAgreement by agreementId returns the agreement's provisions.
optionExplanations.D: Creates an AI-written summary rather than returning structured provisions.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the ID is known and one agreement's provisions are needed. The trap is A: it is the Agreement Manager list endpoint, which is for finding agreements, not for retrieving one known record. B is an eSignature endpoint that returns signer tab values, and D generates an AI summary instead of returning provisions.

stem: Every applicant signs the exact same NDA; only the name and date fields change. Which step should prepare the document for signature?

options.text: Prepare Document Template
Use eSignature API
Collect Data with Web Forms
Prepare eSignature Template, followed by Send Documents for Signature

answerText: Prepare eSignature Template, followed by Send Documents for Signature
explanation: Prepare eSignature Template is meant for a single template used by every workflow instance, where the document is always the same. It is followed by the Send Documents for Signature step.

optionExplanations.A: Meant for documents whose content varies by workflow variables; overkill for a fixed NDA.
optionExplanations.B: Not the step for preparing a fixed template for signature.
optionExplanations.C: Collects data but does not prepare a document to sign.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. One fixed template for all instances, then Send Documents for Signature.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the document never changes between instances. The trap is A: Prepare Document Template is for generating different document content from workflow variables with conditional logic, which this NDA does not need. B is for direct API-driven envelope actions, and C only collects data.

stem: Docusign must call a customer-hosted endpoint for an extension action. Which network consideration is important?

options.text: Allow Docusign's requests through the endpoint's firewall to the HTTPS endpoint
Allow the endpoint to make outbound calls to the eSignature API
Enable CORS for the App Center domain
Allow inbound traffic only from signers' browsers

answerText: Allow Docusign's requests through the endpoint's firewall to the HTTPS endpoint
explanation: Docusign's servers must be able to reach the endpoint, so the firewall must allow Docusign's requests (or the endpoint must be exposed through an API proxy).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The firewall must let Docusign's requests reach the endpoint.
optionExplanations.B: Outbound calls to Docusign are the reverse direction; extension actions are inbound calls from Docusign.
optionExplanations.C: CORS governs browser JavaScript, not Docusign's server-to-server calls.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign's servers, not signers' browsers, call the action endpoint.

whyNotOthers: A is right because Docusign is the caller and must get through the firewall. The trap is B: it reverses the direction; the endpoint is called by Docusign, not calling Docusign. C applies to browser calls, and D blocks the very server-to-server calls Docusign makes.

stem: A nightly job uses a dedicated system sender account. Consent was granted once, but no one will be available to sign in when the job runs. The team suggests Confidential Auth Code Grant with refresh tokens instead. Which option should the team keep?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: JSON Web Token Grant
explanation: With consent already granted and no user available at runtime, JWT Grant is the recommended flow; it gets a fresh token by signing a new assertion.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant needs a user sign-in to start, and refresh tokens expire after up to 30 days, so it cannot run unattended indefinitely.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. JWT Grant is designed for unattended service integrations after one-time consent.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE requires an interactive user and has a 24-hour refresh token.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a legacy interactive browser flow.

whyNotOthers: B is right because JWT needs only prior consent, not a sign-in at runtime. The trap is A: refresh tokens can extend a confidential session, but the flow still starts with a user sign-in and the refresh token eventually expires, which then needs a person again. C and D are interactive browser flows.

stem: A team has gone live and wants the production app to behave as it did in development. Besides OAuth settings and endpoints, what must they migrate to the production account?

options.text: Nothing; Go-Live copies the whole developer account into production
Only the envelopes that were sent during testing
Users, templates and the account settings the app relied on
Only the integration key's Connect failure logs

answerText: Users, templates and the account settings the app relied on
explanation: Production account settings and data are separate from developer account data, so users, templates and settings must be added to production with Docusign Admin or the eSignature REST API.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live duplicates only the integration key; account data and settings stay in the developer account.
optionExplanations.B: Test envelopes are not migrated, and demo envelopes are not legally binding anyway.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Users, templates and account settings must be recreated in the production account.
optionExplanations.D: Logs are diagnostic data; they are not what the production app needs to function.

whyNotOthers: C is right because only the integration key is duplicated by Go-Live. The trap is A: it is easy to assume Go-Live copies the account, but it copies only the key (not even its secrets). B is wrong because test envelopes are not migrated (and demo envelopes are not legally binding), and D is not something an app needs to run.

stem: An organization admin must send events from three of the organization's five accounts to one listener, managed from a single place. Which option should be used?

options.text: Account-level Connect set up in eSignature Admin of one account
Organization-level Connect scoped to the selected accounts
eventNotification added by each sending application
An organization-level configuration using legacy XML aggregate messages

answerText: Organization-level Connect scoped to the selected accounts
explanation: Organization-level Connect can listen to all or selected accounts in the organization and is set up in Organization Admin or by API.

optionExplanations.A: An account-level configuration covers only the account it is created in.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Organization-level Connect can target all or selected accounts from one configuration.
optionExplanations.C: eventNotification is per envelope and API only, so web-app sends would be missed.
optionExplanations.D: Organization-level configurations always use JSON SIM; legacy XML and aggregate are account and envelope level only.

whyNotOthers: B is right because org-level Connect supports selecting specific accounts in one configuration. The trap is D: org-level is the right level, but organization-level configurations always use JSON SIM, so legacy XML and aggregate mode are not available there. A covers only one account, and C misses envelopes sent from the web app.

stem: A developer uses the direct documents model to send a PDF contract and wants tabs to stay correctly placed even if minor revisions shift the page text. What is the recommended tab placement strategy?

options.text: anchorString with anchorUnits and anchorXOffset/anchorYOffset
Docusign AI automatic tab placement
Retrieve field values from a web form
xPosition and yPosition fixed positioning

answerText: anchorString with anchorUnits and anchorXOffset/anchorYOffset
explanation: Anchor (string-based) tagging places tabs relative to text in the document, so when text moves the tabs move with it; offsets and anchorUnits fine-tune the position.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Anchor tags with offsets keep tabs next to their anchor text when the document changes.
optionExplanations.B: Automatic AI placement is not the recommended API strategy for keeping tabs aligned to text.
optionExplanations.C: A web form can supply field values, but it does not decide where tabs sit on the document.
optionExplanations.D: Fixed x and y coordinates stay at the same spot even when the text they belong to moves.

whyNotOthers: A is right because anchor tabs follow the anchor text when content shifts. The trap is D: fixed positioning is a valid way to place tabs, but it uses absolute coordinates that no longer line up after a revision. B is not the documented placement strategy for API-sent documents and C supplies values, not positions.

stem: A developer creates 100 web form instances for participants in an internal compliance process using the Web Forms API, and the internal system must map and track each instance back to the individual user record. Which parameter must be supplied in the Instances:createInstance request?

options.text: The web form configuration ID, for one-to-one mapping
The participant's email address as the unique key for all Docusign objects
A unique clientUserId value generated by the developer's internal systems
The API account ID to distinguish instances

answerText: A unique clientUserId value generated by the developer's internal systems
explanation: Each instance needs its own identifier from the internal system, and that is clientUserId.

optionExplanations.A: All 100 instances are created from the same configuration, so its ID is shared and cannot map to individual users.
optionExplanations.B: Email is not a unique key for Docusign objects and is not the identifier createInstance uses for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. clientUserId is the developer-supplied identifier for the user in your system, which gives a one-to-one mapping to the user record.
optionExplanations.D: The account ID is the same for every instance in the account; it identifies the account, not a participant.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a developer-generated clientUserId maps each instance to one user record. The trap is A: it is a real Web Forms identifier, but every instance shares it. B and D fail because email is not a Docusign-wide unique key and the account ID is the same for the whole account.

stem: A nightly job must pick up every agreement in Agreement Manager, including imported legacy ones, and then pull full detail for each new agreement. Which design fits?

options.text: Call Agreements:getAgreement with a wildcard agreementId
Call Agreements:getAgreementsList to enumerate agreements, then Agreements:getAgreement for each new one
Rely on Connect envelope-completed events to find new agreements
Call Agreements:createAgreementSummary for each agreement to get its detail

answerText: Call Agreements:getAgreementsList to enumerate agreements, then Agreements:getAgreement for each new one
explanation: Listing agreements finds every record in the repository, whatever its origin, and getAgreement then retrieves full detail for each new one.

optionExplanations.A: getAgreement takes one specific agreementId; it does not accept wildcards.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Enumerate with the list call, then get detail for each new agreement.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope events miss imported legacy agreements, which never went through eSignature.
optionExplanations.D: Summaries are AI-written text, not the structured agreement detail.

whyNotOthers: B is right because only the agreement list covers all repository records. The trap is C: Connect does report completed envelopes, but imported legacy agreements never had an envelope, so they would be missed. A is invalid because getAgreement needs a specific ID, and D returns AI summaries rather than the structured detail.

stem: An HR onboarding workflow starts with the candidate entering address and tax information. The candidate must then complete identity verification before any signing package is released. Which step order matches?

options.text: Verify Someone's Identity, then Collect Data with Web Forms
Collect Data with Web Forms, then Verify Someone's Identity
Send Documents for Signature, then Verify Someone's Identity
Collect Data with Web Forms, then Send Documents for Signature without verification

answerText: Collect Data with Web Forms, then Verify Someone's Identity
explanation: The stem says the workflow starts with data entry and verifies identity before signing, so the form comes first, then the identity step, then signing.

optionExplanations.A: A valid pattern in other cases, but this workflow must start with the candidate's data entry.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Collect the data first, then verify identity before signing.
optionExplanations.C: Signing happens before verification, which the requirement forbids.
optionExplanations.D: Skips the required identity verification step.

whyNotOthers: B is right because it follows the stated business order. The trap is A: verifying identity before a form is a valid pattern when sensitive pre-filled data must be protected, but here the workflow is defined to start with data entry. C releases the signing package before verification, and D skips verification.

stem: A third-party API used by an extension app accepts XML payloads, but Docusign requires the external response in a specific JSON schema. What should the developer deploy to handle the translation?

options.text: An OAuth 2.0 identity provider
A Docusign Connect listener
An API proxy
Concerto type definitions in the manifest

answerText: An API proxy
explanation: An API proxy sits between Docusign and the third-party service and transforms XML to the required JSON (and back).

optionExplanations.A: An identity provider issues tokens; it does not translate payloads.
optionExplanations.B: A Connect listener receives envelope events; it does not translate extension calls.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An API proxy translates the XML API to the JSON schema Docusign expects.
optionExplanations.D: Concerto models data types; it does not translate an API's XML into JSON.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the proxy performs format translation. The trap is D: Concerto describes data types for Data IO and connected fields, but it does not convert XML responses. A handles authorization, and B receives event notifications.

stem: A JWT integration will impersonate a system user to send envelopes. Before the first token request, which consent must that user (or an admin) grant?

options.text: Consent for the integration key covering the signature and impersonation scopes
Consent for the signature scope only
No consent; adding impersonation to the JWT assertion is enough
Consent for the extended scope so a refresh token is issued

answerText: Consent for the integration key covering the signature and impersonation scopes
explanation: JWT consent must include impersonation, which authorizes the app to act as the user, plus the API scope it needs such as signature.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Consent to signature and impersonation lets the app request tokens as that user.
optionExplanations.B: signature alone does not authorize the app to impersonate the user, so JWT requests would still fail.
optionExplanations.C: Listing impersonation in the assertion does not replace consent from the user or an admin.
optionExplanations.D: extended controls the refresh-token lifecycle in Auth Code flows; JWT never returns a refresh token.

whyNotOthers: A is right because JWT impersonation needs consent to both signature and impersonation. The trap is B: signature covers eSignature calls, but without impersonation the app is not allowed to act as the user. C misunderstands consent, which must be granted by the user or an admin, and D applies only to Auth Code flows because JWT never returns a refresh token.

stem: An app that uses JWT Grant has just gone live. Which production setup lets it obtain access tokens?

options.text: Reuse the developer RSA private key, because it was copied with the key
Add an RSA key pair to the production key and obtain consent in production
Add a secret key only, because JWT Grant does not use RSA keys
Switch to Authorization Code Grant, because JWT Grant needs a separate review

answerText: Add an RSA key pair to the production key and obtain consent in production
explanation: For JWT Grant apps, the After Go-Live guidance says to add RSA key pairs (and redirect URIs as needed for consent) on the production key; consent must also be granted in production.

optionExplanations.A: RSA key pairs are not duplicated with the key; a new pair must be added in production.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Add an RSA key pair in production and grant consent (individual or admin) in production.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant signs its assertion with an RSA private key; a secret alone is not enough.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant apps go live through the same Go-Live process; no flow change is needed.

whyNotOthers: B is right because RSA keys are not copied and production consent is separate. The trap is A: the key value is the same in production, but its RSA keys are not duplicated. C confuses JWT with Authorization Code Grant, and D is wrong because JWT Grant apps go live through the same process.

stem: A new integration's listener should receive small, event-focused messages and be able to subscribe to the widest range of event types. Which message format should the Connect configuration use?

options.text: JSON SIM format
Legacy XML with aggregate mode to reduce message count
Legacy XML SIM matching the SOAP object model
XML messages that always include the full envelope summary

answerText: JSON SIM format
explanation: JSON SIM is event-focused: messages are smaller, customizable and easier to process, and it supports more event types, so Docusign recommends it for all apps.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. JSON SIM sends smaller, event-focused messages and supports more event types.
optionExplanations.B: Aggregate mode cuts message count but is legacy XML with envelope-focused payloads.
optionExplanations.C: Legacy XML SIM suits existing SOAP integrations, not a new app needing small messages.
optionExplanations.D: Including the full envelope summary in every message makes payloads larger, not smaller.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the clues (small, event-focused, more event types) describe Connect 2.0. The trap is B: aggregate mode reduces the number of messages, but it is a legacy XML option and messages stay envelope-focused. C is only worth considering for an existing SOAP integration, and D is the opposite of a small payload.

stem: A sender must prepare and edit an envelope from inside a custom app before it is sent. Which endpoint provides that experience?

options.text: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
EnvelopeViews:createSender
Envelopes:update with status sent
clientUserId on the sender

answerText: EnvelopeViews:createSender
explanation: Embedded sending uses EnvelopeViews:createSender on a draft envelope, giving a sender view URL where the user tags and sends inside the app.

optionExplanations.A: createRecipient opens the signing ceremony for a recipient, not the sender's preparation view.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. EnvelopeViews:createSender returns a sender view for tagging and sending inside the app.
optionExplanations.C: Updating to sent sends the envelope immediately with no chance to prepare it in the app.
optionExplanations.D: clientUserId marks embedded recipients for signing; it does not give a sender a preparation view.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the sender view is the embedded preparation experience. The trap is A: createRecipient is also an embedded view, but it opens a signing session for a recipient. C sends without any preparation step and D is a recipient property for embedded signing.

stem: Sofia's integration must make signers enter a code that Docusign sends to their mobile phone before they can access the envelope. Which recipient authentication method applies?

options.text: Knowledge-based authentication (KBA)
Phone authentication
Access code
ID verification with a government photo ID

answerText: Phone authentication
explanation: A code sent by Docusign to the signer's phone is phone authentication.

optionExplanations.A: KBA challenges the signer with questions from public records (US only); no code is sent to the phone.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Phone authentication sends a code by SMS or call; the recipient must enter it to access the envelope.
optionExplanations.C: The sender defines the access code and must share it out of band; Docusign does not send it to the phone.
optionExplanations.D: IDV checks an identity document, which is heavier than needed and does not match the code-to-phone requirement.

whyNotOthers: B is right because phone authentication is the method where Docusign sends the code to the phone. The trap is A: KBA is a well-known stronger recipient authentication option, but it uses questions, not codes. C and D fail because an access code is sender-defined and shared out of band, and IDV checks an ID document.

stem: After an acquisition, 5,000 contracts signed in another vendor's tool must appear in Agreement Manager search results with extracted data. Which capability fits?

options.text: Bulk import the acquired contracts into Agreement Manager
Send them through eSignature Bulk Send so they become agreements
Call Agreements:createAgreementSummary on each contract file
Save each contract as an eSignature template

answerText: Bulk import the acquired contracts into Agreement Manager
explanation: Bulk import is how existing, non-Docusign agreements enter Agreement Manager, where AI extraction runs on them.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bulk import brings the acquired contracts into Agreement Manager for AI extraction.
optionExplanations.B: Bulk Send sends new envelopes for signature; it is not an import of signed contracts.
optionExplanations.C: Summaries can only be created for agreements already in Agreement Manager.
optionExplanations.D: Templates are reusable sending blueprints, not agreement records.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the contracts are already signed and only need to be added to the repository. The trap is B: Bulk Send is also a bulk eSignature feature, but it sends new envelopes for signing, which is not needed for already-executed contracts. C works only on agreements already in Agreement Manager, and D creates reusable sending templates, not agreement records.

stem: An ISV is building a new extension app so Maestro workflows can save completed agreements to its cloud storage service. Which extension type should it build?

options.text: A connected fields extension
A file output cloud storage extension
A file archive extension
A bank account verification extension

answerText: A file output cloud storage extension
explanation: File output cloud storage is the extension type for saving files from Maestro workflows, and it is the one to use for new apps.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields verify tab data in eSignature and are not supported in Maestro.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. File output cloud storage is the current extension type for saving workflow files.
optionExplanations.C: File archive is legacy; new apps should use file output cloud storage.
optionExplanations.D: Bank account verification checks account data; it does not store documents.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the app is new and stores workflow files. The trap is C: file archive does the same job, but it is the legacy type and new apps should use file output cloud storage. A is not supported in Maestro, and D verifies bank data rather than storing files.

stem: A Maestro workflow must read and write structured records in a customer's system of record. Which extension type fits?

options.text: File IO (file output cloud storage)
Connected Fields
Data Verification
Data IO

answerText: Data IO
explanation: Data IO extensions read data from and write data to a system of record from Maestro workflows.

optionExplanations.A: File IO writes documents to storage, not structured records.
optionExplanations.B: Connected fields verify field values in eSignature and are not supported in Maestro.
optionExplanations.C: Data Verification checks standard values like addresses; it does not read/write records.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Data IO reads and writes system-of-record data from Maestro workflows.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the requirement is structured record read/write in a workflow. The trap is B: connected fields also talk to a system of record, but for field verification in eSignature, and they are not supported in Maestro. A writes documents, not records, and C verifies standard data types.

stem: An app only needs to send envelopes and read user account information. A developer adds signature, extended, and aow_manage in case new features are added later. What should the developer do when requesting consent?

options.text: Keep all three so future features need no re-consent
Request impersonation only, because it includes signature
Reuse the scope list from the team's other integration key
Request only the minimum scopes required for those operations

answerText: Request only the minimum scopes required for those operations
explanation: Scopes should match the operations the app performs today; extra scopes such as aow_manage (Maestro) widen access without a current need.

optionExplanations.A: This over-requests: aow_manage and extended give access the app does not currently use.
optionExplanations.B: impersonation lets an app act as a user through JWT; it does not include the signature API scope.
optionExplanations.C: Another integration's scopes reflect its own operations, not this app's needs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Request only the scopes needed for sending envelopes and reading account info.

whyNotOthers: D is right because least privilege means requesting only what current operations require. The trap is A: avoiding future re-consent sounds practical, but it grants Maestro access and long-lived refresh tokens the app does not use. B is wrong because impersonation does not include signature, and C copies scopes that may not match this app.

stem: Nadia completed Go-Live for an app that uses the template reference model to create envelopes. What template work must she do so the app works in production as it did in development?

options.text: Convert the code to composite templates, because the template reference model is not supported in production
Delete the developer template first, then rebuild it in production and update the template ID
Reference the same template ID, because templates were deployed to production during Go-Live
Deploy the template to production, then update the app to use the new production template ID

answerText: Deploy the template to production, then update the app to use the new production template ID
explanation: Templates are not copied during Go-Live; you must add the template to the production account, which gives it a new production template ID, and point the app at that ID.

optionExplanations.A: The template reference model is fully supported in production.
optionExplanations.B: Deleting the developer template is not required; the developer environment stays in use for testing.
optionExplanations.C: Go-Live does not deploy templates, so there is no automatically deployed ID to reference.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Add the template to production and update the app to its new production template ID.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the production template has its own ID. The trap is B: rebuilding in production and updating the ID is reasonable, but deleting the developer template is unnecessary, since the developer key and data keep working for testing. A is wrong because the template reference model works in production, and C is wrong because Go-Live copies only the integration key.

stem: A listener sits behind an API gateway that rejects any request without an Authorization header. Which account-level Connect security option satisfies the gateway?

options.text: Put a username and password in the listener URL query string
Send the integration key in the eventNotification object
HMAC signatures in X-DocuSign-Signature headers only
Basic authentication or OAuth 2.0 for Connect on the configuration

answerText: Basic authentication or OAuth 2.0 for Connect on the configuration
explanation: Basic authentication adds a username and password header, and OAuth for Connect sends an access token in the Authorization header with every message.

optionExplanations.A: Credentials in a query string are exposed in logs and are not a Connect security feature.
optionExplanations.B: The integration key identifies an app for API auth; it does not authenticate Connect messages.
optionExplanations.C: HMAC uses X-DocuSign-Signature headers, not an Authorization header.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Basic auth and OAuth for Connect both send credentials in the Authorization header.

whyNotOthers: D is right because both options put credentials in the Authorization header the gateway checks. The trap is C: HMAC is a strong control, but its values go in X-DocuSign-Signature headers, not the Authorization header, so the gateway would still reject the request. A exposes credentials in the URL, and B is not a Connect authentication mechanism.

stem: A developer needs to send separate, personalized copies of the same envelope to thousands of recipients, each signing their own copy. Which feature is designed for that?

options.text: Bulk Send (bulk send list applied to a draft envelope)
Envelopes:create called in a loop with transactionId
One envelope with all recipients at the same routing order
A composite template with one inline template per recipient

answerText: Bulk Send (bulk send list applied to a draft envelope)
explanation: Bulk Send creates one envelope per recipient from a bulk send list and a draft envelope or template, processed from a queue. The clue is a separate copy per recipient.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bulk Send generates a separate envelope for each recipient on the bulk send list.
optionExplanations.B: Looping Envelopes:create rebuilds bulk sending in custom code and consumes many API calls.
optionExplanations.C: Same routing order means parallel signing on one envelope, not separate copies.
optionExplanations.D: A composite template still produces a single envelope, not one envelope per recipient.

whyNotOthers: A is right because Bulk Send is built for many personalized copies. The trap is C: parallel routing does send to many recipients at once, but they all sign one shared envelope instead of their own copy. B reimplements bulk sending in custom code and D still builds one envelope.

stem: A financial-aid office sends envelopes by email. After a student finishes signing, they should be redirected to the office's help page. Which option should be used?

options.text: Brand destination URLs
returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
Branding signing resource file
A Connect webhook

answerText: Brand destination URLs
explanation: Email-delivered signing is remote signing, so the redirect is a brand destination URL.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Destination URLs on a brand redirect remote signers after events such as signing complete; apply the brand with brandId.
optionExplanations.B: returnUrl applies to embedded signing sessions only, not to email (remote) signing.
optionExplanations.C: Resource files customize the text and appearance of the signing experience; they do not set the redirect destination.
optionExplanations.D: Connect sends event notifications to your server and cannot redirect a browser.

whyNotOthers: A is right because brand destination URLs are the redirect setting for remote signers. The trap is B: it is a real redirect setting, but only for embedded signing. C and D fail because resource files change appearance and Connect is a server notification.

stem: An audit export must include extracted metadata and the signed file for every agreement of a given type. The agreement IDs are not known in advance. Which plan is correct?

options.text: Agreements:getAgreementsList to find them, Agreements:getAgreement for data, then a separate document download
Agreements:getAgreement alone, because it returns metadata and the file
Agreements:createAgreementSummary for each agreement, used as the audit copy
Agreements:getAgreementsList alone, because its response includes each file

answerText: Agreements:getAgreementsList to find them, Agreements:getAgreement for data, then a separate document download
explanation: The IDs are unknown, so listing comes first; getAgreement then returns the extracted data, and the file needs a separate document download.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. List to find agreements, getAgreement for extracted data, and a separate download for the file.
optionExplanations.B: getAgreement needs a known ID and returns extracted data, not the signed file.
optionExplanations.C: An AI summary is not an acceptable audit copy of the signed agreement.
optionExplanations.D: The list response contains agreement records, not document files.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it covers all three needs: finding records, reading data, and getting the file. The trap is B: getAgreement does provide the metadata, but it needs a known ID and does not return the document file. C replaces the signed file with AI-written text, and D wrongly assumes the list response carries the documents.

stem: A workflow must route by a Job Location field with three values: US, Canada, and Other. If the value is blank or unexpected, HR must be emailed. Which configuration fits?

options.text: A Multi Branch Rule step with a path per value plus a No Conditions Met path to a Send an Email step
A Branching Rule step that tests only Job Location = US (true or false)
Three separate published workflows, with participants choosing which to start
A Show a Confirmation Screen step telling the participant to restart

answerText: A Multi Branch Rule step with a path per value plus a No Conditions Met path to a Send an Email step
explanation: A Multi Branch Rule step creates several paths from one field and includes a No Conditions Met path, which can notify HR with a Send an Email step.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. One path per location, and No Conditions Met emails HR for blank or unexpected values.
optionExplanations.B: A two-way branch cannot separate Canada, Other and blank values.
optionExplanations.C: Duplicating workflows adds maintenance and depends on users choosing correctly.
optionExplanations.D: A confirmation screen does not route the process or notify HR.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it handles three values plus a fallback in one step. The trap is B: a single Branching Rule gives only true and false paths, so Canada, Other and blank values would all fall into one path. C duplicates the process and relies on the participant to choose correctly, and D never notifies HR.

stem: A Maestro workflow needs to save completed documents to an external repository using an installable extension app. Which extension type fits?

options.text: Connected Fields
Data Verification
File IO (file output cloud storage)
Data IO with CreateRecord

answerText: File IO (file output cloud storage)
explanation: File IO extensions write documents to cloud storage from Maestro workflows.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields verify field values in eSignature, not file storage.
optionExplanations.B: Data Verification checks standard values such as addresses.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. File IO (file output cloud storage) writes documents to external storage.
optionExplanations.D: Data IO writes records, not documents.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the requirement is storing documents. The trap is D: Data IO also writes to external systems, but it writes structured records, not files. A and B verify field values during preparation and signing.

stem: An implementation note must tell developers where to get the account ID and base URI after an access token is issued. Which endpoint should it name?

options.text: /oauth/token
The coid claim of the ID token
/oauth/userinfo
/oauth/auth

answerText: /oauth/userinfo
explanation: /oauth/userinfo, called with the access token, returns the accounts with their account_id and base_uri values.

optionExplanations.A: /oauth/token returns access and refresh tokens, not account IDs or base URIs.
optionExplanations.B: coid lists organizations that granted admin consent; it does not give account IDs or base URIs.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. /oauth/userinfo returns account_id and base_uri for each of the user's accounts.
optionExplanations.D: /oauth/auth starts the sign-in and consent step; it does not return account context.

whyNotOthers: C is right because userinfo is the endpoint that returns account context. The trap is A: the token endpoint is the step just before, but its response contains tokens and expiry, not accounts. B lists organizations that granted admin consent, and D starts sign-in and consent.

stem: An integration cannot use Connect and must poll envelope status. What is the most frequent polling allowed for a single envelope?

options.text: Once every 15 minutes
Once every minute
Once every 5 minutes
Once per hour for the whole account

answerText: Once every 15 minutes
explanation: Docusign limits status polling to at most one request per envelope every 15 minutes; violating it can fail Go-Live review.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Poll a given envelope no more than once every 15 minutes.
optionExplanations.B: Polling every minute is 15 times the allowed rate and hurts the efficiency score.
optionExplanations.C: Every 5 minutes still exceeds the once-per-15-minutes rule.
optionExplanations.D: The rule is per envelope, not one poll per hour for the whole account.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the polling rule is once per 15 minutes per envelope. The trap is C: it sounds conservative, but 5 minutes is still three times the allowed rate. B is far too frequent, and D wrongly applies the rule per account instead of per envelope.

stem: Which listener responses does Docusign Connect treat as failed deliveries to be retried?

options.text: Only HTTP 5xx responses; 4xx responses are final
Only network connection failures
Any non-2xx response or a timeout
None; Connect delivers each event once

answerText: Any non-2xx response or a timeout
