explanation: Any response outside the 2xx range, or no response before the timeout, counts as a failure and the event is retried.

optionExplanations.A: Connect does not distinguish 4xx from 5xx; both are failures and are retried.
optionExplanations.B: Error status codes and timeouts are also failures, not only connection errors.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Non-2xx responses and timeouts are failures that Connect retries.
optionExplanations.D: Connect retries failed deliveries with exponential back-off.

whyNotOthers: C is right because only a 2xx response acknowledges the message. The trap is A: many HTTP clients treat 4xx as non-retryable, but Connect retries any non-2xx response. B ignores error responses and timeouts, and D ignores Connect's retry process entirely.

stem: An Envelopes:create request contains documents, recipients and an emailSubject, and must go out to recipients without any further API call. Which status value belongs in the request?

options.text: created
delivered
completed
sent

answerText: sent
explanation: With the direct documents model, status sent sends the envelope in the same call. The clue is 'without any further API call', which rules out creating a draft first.

optionExplanations.A: created builds a draft envelope; a later update to sent would be needed, which the stem rules out.
optionExplanations.B: delivered is set by Docusign when a recipient opens the envelope; the integration cannot request it on create.
optionExplanations.C: completed is set by Docusign after all recipients finish; it is not a value used to send an envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. status sent sends the envelope to recipients as soon as Envelopes:create succeeds.

whyNotOthers: D is right because sent delivers the envelope immediately. The trap is A: created is accepted by Envelopes:create but leaves a draft that needs a second call to send. B and C are statuses Docusign assigns as recipients open and finish the envelope; the sender does not set them.

stem: Grace's app must send an envelope whose fields are verified against an external system through a Connected Fields extension. Which API sequence creates and sends it?

options.text: Envelopes:create first, then GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups to attach extensionData
AccountSignatureProviders:list, then recipientSignatureProviders on the signer
Configurations:getForm, then formValues on Instances:createInstance
TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, put the data in each tab's extensionData, then Envelopes:create

answerText: TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, put the data in each tab's extensionData, then Envelopes:create
explanation: Connected Fields are sent by getting the tab groups, filling each tab's extensionData, then calling Envelopes:create.

optionExplanations.A: The steps are right but the order is wrong: the extensionData must be on the tabs when the envelope is created.
optionExplanations.B: This sets up EU standards-based signatures, not connected fields.
optionExplanations.C: This prefills a web form instance; it does not create connected fields on an envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. This is the documented Connected Fields send flow: get the tab groups, populate extensionData on each tab, then create the envelope.

whyNotOthers: D is right because it follows the documented order: GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups, extensionData, Envelopes:create. The trap is A: it names the right calls but reverses the order, so the tabs would be created without their extension data. B and C fail because they configure SBS signature providers and web form prefill.

stem: Which endpoint returns the full structured data of one specific agreement so it can be sent to an external system?

options.text: Agreements:createAgreementSummary
Workflows:getWorkflowsList
Agreements:getAgreementsList
Agreements:getAgreement

answerText: Agreements:getAgreement
explanation: Agreements:getAgreement returns one agreement's full structured record (type, parties, provisions) for sending to an external system.

optionExplanations.A: Generates an AI-written summary of an agreement, not its structured fields.
optionExplanations.B: Lists Maestro workflow definitions; it returns no agreement data.
optionExplanations.C: Lists agreements across the account; it is the search step, not the single-agreement retrieval.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. getAgreement returns the full structured data of one agreement.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the question asks for one specific agreement's full data. The trap is C: getAgreementsList also returns agreement data, but it is the search and index step across many agreements, not the single-record call. A generates an AI prose summary, and B lists Workflow Builder workflows, which have nothing to do with agreement data.

stem: A citizen-services portal shows a 'Start application' button. The portal is a static page with no backend, and applicants should start the Maestro workflow themselves by opening a URL. Which start method matches?

options.text: Started by an envelope-completed event
From a link
Manually in Docusign by an administrator
From an API call with trigger_inputs

answerText: From a link
explanation: From a link provides a URL that starts a new workflow instance when opened, designed for self-service workflows started by participants.

optionExplanations.A: The applicant starts this process; it is not a reaction to a completed envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The workflow link starts a new instance when the applicant opens it.
optionExplanations.C: Manual start is done by internal users, not by public applicants.
optionExplanations.D: An API trigger needs a backend with an access token; the portal has none.

whyNotOthers: B is right because applicants open a URL themselves and the portal has no backend. The trap is D: From an API call is the method for passing starting values, but it needs server code with an OAuth token, which the static portal lacks. A is not how this workflow is started, and C needs an internal user to press Run Workflow.

stem: A developer configures an extension app connection using OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Grant. Which four values must come from the external API service or identity provider?

options.text: Publisher name, app name, short description and long description
Client ID, client secret, token URL and authorization URL
Client ID, public key, JWT and authorization URL
Integration key, API account ID, redirect URI and Docusign scopes

answerText: Client ID, client secret, token URL and authorization URL
explanation: Authorization Code Grant needs the client ID, client secret, token URL and authorization URL from the external provider.

optionExplanations.A: These are App Center listing details, not OAuth parameters.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Client ID, client secret, token URL and authorization URL come from the external provider.
optionExplanations.C: Public keys and JWTs belong to JWT Grant, not an Authorization Code connection.
optionExplanations.D: These identify your app to Docusign; the connection authenticates Docusign to the external API.

whyNotOthers: B is right because those are the provider values for an Authorization Code connection. The trap is D: those are Docusign-side values for your app calling Docusign, the opposite direction. A are listing details and C mixes in JWT Grant artifacts.

stem: A single-page application runs entirely in the user's browser to send documents, so a secret cannot be stored securely. Which OAuth flow does Docusign recommend for authenticating individual users?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
Implicit Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE is the recommended flow for clients that cannot store a secret while still authenticating each user interactively.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant requires a securely stored client secret, which a pure browser SPA cannot provide.
optionExplanations.B: Implicit Grant was the old SPA answer but is legacy; Docusign recommends the PKCE code flow instead.
optionExplanations.C: JWT Grant is for unattended service integrations, not for authenticating individual interactive users.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Browser-only client with interactive users: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the SPA cannot keep a secret and users sign in. The trap is B: Implicit Grant was the historical SPA answer but is legacy because it exposes the token in the redirect URL. A needs a secret the browser cannot protect, and C is for unattended service accounts.

stem: After a developer submits Go-Live and selects the production account, the key shows the status Pending approval. What does this mean?

options.text: The request failed and must be resubmitted with a different integration type
The app must make more eSignature API calls before review starts
The production account must be upgraded before review can begin
The integration needs manual approval, which may take up to 48 hours

answerText: The integration needs manual approval, which may take up to 48 hours
explanation: The course defines Pending approval as a manual approval process that may take up to 48 hours; App is live means the key is already available in production.

optionExplanations.A: Pending approval is not a rejection; you are asked for corrections only if review finds issues.
optionExplanations.B: There is no longer a required number of API calls before Go-Live.
optionExplanations.C: The status does not indicate a plan upgrade; it indicates manual review.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pending approval means manual review, which may take up to 48 hours.

whyNotOthers: D is right because Pending approval signals manual review. The trap is A: if issues are found you are asked to make corrections, but Pending approval itself is not a failure. B refers to the removed 20 API call requirement, and C is not what the status means.

stem: Connect logs show the same event delivered twice after the listener timed out on the first attempt. What should the integration do?

options.text: Spend longer processing before returning 200
Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
Return a non-2xx response to the second copy to reject it
Switch to envelope-level eventNotification to guarantee single delivery

answerText: Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
explanation: The timeout caused a retry, so the same event arrived twice; idempotent processing keeps the second copy from changing anything.

optionExplanations.A: Slower responses cause more timeouts and therefore more retries.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Detect already-processed events so redelivery has no effect.
optionExplanations.C: Any non-2xx response counts as a failed delivery and is retried.
optionExplanations.D: Envelope-level webhooks do not guarantee single delivery.

whyNotOthers: B is right because duplicates are expected after timeouts and retries. The trap is C: rejecting the copy with a non-2xx response is itself a failure, so Connect retries again. A makes timeouts more likely, and D does not help because envelope-level webhooks follow the same delivery and retry behavior.

stem: An app will call EnvelopeViews:createSender so a user can tag the envelope inside the app before it goes out. Which status must the envelope have when it is created?

options.text: sent
delivered
created
completed

answerText: created
explanation: Embedded sending works on a draft envelope, so the envelope is created with status created and then opened in the sender view. The clue is that the user still has to tag it before it goes out.

optionExplanations.A: sent delivers the envelope at once, so the user would have no chance to tag it first.
optionExplanations.B: delivered is set by Docusign when a recipient opens the envelope; it is not a create value.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A draft (status created) envelope is what EnvelopeViews:createSender opens for tagging and sending.
optionExplanations.D: completed is a terminal status after all recipients finish; nothing can be prepared at that point.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the sender view is requested for a draft envelope created with status created. The trap is A: sent is the usual create value, but a sent envelope is already out of the sender's hands and cannot be prepared first. B and D are statuses Docusign assigns as recipients open and finish the envelope.

stem: After a signer completes ID Verification, a system must pull the retained evidence about that event. Which API is relevant?

options.text: AccountSignatureProviders:list
The Connect envelope-completed payload
ID Evidence API
Docusign JS client SDK

answerText: ID Evidence API
explanation: Retained IDV data is retrieved after the event with the ID Evidence API.

optionExplanations.A: This lists signature providers for standards-based signatures; it returns no ID verification evidence.
optionExplanations.B: This envelope event payload reports envelope status; it does not include the retained ID verification data.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The ID Evidence API retrieves evidence (such as ID images and events) for a completed ID verification.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign JS renders embedded experiences in a browser; it does not retrieve evidence.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the ID Evidence API is the API built to retrieve ID verification evidence. The trap is A: it sounds like an identity-related list call, but it returns SBS signature providers. B and D fail because the Connect envelope payload does not carry ID evidence and Docusign JS is client-side rendering.

stem: A compliance dashboard already has an agreementId from a renewal workflow. The product owner wants that agreement's extracted provisions and key fields as data, not a search result page. Which operation fits best?

options.text: Agreements:getAgreementsList
Agreements:getAgreement
eSignature EnvelopeFormData:get on the source envelope
Agreements:createAgreementSummary

answerText: Agreements:getAgreement
explanation: With the agreementId known, getAgreement returns that agreement's extracted provisions and key fields as structured data.

optionExplanations.A: Returns a list of agreements, which the product owner explicitly does not want.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. getAgreement returns one agreement's extracted provisions and key fields.
optionExplanations.C: Returns tab values entered during signing, not AI-extracted provisions.
optionExplanations.D: Returns prose generated by AI, not discrete fields for a dashboard.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the ID is known and structured fields are required. The trap is D: createAgreementSummary works on the same known agreement, but it returns an AI-written summary, not field values a dashboard can display. A returns search results across agreements, and C returns signer tab values from the envelope, not extracted provisions.

stem: An app is ready to call TriggerWorkflow. Where does it get the URL to send the trigger request to?

options.text: Build it from the eSignature base path /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows
Reuse the workflow instance URL returned by an earlier trigger
From the GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements response; the URL carries mtid and mtsec query parameters
From the workflow-started Connect event

answerText: From the GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements response; the URL carries mtid and mtsec query parameters
explanation: GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements returns the trigger URL. It includes the mtid and mtsec query parameters that the Maestro service generates at publish time to identify and authenticate a valid workflow.

optionExplanations.A: Maestro does not use the eSignature /restapi/v2.1 base path.
optionExplanations.B: An instance URL opens an existing instance; it does not trigger a new one.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The trigger requirements response provides the trigger URL with mtid and mtsec.
optionExplanations.D: workflow-started is sent after an instance exists, so it cannot provide the URL to start one.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the trigger requirements call returns the URL to trigger. The trap is B: an earlier instance URL looks similar, but it opens that existing instance for a participant; it does not start a new one. A uses the eSignature base path, while Maestro uses api-d.docusign.com/v1 or api.docusign.com/v1, and D arrives only after an instance has started.

stem: A company wants eSignature fields such as an internal policy number to be verified against its own system of record while senders add fields and signers sign. Which extension type applies?

options.text: Data IO in a Maestro workflow
Connected Fields
Data Verification (for example postal address verification)
File IO

answerText: Connected Fields
explanation: Connected fields perform custom data verification of any value type against your system of record, at the Add Fields view and during signing.

optionExplanations.A: Data IO runs in Maestro workflows, not at Add Fields or signing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connected fields verify custom values against your system of record during prepare and signing.
optionExplanations.C: Data verification extensions cover standard types such as addresses, not internal policy numbers.
optionExplanations.D: File IO writes documents to storage.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the value is custom (an internal policy number) and checked against the company's own system. The trap is C: data verification extensions verify specific standard types like addresses or bank accounts, not custom internal values. A runs in workflows, not in Add Fields or signing, and D stores files.

stem: A native mobile app lets each user sign in to send envelopes. Developers propose shipping the client secret inside the app binary so they can use the confidential flow. Which option should the team keep?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
Implicit Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: A secret inside an app binary can be extracted, so the app is a public client and must use Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant would require a secret embedded in the binary, where it can be extracted.
optionExplanations.B: Implicit Grant is legacy and not recommended by Docusign.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A native app is a public client, so it uses Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant is for services with no user present and would need a private key in the app, which is worse.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a native app cannot truly protect a secret. The trap is A: the confidential flow is a valid code flow, but shipping the secret in the binary exposes it to anyone who unpacks the app. B is the legacy flow, and D is for unattended services.

stem: A developer clicks Start Go live and must log in to the production account that will host the integration. What must be true of that login?

options.text: It must belong to a Docusign Partner Program member
It must use the same email address as the developer account
It must have administrator privileges on the production account
It must be on an account with a paid Docusign support plan

answerText: It must have administrator privileges on the production account
explanation: The developer submitting the Go-Live request must have administrator privileges on the production account.

optionExplanations.A: Partner Program membership is required only for a Public integration, not for every Go-Live.
optionExplanations.B: The production account can use a different email address than the developer account.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The submitter must be an administrator on the production account.
optionExplanations.D: A paid support plan is not a Go-Live requirement; it only affects access to support cases.

whyNotOthers: C is right because admin access to the production account is a Go-Live requirement. The trap is B: many people assume the accounts must match, but the production login can use a different email address from the developer account. A applies only to Public integrations, and D is needed only to open support cases.

stem: Security policy says signed PDFs must not travel inside webhook payloads; the app will download them through the API with its own token. Which option should be used?

options.text: Leave documents out of the Connect payload and download them by API when needed
Include documents but encrypt the listener's disk
Include documents and delete them after processing
Enable HMAC so document contents are hidden in transit

answerText: Leave documents out of the Connect payload and download them by API when needed
explanation: Configuring the Connect payload without documents keeps PDFs out of webhook messages, and the app retrieves them by API when required.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Omit documents from the payload and fetch them through the API.
optionExplanations.B: Documents would still travel in the webhook payload.
optionExplanations.C: Documents would still be sent in the payload before deletion.
optionExplanations.D: HMAC signs messages; it does not encrypt or remove document content.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it is the only option that keeps PDFs out of the payload. The trap is D: HMAC is a Connect security feature, but it signs the message for authenticity and integrity; it does not hide or remove the document contents. B and C still send the PDFs in the payload, breaking the policy.

stem: A sent envelope must be canceled permanently, and the cancellation must record why. What should the Envelopes:update request contain?

options.text: status created with an emailBlurb
status voided with a voidedReason
status declined with a declinedReason
status completed with a note

answerText: status voided with a voidedReason
explanation: Voiding an envelope is done with status voided plus a voidedReason. The clue is a permanent cancellation that records the reason.

optionExplanations.A: created plus emailBlurb describes a draft and its email text; it does not cancel anything.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. status voided with voidedReason permanently cancels the envelope and records the reason.
optionExplanations.C: declined and declinedReason belong to a recipient who refuses to sign, not to the sender cancelling.
optionExplanations.D: completed is set by Docusign when all recipients finish; it cannot be used to cancel.

whyNotOthers: B is right because a void request sets status voided and supplies voidedReason. The trap is C: declinedReason is real, but it records why a recipient declined, not a sender cancellation. A creates or describes a draft message and D is a status only Docusign sets.

stem: A developer embeds a Docusign web form in a customer portal. Instances:createInstance has returned the instance URL. Which component is loaded in the portal page to display it?

options.text: The embedded sending view from EnvelopeViews:createSender
Docusign JS client SDK
A PowerForm URL
A Connect webhook listener

answerText: Docusign JS client SDK
explanation: The instance URL comes from createInstance, and the documented client-side component for showing it inline is Docusign JS.

optionExplanations.A: The sender view lets a sender prepare an envelope inside your app; it does not display a web form instance to a participant.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Docusign JS is the client SDK used to render a web form instance URL in a host page.
optionExplanations.C: A PowerForm is a separate self-service signing link for templates; it does not render a Web Forms API instance.
optionExplanations.D: Connect pushes event notifications to your server; it renders nothing in the browser.

whyNotOthers: B is right because Docusign provides Docusign JS to embed web form instances in a website. The trap is A: it is a real embedded view, but it is for senders preparing envelopes, not for participants filling a web form. C and D fail because a PowerForm is a different self-service feature and Connect is server-side event delivery.

stem: A contract analytics page lets users filter agreements by counterparty, expiration month and type before opening one record. The integration does not know the agreementId until the filter results return. Which operation comes first?

options.text: Agreements:getAgreement
Agreements:createAgreementSummary
Agreements:getAgreementsList
eSignature Envelopes:listStatusChanges

answerText: Agreements:getAgreementsList
explanation: getAgreementsList is the list and search step that runs before retrieving a specific agreement when its ID is not yet known.

optionExplanations.A: Needed after the user picks a result; it requires the agreementId first.
optionExplanations.B: Summarizes one known agreement; it cannot filter agreements.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. List agreements first, then open the chosen one.
optionExplanations.D: Lists envelope changes; it cannot filter on extracted counterparty or expiration data.

whyNotOthers: C is right because filtering happens before any agreementId exists. The trap is A: getAgreement is the call for opening the record, but it comes second because it needs the agreementId. B also needs a known agreement, and D lists envelope status changes rather than agreements filtered by extracted fields.

stem: A workflow starts correctly from a test, but production triggers fail whenever the app omits accountType, which the designer marked as a required starting variable. Where should the developer investigate first?

options.text: Workflow trigger requirements and starting-variable mapping
Whether the token includes aow_manage
Whether new instances of the workflow are paused
The Connect configuration's message format

answerText: Workflow trigger requirements and starting-variable mapping
explanation: The failure appears only when accountType is missing, and the designer made it a required starting variable. That points to the trigger requirements and how the app maps values into the trigger inputs.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Check the required inputs in the trigger requirements and map accountType on every call.
optionExplanations.B: A scope problem would fail every call, not only calls missing accountType.
optionExplanations.C: Paused workflows reject all new instances regardless of inputs.
optionExplanations.D: Connect message format affects notifications, not trigger validation.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the deciding clue is that failures track one missing required value. The trap is B: a missing scope would fail every trigger call, not only those without accountType. C would block all new instances, and D affects event delivery, not starting a workflow.

stem: A signer enters a bank account number that must be validated in real time against a standard bank verification service while signing. Which extension pattern fits?

options.text: Data Verification (bank account verification) at eSignature signing
File IO in a Maestro workflow
Data IO in a Maestro workflow
ID Verification of the signer before opening the envelope

answerText: Data Verification (bank account verification) at eSignature signing
explanation: Data Verification checks signer-entered standard data such as bank accounts in real time during signing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bank account verification is a Data Verification extension run at signing.
optionExplanations.B: File IO stores documents; it does not validate entered values.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO reads/writes records in workflows; it does not verify a field during signing.
optionExplanations.D: ID Verification confirms who the signer is, not whether the bank account is valid.

whyNotOthers: A is right because bank account is a standard data verification type checked at signing. The trap is C: Data IO also talks to external systems, but it runs in Maestro workflows and reads/writes records rather than verifying a field as it is entered. B stores files, and D verifies identity, not the bank data.

stem: A partner's REST calls return 401 Unauthorized. The code sends Authorization: Bearer, but with the wrong value. Which value belongs after Bearer?

options.text: The access token returned by /oauth/token
The refresh token
The ID token returned when openid is requested
The integration key

answerText: The access token returned by /oauth/token
explanation: The Bearer header carries the access token; refresh tokens and ID tokens are never used to call the APIs.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. API calls use Authorization: Bearer <access_token>.
optionExplanations.B: A refresh token is only exchanged at /oauth/token for a new access token; APIs reject it.
optionExplanations.C: The ID token records identity and consent details; it is not used to call APIs.
optionExplanations.D: The integration key identifies the app; it is not a credential for API calls.

whyNotOthers: A is right because only the access token authorizes API calls. The trap is B: the refresh token comes back in the same response, but it is only sent to /oauth/token to get a new access token. C has no system function for calling APIs, and D identifies the app rather than authorizing a request.

stem: A company builds an app that its own employees and its customers' employees will use directly. Which integration type should it select?

options.text: Public integration
Private custom integration
Third-party integration key
Embedded integration

answerText: Private custom integration
explanation: When the integration is directly used by your employees or your customers' employees, the classification is Private custom integration.

optionExplanations.A: Public integration is a partner app for many Docusign customers using their own accounts.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Use by your employees or your customers' employees is a Private custom integration.
optionExplanations.C: Third-party integration key is for a partner product that requires the customer's own key.
optionExplanations.D: Embedded integration needs an ISV Embed license and serves customers without their own Docusign accounts.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the clue is direct use by the company's own employees or its customers' employees. The trap is A: customers are involved, but Public integration is for a partner app that many Docusign customers connect to their own accounts. C is for a customer supplying its own key to a partner product, and D is for vendors offering Docusign features through their own account.

stem: A QA tester confirms that envelope X, sent by API, posts events to a special listener while every other envelope in the account still uses the existing account webhook. Which configuration produces exactly this behavior?

options.text: A new account-level Connect configuration with all users selected
An organization-level Connect configuration for selected accounts
Polling Envelopes:listStatusChanges for envelope X
An eventNotification object in the Envelopes:create request for envelope X

answerText: An eventNotification object in the Envelopes:create request for envelope X
explanation: Only envelope-level Connect (eventNotification on Envelopes:create) targets one envelope while the account-level configuration keeps serving all other envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: An account-level configuration for all users sends events for every envelope in the account, not only envelope X.
optionExplanations.B: Organization-level Connect covers whole accounts in the org, not a single envelope.
optionExplanations.C: listStatusChanges is a polling call; it does not push anything to a listener.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. eventNotification scopes the webhook to the envelope it is created with.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the special listener receives events for envelope X only. The trap is A: an account-level configuration with all users selected would post every envelope in the account to the special listener. B is wider again, and C is polling, which is not a webhook at all and adds API calls.

stem: A developer is implementing embedded signing. Which parameter must be included in the recipient definition when creating the envelope to signal that the signer will be embedded rather than remote?

options.text: recipientId
clientUserId
returnUrl
accountId

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: Setting clientUserId on the recipient flags it as embedded (captive) instead of remote, which enables the embedded signing session.

optionExplanations.A: recipientId identifies every recipient, embedded or remote; it does not mark embedding.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. clientUserId on the recipient marks it as an embedded signer.
optionExplanations.C: returnUrl belongs to the createRecipient request, where it sets the redirect after signing.
optionExplanations.D: accountId is part of the request URL path; it says nothing about the recipient type.

whyNotOthers: B is right because clientUserId in the recipient definition is what makes the signer embedded. The trap is C: returnUrl is required for embedded signing, but it goes in the createRecipient request, not in the recipient definition. A exists for every recipient and D is part of the request URL.

stem: An HR onboarding workflow in Workflow Builder must first capture the new hire's personal information and then verify their government-issued ID. Which step sequence matches this?

options.text: Set Up Invite step, then Add a Branching Rule step
Collect Data with Web Forms step, then Verify Someone's Identity step
Verify Someone's Identity step, then Collect Data with Web Forms step
Get Signatures step, then Collect Data with Web Forms step

answerText: Collect Data with Web Forms step, then Verify Someone's Identity step
explanation: Collect Data with Web Forms captures the information first, then Verify Someone's Identity confirms the government ID, matching the stated order.

optionExplanations.A: Neither step collects data or verifies an ID; one configures how participants are invited and the other adds conditional routing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Collect Data with Web Forms gathers the personal information, then Verify Someone's Identity checks the government ID, in the required order.
optionExplanations.C: These are the right steps in the wrong order: the requirement is to collect the data first, then verify the ID.
optionExplanations.D: Get Signatures collects signatures, not ID verification, and it is placed before data collection.

whyNotOthers: B is right because it uses the two correct steps in the order the stem requires. The trap is C: the steps are correct but reversed. A and D fail because they do not include an identity verification step.

stem: A legal team has thousands of signed agreements from outside Docusign. They want them in Agreement Manager so future searches and analytics include them. Which capability is the right fit?

options.text: Re-send each agreement for signature as a new envelope
Bulk import the agreements into Agreement Manager
Configure Connect to publish events for the old agreements
Upload each agreement as an eSignature template

answerText: Bulk import the agreements into Agreement Manager
explanation: Bulk import brings existing agreements and their content into Agreement Manager, where they become searchable with AI-extracted data.

optionExplanations.A: Already-signed agreements do not need to be re-signed; import is the intended path.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Bulk import adds the legacy agreements to Agreement Manager for search and analytics.
optionExplanations.C: Connect reports events for Docusign envelopes; agreements from outside Docusign have none.
optionExplanations.D: Templates are reusable sending blueprints and do not create agreement records.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the agreements are already signed and only need to enter the repository. The trap is A: completed envelopes do appear in Agreement Manager, but re-signing executed contracts is unnecessary and creates new signing events. C only publishes events about Docusign envelopes, which these agreements never had, and D creates sending templates, not agreement records.

stem: A team embeds a workflow instance in an iframe. The workflow includes a Verify Someone's Identity step. Which verification method is supported in embedded workflow instances?

options.text: Phone authentication
ID verification with a government photo ID
Collect Data from an ID
Any method; embedding has no step restrictions

answerText: Phone authentication
explanation: For Verify Someone's Identity steps in embedded workflow instances, only the Phone Authentication method is supported.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Phone authentication is the only verification method supported for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.B: Works in a normal workflow, but is not supported when the instance is embedded.
optionExplanations.C: Collect Data from an ID is a step type, and it is not supported in embedded instances.
optionExplanations.D: Embedding has documented restrictions on identity and ID-related steps.

whyNotOthers: A is right because Docusign limits embedded identity steps to phone authentication. The trap is B: ID verification is a valid method in non-embedded workflows, but not in an embedded instance. C is a step type that is itself unsupported when embedded, and D ignores the documented restrictions.

stem: Which IT infrastructure change helps ensure Docusign can reliably send requests to the external API service behind an extension app?

options.text: Configure the network firewall to allow Docusign's requests
Enable CORS on the endpoint
Require multi-factor authentication on the endpoint
Add a CNAME entry to DNS

answerText: Configure the network firewall to allow Docusign's requests
explanation: The firewall must allow Docusign's requests to reach the external endpoint; otherwise the calls are blocked.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Allowing Docusign through the firewall keeps the endpoint reachable.
optionExplanations.B: CORS applies to browsers, not to Docusign's server-to-server calls.
optionExplanations.C: MFA is for interactive users; Docusign authorizes through the app's OAuth connection.
optionExplanations.D: A DNS alias does not make a firewalled endpoint reachable.

whyNotOthers: A is right because Docusign's server-to-server calls must get through the firewall. The trap is B: CORS controls browser cross-origin JavaScript, not server calls. C is an interactive user control that machine calls cannot satisfy, and D does not open network access.

stem: Users sign in interactively. The backend then exchanges the authorization code at /oauth/token, sending an Authorization: Basic header built from base64(integrationKey:secretKey). Which OAuth flow is this?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant
Implicit Grant
Confidential Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Sending the integration key and secret key in a Basic header during the code exchange is the defining step of Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Public Auth Code Grant also redeems a code at /oauth/token, but it sends a code_verifier and never a secret key.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant posts a signed assertion to /oauth/token; there is no authorization code and no Basic secret header.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant returns the token directly to the browser, so there is no code exchange at /oauth/token.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The Basic header with base64(integrationKey:secretKey) on the code exchange is the confidential flow.

whyNotOthers: D is right because only the confidential flow authenticates the code exchange with the secret key in a Basic header. The trap is A: Public Auth Code also exchanges a code at /oauth/token, but it sends a code_verifier in the body and no secret. B posts a signed JWT assertion instead of a code, and C never performs a code exchange.

stem: After Go-Live, how should an eSignature app determine the production base URI for a user's account?

options.text: Call userinfo after production authentication and use the account's base_uri
Hardcode https://www.docusign.net/restapi for all production accounts
Reuse the base_uri that userinfo returned in the developer environment
Use the authentication host account.docusign.com as the API base

answerText: Call userinfo after production authentication and use the account's base_uri
explanation: The account's production base URI comes from the base_uri field of the userinfo response after authenticating in production (it is also shown as Account Base URI on Apps and Keys).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Read base_uri from the production userinfo response and cache it.
optionExplanations.B: Production accounts live on different servers, so one hardcoded host is wrong for many accounts.
optionExplanations.C: The developer environment's userinfo returns the demo host, not the production one.
optionExplanations.D: account.docusign.com is the OAuth host; API calls go to the account's base URI.

whyNotOthers: A is right because each production account lives on a specific server returned by userinfo. The trap is B: it is a production host, but hardcoding one server fails for accounts on other data centers. C returns the demo host, and D confuses the authentication service with the API host.

stem: A developer proposes checking each in-flight envelope's status every 5 minutes to update a CRM. What should the guidance recommend instead?

options.text: Keep the 5-minute poll; per-envelope polling has no limit
Poll every 15 minutes per envelope and skip webhooks
Subscribe to Connect events instead of polling
Poll every 5 minutes but only during business hours

answerText: Subscribe to Connect events instead of polling
explanation: Polling is limited to once per 15 minutes per envelope, and Connect removes the need to poll by pushing status changes as they happen.

optionExplanations.A: Per-envelope polling is limited to once every 15 minutes; 5 minutes violates it.
optionExplanations.B: Allowed, but still wastes calls and adds delay; Connect is the recommended design.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect pushes events, so no per-envelope polling is needed.
optionExplanations.D: Limiting the hours does not change the 5-minute interval, which still breaks the polling limit.

whyNotOthers: C is right because Connect delivers each status change immediately without API calls. The trap is B: it fixes the limit violation but keeps a slower, call-heavy polling design that Docusign discourages. A and D both poll every 5 minutes, which breaks the once-per-15-minutes-per-envelope rule.

stem: A sender service creates envelopes during a high-volume window. If Envelopes:create times out, the service retries the same request. Which value should the app supply so Docusign can recognize the retry as the same transaction?

options.text: envelopeId
transactionId
recipientId
batchId

answerText: transactionId
explanation: The client sets transactionId on the envelope definition, so a timed-out request can be recognized instead of producing a second envelope.

optionExplanations.A: envelopeId is assigned by Docusign in the response; a timed-out call may never return it to the client.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. transactionId is the client-supplied value that identifies the create transaction across retries.
optionExplanations.C: recipientId identifies a recipient inside the envelope; it cannot identify the create transaction.
optionExplanations.D: batchId belongs to bulk send batches, not to single Envelopes:create calls.

whyNotOthers: B is right because transactionId is generated by the sender and travels with the create request. The trap is A: envelopeId is the envelope's identifier, but Docusign assigns it and a timed-out call may never return it. C identifies a recipient and D a bulk send batch.

stem: A financial-aid office embeds one web form instance per applicant and must later match each instance to the applicant's record. Which value should the app supply on createInstance?

options.text: clientUserId
recipients[].roleName
The API account ID
The envelopeId

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: Per-applicant correlation from your own system is done with clientUserId.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. clientUserId is the app's own identifier for the user, required for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.B: roleName maps participants to template roles in remote instances; it names a role, not a specific applicant.
optionExplanations.C: The account ID is identical for every instance in the account.
optionExplanations.D: An embedded instance has no envelope until the first submit, so no envelopeId exists when the instance is created.

whyNotOthers: A is right because clientUserId carries the applicant identifier from your system. The trap is B: it is part of createInstance, but it is used for remote instances and identifies a role such as 'Applicant', not which applicant. C and D fail because the account ID is shared and the envelopeId does not exist yet at creation.

stem: A renewal review task needs a copy of the prior signed agreement file attached. The agreement already exists in Agreement Manager and its ID is known. Which approach fits?

options.text: Download the agreement document for that agreement
Attach the output of Agreements:createAgreementSummary
Attach the response of Agreements:getAgreementsList
Create a new envelope containing the agreement

answerText: Download the agreement document for that agreement
explanation: The task needs the signed file itself, so the agreement document is downloaded for that agreement.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Downloading the agreement document gives the review task the signed file.
optionExplanations.B: An AI summary is not a copy of the signed agreement.
optionExplanations.C: The list response contains agreement records, not the agreement file.
optionExplanations.D: A new envelope starts a new signing process; it does not retrieve the existing signed copy.

whyNotOthers: A is right because only the document download yields a copy of the signed file. The trap is B: a summary helps reviewers, but it is AI-written text, not the prior signed agreement. C returns agreement records rather than a file, and D starts a new signing transaction instead of retrieving the existing document.

stem: A company built an extension app that reads its internal HR system for use in its own Maestro workflows. No other Docusign customer should see or install it. How should the app be distributed?

options.text: Publish it publicly in the App Center
Register it as a Connect listener
Expose it as a connected fields extension
Use private distribution so only the company's organization can install it

answerText: Use private distribution so only the company's organization can install it
explanation: Private distribution is meant for org-only extension apps. The company's admin then installs it so the workflow can use its steps.

optionExplanations.A: Public listing exposes the app to all customers, which the company does not want.
optionExplanations.B: Connect pushes event notifications; it does not provide workflow steps.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Private distribution limits the app to the company's own organization.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the app is for this organization only. The trap is A: public App Center listing is the normal path for extension apps, but it goes through public review and makes the app available to every customer. B only receives events, and C is an eSignature feature not supported in Maestro.

stem: An architect explains extension apps to a team that has only built eSignature API integrations. Which statement correctly describes how an extension app's calls flow?

options.text: Your service calls Docusign APIs using JWT Grant and an integration key
Docusign pushes envelope status events to your listener through Connect
Signers are redirected to your site and returned with a signing token
Docusign calls your external service through actions defined in the app

answerText: Docusign calls your external service through actions defined in the app
explanation: With an extension app, Docusign is the caller: it invokes the external endpoints described by the app's actions, using the app's connection for authorization.

optionExplanations.A: This is a standard eSignature API integration (your code calls Docusign), not how an extension app works.
optionExplanations.B: Connect sends event notifications; it does not execute extension actions such as verify or write record.
optionExplanations.C: Redirect-based signing is an embedded/remote signing pattern, unrelated to how extension actions are invoked.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Docusign invokes the external endpoints declared in the app's actions, authorized through the app's connection.

whyNotOthers: D is right because extension apps reverse the usual integration direction: Docusign calls your service via manifest actions. The trap is A, which describes a normal API integration where your code calls Docusign. B describes Connect notifications and C describes a redirect pattern, neither of which is the extension app call model.

stem: A legacy browser-only SPA uses Implicit Grant. The team must follow current Docusign guidance for a client that cannot protect a secret and signs in each user. Which flow should it use?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Keep Implicit Grant but request fewer scopes

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: Docusign recommends replacing Implicit Grant with Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE for clients that cannot store a secret.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant needs a client secret, which a browser-only SPA cannot protect.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is for service integrations without a user present, not per-user browser sign-in.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE is the recommended replacement for Implicit Grant.
optionExplanations.D: Least privilege is good, but it leaves the app on the legacy Implicit flow that Docusign no longer recommends.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the client is public and the guidance is to migrate off Implicit to the PKCE code flow. The trap is D: requesting fewer scopes is good practice, but it does not fix the legacy flow itself. A needs a secret the SPA cannot hold, and B does not sign users in.

stem: A developer wants the same codebase to run in the developer environment and in production without breaking template references. What is the best approach?

options.text: Hardcode the developer templateId, because Go-Live maps it to production
Reference templates by the demo templateId and let production redirect it
Re-run Go-Live whenever a template changes so production stays in sync
Keep template IDs in environment-specific configuration, one set per environment

answerText: Keep template IDs in environment-specific configuration, one set per environment
explanation: Template IDs differ between the developer and production accounts, so they should be stored as per-environment configuration rather than hardcoded.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live does not map or copy templates; the developer templateId does not exist in production.
optionExplanations.B: Production does not redirect demo template IDs; the production template has its own ID.
optionExplanations.C: Go-Live promotes the integration key only; it never synchronizes templates.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Store template IDs per environment so each deployment uses its own account's templates.

whyNotOthers: D is right because each environment has its own template IDs. The trap is A: it assumes Go-Live carries templates and their IDs into production, but Go-Live only duplicates the integration key. B is the same mistake, and C is wrong because Go-Live never copies templates.

stem: A developer needs real-time updates for envelopes sent across three Docusign accounts under one corporate organization, to centralize logging and monitoring. Which Connect configuration should be implemented?

options.text: Recipient Connect
Envelope-level Connect (eventNotification)
Organization-level Connect
Account-level Connect

answerText: Organization-level Connect
explanation: Organization-level Connect spans the accounts in the organization, centralizing event delivery in one configuration.

optionExplanations.A: Recipient Connect does not centralize events from several accounts.
optionExplanations.B: Envelope-level Connect applies to one envelope at a time, not all envelopes in three accounts.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Organization-level Connect covers all or selected accounts in the organization.
optionExplanations.D: Account-level Connect covers only one account; three separate configurations would be needed.

whyNotOthers: C is right because only org-level Connect covers multiple accounts from one place. The trap is D: account-level Connect works for one account, so it would need three separate configurations instead of one central one. B applies to a single API-sent envelope, and A is not the level that aggregates events across accounts.

stem: A request uses the template reference model with one saved template. The developer must point the call at that template, then map recipients into its roles. Which identifier points at the template?

options.text: templateId
roleName
envelopeId
clientUserId

answerText: templateId
explanation: templateId identifies the saved template; templateRoles with roleName then map recipients into it.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. templateId tells Docusign which saved template to build the envelope from.
optionExplanations.B: roleName is used in templateRoles to match a recipient to a role inside the template.
optionExplanations.C: envelopeId identifies an existing envelope, not the template used to create one.
optionExplanations.D: clientUserId marks a recipient for embedded signing; it does not reference a template.

whyNotOthers: A is right because templateId is the template reference. The trap is B: roleName is required for the recipient mapping step, but it names a role, not the template. C identifies an envelope that already exists and D marks an embedded recipient.

stem: Maya must ensure that a signer presents a government-issued photo ID before signing an envelope. Which recipient setting enforces this?

options.text: authenticationMethod recorded during embedded signing
An accessCode shared with the signer
idCheckConfigurationName set for KBA
identityVerification with the workflowId of the account's ID verification configuration

answerText: identityVerification with the workflowId of the account's ID verification configuration
explanation: The clue is a government-issued photo ID, which is ID verification configured with identityVerification.workflowId.

optionExplanations.A: This only writes your app's own authentication method to the certificate; Docusign does not challenge the signer.
optionExplanations.B: An access code proves the signer knows a secret, not that they hold a valid government ID.
optionExplanations.C: KBA verifies identity with public-record questions (US only), not with a photo ID.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Adding identityVerification.workflowId for an IDV configuration makes the recipient verify a photo ID before accessing the documents.

whyNotOthers: D is right because IDV is the method that checks a government photo ID, applied via identityVerification.workflowId. The trap is A: it looks like an identity setting, but it only records and never enforces. B and C fail because an access code and KBA are lighter methods that do not inspect an ID document.

stem: A custom app must show the parties array and provisions (for example governing_law and expiration_date) of one specific agreement. Which operation returns them?

options.text: Agreements:getAgreementsList
eSignature Envelopes:get
Agreements:getAgreement
Agreements:createAgreementSummary

answerText: Agreements:getAgreement
explanation: getAgreement returns one agreement's record, including its parties array and provisions object with fields such as governing_law and expiration_date.

optionExplanations.A: Lists agreements to find candidates; the app needs one specific agreement's record.
optionExplanations.B: Returns envelope metadata, not Agreement Manager parties and provisions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. getAgreement returns the parties and provisions for one agreement.
optionExplanations.D: Returns an AI summary rather than the parties array and provisions object.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the app needs the structured fields of one specific agreement. The trap is A: getAgreementsList is also an Agreement Manager read call, but it is used to find agreements, not to retrieve one specific record. B returns envelope status and recipients, not extracted provisions, and D returns AI-written prose.

stem: A developer wants Docusign Connect to send events about Maestro workflows (for example workflow-completed). Which Connect configuration detail is required?

options.text: The messages must exclude all envelope and recipient data.
The messages must have retries enabled.
The messages must be authenticated using HMAC.
The messages must use the JSON SIM format.

answerText: The messages must use the JSON SIM format.
explanation: Maestro workflow events are only available in the JSON SIM event message format.

optionExplanations.A: Excluding envelope data is not a requirement for workflow events.
optionExplanations.B: Retries improve delivery but do not enable workflow events.
optionExplanations.C: HMAC is recommended for security but is optional and does not enable workflow events.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Maestro workflow events are delivered only in JSON SIM format.

whyNotOthers: D is right because workflow events exist only in JSON SIM. The trap is C: HMAC is a recommended way to secure Connect messages, but it is optional and does not decide which events you receive. A and B are unrelated settings: excluding data or enabling retries does not make workflow events available.

stem: A private extension app has been approved. What must the developer do so that a specific customer's administrators can install it?

options.text: Click the button that makes the app available to all App Center customers
Set publicationRegions to the customer's region in the manifest
Add the customer's production account ID (GUID) to the app's allowed accounts
Send the customer the app's OAuth client ID and secret

answerText: Add the customer's production account ID (GUID) to the app's allowed accounts
explanation: For a private app, after approval the developer adds the production account IDs (GUIDs) allowed to install it; administrators of those accounts can then install it.

optionExplanations.A: Listing the app for all customers is the public publishing step, which a private app does not use.
optionExplanations.B: publicationRegions applies to public apps and controls regions, not specific accounts.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Private apps are shared by adding the production account IDs (GUIDs) of the allowed accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Connection credentials are for Docusign's calls to the external API; they do not control who can install the app.

whyNotOthers: C is right because private sharing is done by listing production account IDs. The trap is A: clicking to list the app for all customers is the public publishing step. B applies to public apps only, and D shares connection credentials, which does not grant install rights.

stem: A security architect reviews a service that has no user present. Its access token expires after one hour, no refresh token is returned, and the service signs a new assertion to get the next token. Which authentication model is this?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: JSON Web Token Grant
explanation: A 1-hour access token, no refresh token, and a newly signed assertion for each new token are the defining traits of JWT Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant returns an 8-hour access token plus a refresh token, which does not match the stem.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. JWT Grant: 1-hour access token, no refresh token, new signed assertion each time.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE needs an interactive user and returns a refresh token valid 24 hours.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a legacy interactive browser flow, not a service model.

whyNotOthers: B is right because only JWT Grant returns no refresh token and renews by signing a new assertion. The trap is A: Confidential Auth Code is also server-side, but its access token lasts 8 hours and it returns a refresh token. C returns a 24-hour refresh token, and D is a legacy browser flow.

stem: After Go-Live, which two values must the application itself switch from demo to production, as opposed to credentials you re-add on the production key in Apps and Keys? (Select two)

options.text: Redirect URI
Integration key (client ID)
Production API endpoints
Account Base URI
Secret or RSA key pair

answerText: Production API endpoints; Account Base URI
explanation: The application must call production endpoints (for example account.docusign.com for OAuth) and the account's production base URI instead of the demo hosts. This is the keyed answer in the source exam question.

optionExplanations.A: Redirect URIs must be re-added on the production key in Apps and Keys, which the stem excludes.
optionExplanations.B: The production key keeps the same value as the demo key, so the client ID does not change.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The app must switch to production endpoints such as https://account.docusign.com.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The app must call the account's production base URI, obtained from userinfo.
optionExplanations.E: Secrets and RSA keys are re-added on the production key in Apps and Keys, which the stem excludes.

whyNotOthers: C and D are right because they are values the code uses to route calls to production. The trap is B: the integration key is duplicated with the same value, so the app does not need a new client ID. A and E must be re-added on the production key in Apps and Keys, which the stem excludes; the source question keys C and D, so remember that pairing.

stem: A company needs one webhook that also captures envelopes that users in any of its organization's accounts receive from external senders. Which Connect level fits?

options.text: Account-level Connect configured in one account
Organization-level Connect
eventNotification on every envelope the company sends
Polling Envelopes:listStatusChanges for each account

answerText: Organization-level Connect
explanation: Organization-level Connect covers envelopes sent from or received by the organization's accounts, including envelopes received from external parties.

optionExplanations.A: One account-level configuration sees only that account's envelopes.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Org-level Connect covers envelopes sent or received by all or selected accounts.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope-level webhooks exist only on envelopes you send by API; they cannot cover envelopes received from external senders.
optionExplanations.D: Polling is not a webhook and adds API traffic per account.

whyNotOthers: B is right because it is a single configuration across accounts and includes received envelopes. The trap is C: eventNotification is set only by the sender at creation time, so it can never cover envelopes your users receive from external senders. A covers one account only, and D is polling, not a webhook.

stem: A request must combine a server template, inline recipient data, and an extra document supplied at runtime, all in one envelope. Which model supports that structure?

options.text: Template reference model (templateId plus templateRoles)
Direct documents model with fixed-position tabs
Composite templates model
Bulk send list applied to a draft envelope

answerText: Composite templates model
explanation: Composite templates mix server templates, inline templates and directly supplied documents in one envelope. The clue is combining all three.

optionExplanations.A: The template reference model uses one saved template as is; it cannot add an extra runtime document.
optionExplanations.B: Direct documents can supply the extra document but cannot apply the saved server template.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Composite templates combine server templates, inline templates and documents in one envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Bulk send creates one envelope per list recipient; it does not combine templates and documents.

whyNotOthers: C is right because only the composite templates model combines a saved template with a runtime document and inline data. The trap is A: it does use the saved template, but it cannot add a separate runtime document alongside it. B ignores the saved template and D sends copies to many recipients, which is a different requirement.

stem: A design requires that a signer receive a one-time code by SMS and enter it before the envelope opens. Which Docusign feature category applies?

options.text: The phone number verification extension (Verify.Version1.PhoneNumber)
Brand destination URLs
Recipient authentication (phone authentication)
authenticationMethod on createRecipient

answerText: Recipient authentication (phone authentication)
explanation: Requiring a code before the envelope opens is recipient authentication, specifically phone authentication.

optionExplanations.A: This extension validates a phone number value entered in a field; it does not gate access to the envelope with a code.
optionExplanations.B: Destination URLs redirect remote signers after events; they do not authenticate anyone.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Gating access to the envelope with an SMS code is a recipient authentication method: phone authentication.
optionExplanations.D: This only records your app's authentication on the certificate; nothing is sent to the signer.

whyNotOthers: C is right because recipient authentication controls access to the envelope, and phone authentication sends the SMS code. The trap is A: it is phone-related and runs inside eSignature, but it verifies a data value, not the signer's access. B and D fail because destination URLs only redirect and authenticationMethod only records.

stem: An app has only a counterparty name and must display that counterparty's agreement in full. In which order should it call the Agreement Manager API?

options.text: Agreements:getAgreement first, then Agreements:getAgreementsList to confirm
Agreements:getAgreementsList to find the agreement, then Agreements:getAgreement for its detail
Agreements:createAgreementSummary first to locate the agreement
eSignature Envelopes:get first, using the counterparty name

answerText: Agreements:getAgreementsList to find the agreement, then Agreements:getAgreement for its detail
explanation: With only a counterparty name, the app must list or search agreements to get the agreementId, then call getAgreement for the full record.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong order; getAgreement requires the agreementId that only the list step provides.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Search with the list call, then retrieve the full record by ID.
optionExplanations.C: createAgreementSummary works on a known agreement; it cannot locate one.
optionExplanations.D: Envelopes:get needs an envelopeId and returns envelope data, not agreements.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the agreementId comes from the list step. The trap is A: both calls are correct, but in the wrong order, since getAgreement cannot run without an agreementId. C needs a known agreement and does not search, and D is an eSignature call that needs an envelopeId, not a counterparty name.

stem: A services contract must include or hide clauses depending on the customer's region, which is a workflow variable. Which step should generate the document before signing?

options.text: Prepare eSignature Template
Collect Data with Web Forms
Prepare Document Template with conditional show/hide logic, followed by Send Documents for Signature
Use eSignature API with one fixed document

answerText: Prepare Document Template with conditional show/hide logic, followed by Send Documents for Signature
explanation: Prepare Document Template generates different document content from workflow variables using conditional show/hide logic defined on the template. It is followed by Send Documents for Signature.

optionExplanations.A: Meant for one unchanging template; it cannot show or hide clauses by region.
optionExplanations.B: Collects values but does not generate the contract.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Conditional logic on the document template produces region-specific content.
optionExplanations.D: A fixed document cannot vary its clauses by region.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the content itself changes with the region variable. The trap is A: Prepare eSignature Template fills fields on one template, but it is meant for a document that is exactly the same for every instance. B only collects data, and D sends a fixed document that cannot vary its clauses.

stem: A software vendor wants Docusign customers globally to use its compliance document storage service within Maestro workflows. How should the developer configure distribution?

options.text: Set distribution to PRIVATE, because public apps cannot be used in Maestro
Set distribution to PUBLIC and be (or become) a Docusign partner
Set distribution to PRIVATE and list every customer's account ID
Set distribution to PUBLIC and classify the integration key as customer or SI

answerText: Set distribution to PUBLIC and be (or become) a Docusign partner
explanation: Broad availability requires PUBLIC distribution, and only Docusign partners may publish public extension apps.

optionExplanations.A: Public apps can be used in Maestro; distribution does not limit the extension point.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. PUBLIC distribution gives broad availability, and publishing a public app requires Docusign partner status.
optionExplanations.C: Private sharing is for a limited list of production accounts, not every customer worldwide.
optionExplanations.D: Integration key classification is part of eSignature go-live, not extension app distribution.

whyNotOthers: B is right because global availability means public, and public publishing requires partner status. The trap is D: classifying an integration key as customer or SI belongs to eSignature go-live, not extension app publishing. A is false because public apps work in Maestro, and C misuses private sharing, which is limited to listed accounts.

stem: A small customer without Docusign Access Management or a claimed domain installs a JWT integration. The system user has never consented. How should consent be obtained?

options.text: Have the user grant individual consent once by opening the /oauth/auth consent URL in a browser
Use admin consent for external applications (scope=openid plus admin_consent_scope)
Call /oauth/userinfo with the integration key to activate the user
Regenerate the RSA key pair on the integration key

answerText: Have the user grant individual consent once by opening the /oauth/auth consent URL in a browser
explanation: Without Access Management and a claimed domain, admin consent is not available, so the user grants individual consent once through the /oauth/auth URL.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Individual consent through the /oauth/auth URL is the path when admin consent is not available.
optionExplanations.B: Admin consent needs Access Management and a claimed domain, which this customer does not have.
optionExplanations.C: /oauth/userinfo returns account and base URI details for an existing token; it does not grant consent.
optionExplanations.D: A new RSA key pair changes the signing key but does not record consent.

whyNotOthers: A is right because individual consent is the fallback when admin consent is not possible. The trap is B: admin consent for external apps is the ISV pattern, but it requires Access Management and a claimed domain, which this customer lacks. C needs an existing access token and does not grant consent, and D only changes signing keys.

stem: After an integration key is promoted, which account manages the production version of the key?

options.text: The developer account where the key was created
Every customer account that uses the integration
The production account selected during Go-Live
A Docusign-owned account managed by Docusign Support

answerText: The production account selected during Go-Live
explanation: The production key is tied to the production account selected during Go-Live (the OAuth management account), where its production OAuth settings are configured; the key can still make calls against other production accounts.

optionExplanations.A: The developer account manages only the demo version; production settings live in the production account.
optionExplanations.B: Customers can use the key, but it is managed by one production account.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The production account chosen during Go-Live manages the production key.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign does not manage the key for you; you select your own production account.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the production key belongs to the production account you selected. The trap is A: the developer account still manages the demo version of the key, but production settings are configured separately in the production account. B and D are wrong because a production key is managed by exactly one production account that you choose.

stem: An admin creates an organization-level Connect configuration, and the listener developer asks which message format to parse. What is the answer?

options.text: JSON SIM format; organization-level configurations always use it
Legacy XML, the default for organization-level configurations
XML aggregate mode, selected in Organization Admin
Whatever format each account's account-level configuration uses

answerText: JSON SIM format; organization-level configurations always use it
explanation: All organization-level Connect configurations use the JSON SIM model, so the listener must parse JSON SIM messages.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Organization-level configurations always use JSON SIM.
optionExplanations.B: Legacy XML is not available for organization-level configurations.
optionExplanations.C: Aggregate mode is a legacy XML option for account and envelope level only.
optionExplanations.D: An org-level configuration has its own format, always JSON SIM, regardless of account-level settings.

whyNotOthers: A is right because org-level Connect supports only JSON SIM. The trap is D: account-level configurations can use legacy formats, but that setting does not carry over to an org-level configuration. B and C name legacy options that exist only at account and envelope level.

stem: A tab uses anchorString 'Sign here:'. The signature field must appear slightly to the right of that text. Which properties shift the tab relative to the anchor?

options.text: xPosition and yPosition
anchorXOffset and anchorYOffset with anchorUnits
anchorIgnoreIfNotPresent
tabLabel and tabOrder

answerText: anchorXOffset and anchorYOffset with anchorUnits
explanation: anchorXOffset and anchorYOffset, measured in anchorUnits, move the tab relative to the anchor text. The clue is shifting relative to the anchor.

optionExplanations.A: xPosition and yPosition are absolute page coordinates used for fixed positioning.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anchor offsets in anchorUnits shift the tab relative to the anchor text.
optionExplanations.C: anchorIgnoreIfNotPresent handles a missing anchor string; it does not shift the tab.
optionExplanations.D: tabLabel and tabOrder identify and order tabs; they do not set a position relative to text.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the anchor offsets position the tab relative to the found text. The trap is A: xPosition and yPosition also move tabs, but they are absolute page coordinates for fixed positioning, not offsets from the anchor. C controls what happens when the anchor text is missing and D names and orders tabs.

stem: An implementation note covers remote signers who must be redirected to a custom page after finishing. Which branding feature is relevant?

options.text: Branding signing resource file
Brand destination URLs
Brand logo and color settings
returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient

answerText: Brand destination URLs
explanation: Among branding settings, the post-signing redirect for remote signers is the destination URLs setting.

optionExplanations.A: Resource files are part of a brand too, but they change the signing UI text and appearance, not the post-signing redirect.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Destination URLs are the brand setting that controls where remote signers are sent after signing events.
optionExplanations.C: Logos and colors change the look of emails and signing pages; they do not redirect anyone.
optionExplanations.D: returnUrl is not a branding feature and applies to embedded signing only.

whyNotOthers: B is right because destination URLs are the brand setting for remote-signer redirects. The trap is A: it is also a brand setting that affects the signing experience, but it controls content and appearance. C and D fail because logos and colors are visual only and returnUrl is an embedded-signing parameter, not branding.

stem: A bank workflow will show participants a web form pre-filled with their account details from the system of record. Those details must not be shown until the participant's identity is confirmed. Which order fits?

options.text: Collect Data with Web Forms, then Verify Someone's Identity
Verify Someone's Identity, then Collect Data with Web Forms
Send Documents for Signature with an access code, then the web form
A Show a Confirmation Screen warning, then the web form

answerText: Verify Someone's Identity, then Collect Data with Web Forms
explanation: Placing the identity step before the web form verifies the participant before any sensitive pre-filled data is displayed.

optionExplanations.A: The pre-filled form would show account data before identity is verified.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Verify identity first, then show the pre-filled form.
optionExplanations.C: An access code on a signing step does not protect the earlier form.
optionExplanations.D: A warning screen does not verify identity.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the clue is that pre-filled data must stay hidden until identity is confirmed. The trap is A: collecting data first is the usual order, but here the form already shows sensitive data, so verification must come before it. C relies on an access code for a different step, and D only warns the user.

stem: An ISV that is not yet a Docusign partner submits a PUBLIC extension app for review. What happens?

options.text: The app is rejected immediately and must be resubmitted as private
Docusign contacts the ISV about partner onboarding; the app stays In Review until done
