The app is published right away because partner status is checked later
The app is published only in the developer's own region

answerText: Docusign contacts the ISV about partner onboarding; the app stays In Review until done
explanation: Only Docusign partners may publish public apps. Docusign verifies partner status during review and, if needed, works with the developer on partner onboarding while the app stays In Review.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign does not reject it outright; it contacts the developer about joining the partner program.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Partner status is verified during review, and the app remains In Review until onboarding completes.
optionExplanations.C: Partner status is verified during review, before publication, not afterwards.
optionExplanations.D: There is no region fallback for non-partners; regions are a separate publicationRegions setting.

whyNotOthers: B is right because partner status is checked during review and onboarding happens before publication. The trap is A: Docusign does not simply reject the app; it starts partner onboarding. C ignores the partner requirement, and D invents a region-based fallback.

stem: Knowledge check: an app only needs to send envelopes and read user account information. What should the developer do when requesting OAuth consent?

options.text: Request every scope now so users never see a second consent screen
Request impersonation so the app can act as any user later
Copy the scopes used in the Docusign quickstart sample
Request only the minimum scopes required for those operations

answerText: Request only the minimum scopes required for those operations
explanation: Least-privilege scope selection lowers risk and keeps the consent request limited to what the app actually does.

optionExplanations.A: Asking for every scope breaks least privilege and asks users to approve access the app does not need.
optionExplanations.B: impersonation is for JWT service integrations and widens what the app can do without need.
optionExplanations.C: Sample scopes are chosen for the sample; they may not match this app's operations.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Request only the scopes needed to send envelopes and read account info.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the app's needs are narrow and least privilege applies. The trap is A: avoiding repeat consent sounds user-friendly, but it grants access the app never uses. B adds impersonation that a signed-in user flow does not need, and C copies scopes chosen for a sample, not this app.

stem: Two separate integrations on the same production account each make about 2,000 API calls per hour. What happens?

options.text: Each integration key has its own 3,000-call hourly limit, so both are fine
Together they exceed the 3,000 calls per hour shared by the account, so calls are blocked
Excess calls are queued and processed at the start of the next hour
Only the burst limit applies to production accounts, so the hourly total does not matter

answerText: Together they exceed the 3,000 calls per hour shared by the account, so calls are blocked
explanation: The default hourly limit is 3,000 calls per account, shared by all integrations; once it is exceeded, calls are blocked until the next hour.

optionExplanations.A: The hourly limit is per account and shared by all integration keys.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. 4,000 combined calls exceed the 3,000 per hour account limit, so further calls are blocked.
optionExplanations.C: Excess calls are rejected, not queued, until the hour resets.
optionExplanations.D: Hourly and burst limits both apply in production.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the limit is per account, so 4,000 combined calls exceed it. The trap is A: it would be true if the limit were per integration key, but it is shared across all apps on the account. C is wrong because excess calls fail rather than queue, and D ignores that hourly and burst limits both apply.

stem: A security policy requires the listener to verify Docusign's client certificate during the TLS handshake before accepting any Connect message. Which control helps validate message authenticity this way?

options.text: A self-signed server certificate on the listener
Basic authentication with a shared password
HMAC signature validation of the message body
Mutual TLS between Docusign and the listener

answerText: Mutual TLS between Docusign and the listener
explanation: Mutual TLS has Docusign present a client certificate that the listener verifies during the handshake, which is the check the policy demands.

optionExplanations.A: A server certificate identifies the listener, not Docusign.
optionExplanations.B: Basic auth sends a username and password header; no client certificate is involved.
optionExplanations.C: HMAC verifies the body with a shared key after the connection is made, not a TLS client certificate.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Mutual TLS lets the listener verify Docusign's client certificate.

whyNotOthers: D is right because only mutual TLS authenticates Docusign at the TLS layer with a certificate. The trap is C: HMAC also proves authenticity, but it checks a hash of the body after the connection is accepted, not a client certificate in the handshake. A secures only the listener side, and B uses a password header rather than a certificate.

stem: During QA, a test signer still receives a Docusign email invitation, but the requirement is to sign inside the app. What is missing from the signer definition?

options.text: clientUserId
recipientId
routingOrder
EnvelopeViews:createRecipient

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: Without clientUserId the signer is a remote recipient and gets an email invitation. Adding clientUserId makes the signer embedded.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. clientUserId on the signer makes it embedded instead of an emailed remote recipient.
optionExplanations.B: recipientId is required for every recipient and does not change remote signing to embedded.
optionExplanations.C: routingOrder controls signing order; it does not decide whether a signer is embedded.
optionExplanations.D: createRecipient is an API call made after the envelope exists, not part of the signer definition.

whyNotOthers: A is right because clientUserId turns a remote signer into an embedded one. The trap is D: the app will also need to call createRecipient, but that is an endpoint and cannot be added to the signer definition. B and C exist for remote signers too and do not change how the signer is invited.

stem: A signer-provided value must be checked against an external data source while the signer completes the envelope. Which feature is designed for this?

options.text: Connected Fields (data verification extension)
Web Forms formValues prefill
A Data IO extension
Connect extension-executed event

answerText: Connected Fields (data verification extension)
explanation: Verification of signer-entered values during signing is what Connected Fields provide.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Connected Fields run the extension's verify action when the signer completes the required fields.
optionExplanations.B: formValues prefill known data into a web form; they do not verify what a signer enters during signing.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO serves Maestro workflows (read/write a system of record), not field verification during eSignature signing.
optionExplanations.D: This event only reports verification results to your listener after the fact.

whyNotOthers: A is right because Connected Fields verify field values against an external source during signing. The trap is B: it also uses external data, but it fills in values before the form is shown and does not verify signer input. C and D fail because Data IO is a Maestro extension and the Connect event only reports results.

stem: Before the web form step, a workflow must pull the customer's existing account data from Salesforce so the form can be pre-filled. Which step should be used?

options.text: A Read step from the installed Salesforce extension app, placed before Collect Data with Web Forms
A Writeback step to Salesforce, placed after signing
Connected fields added to the web form
A Send an Email step asking the sales rep for the data

answerText: A Read step from the installed Salesforce extension app, placed before Collect Data with Web Forms
explanation: Read steps import data from external systems such as Salesforce into the workflow, so they must run before the form that uses the data.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A Read step imports the Salesforce data before the form needs it.
optionExplanations.B: Writeback sends data to Salesforce; it does not import it, and it runs too late.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.D: Emailing a rep is manual and does not fill the form automatically.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it brings the data into the workflow before the form. The trap is B: a Salesforce writeback step uses the same app, but it pushes data to Salesforce after the fact, the opposite direction. C is not supported in Maestro, and D is a manual workaround.

stem: In an extension app manifest, which object lists, for each extension, the actions that implement it?

options.text: extensions, through actionReferences
actions, through connectionsReference
connections
publisher

answerText: extensions, through actionReferences
explanation: Each extension in the extensions object uses actionReferences to name the actions that implement it.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Extensions reference their implementing actions through actionReferences.
optionExplanations.B: connectionsReference links an action to a connection, the next link in the chain, not extension-to-action.
optionExplanations.C: connections defines authentication; it does not list actions.
optionExplanations.D: publisher holds organization name and contact details shown in the listing.

whyNotOthers: A is right because actionReferences links an extension to its actions. The trap is B: connectionsReference lives on actions and links them to a connection, not to an extension. C holds authentication settings, and D holds publisher contact details.

stem: A corporate web portal lets employees sign in individually to send internal NDAs. The integration server is secured and can safely store client credentials. Which authentication flow should be implemented?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Implicit Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Individual interactive sign-in plus a secure server that can store a secret is Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Interactive users plus a server that can hold a secret means Confidential Authorization Code Grant.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is for unattended service integrations, but here each employee signs in individually.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant is a legacy browser flow that Docusign does not recommend, and the server here can store secrets.
optionExplanations.D: Public Auth Code Grant is for clients that cannot store a secret, such as SPAs or mobile apps; this server can.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the deciding clue is that the server can safely store credentials. The trap is D: Public Auth Code also signs in individual users, but it exists for clients that cannot store a secret; if the server could not, the answer would flip to D. B has no interactive user, and C is a legacy browser flow.

stem: A Confidential Authorization Code Grant app worked in demo but returns authentication errors right after Go-Live. What should be checked first?

options.text: That the production key has its secret and redirect URIs, and the app uses account.docusign.com
That the app still sends the developer secret, since secrets are copied with the key
That the hourly API limit was raised for the production account
That all templates were recreated in the production account

answerText: That the production key has its secret and redirect URIs, and the app uses account.docusign.com
explanation: Authentication errors right after Go-Live usually come from missing production OAuth settings (secret, redirect URIs) or from still using the developer authentication host.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Check the production secret, redirect URIs and the production authentication host first.
optionExplanations.B: Secrets are not copied during Go-Live, so the developer secret fails in production.
optionExplanations.C: Rate limits cause blocked calls, not authentication failures.
optionExplanations.D: Missing templates produce template errors after authentication, not authentication errors.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the clue is authentication errors, which point to OAuth configuration. The trap is B: the key value is the same in production, but secrets are not copied, so the developer secret does not work. C relates to throttling, not authentication, and D would cause template errors, not authentication errors.

stem: A listener processes each payload synchronously for about two minutes before replying, and the Connect logs show many retried deliveries. What should the developer change?

options.text: Keep synchronous processing but always return 200 at the end
Pause the Connect configuration during peak hours
Return 200 immediately and process the payload asynchronously from a queue
Replace Connect with polling for slow-processing envelopes

answerText: Return 200 immediately and process the payload asynchronously from a queue
explanation: Slow responses time out and count as failures, so the listener should acknowledge with 200 right away and do the work asynchronously.

optionExplanations.A: A 200 that arrives after slow processing can still time out and trigger retries.
optionExplanations.B: Pausing defers deliveries; it does not fix the slow listener.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Acknowledge fast, queue the payload, and process it asynchronously.
optionExplanations.D: Polling adds API calls and is limited to once per 15 minutes per envelope.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a fast acknowledgement stops timeouts and the resulting retries. The trap is A: returning 200 is correct, but returning it only after two minutes of work still risks the timeout. B only delays the events, and D brings back the API traffic Connect avoids.

topic: Make an API call to request the signing URL
stem: After a successful Envelopes:create call for an embedded recipient, what is the next API step to start the signing session?

options.text: Redirect the user's browser to docusign.net/embedded.
Display the sending interface so the user can enter tab information.
Send an email notification with the signing link.
Make an API call to request the signing URL.

answerText: Make an API call to request the signing URL.
explanation: The app calls the recipient view endpoint (EnvelopeViews:createRecipient) to get a short-lived signing URL, then redirects the embedded user to it.

optionExplanations.A: There is no fixed embedded URL; each session URL is generated by the API.
optionExplanations.B: A sending interface is embedded sending, used to prepare an envelope, not to sign it.
optionExplanations.C: Emailing a link is remote signing; embedded signers sign through a URL the app requests.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The app requests the signing URL with EnvelopeViews:createRecipient and redirects the user.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the signing URL must be requested from the API for each session. The trap is B: showing a sending interface is embedded sending (createSender), which prepares an envelope rather than signing it. A is not a real fixed URL and C describes remote signing.

stem: A company wants recipients redirected to a contact page after completing remote signing. Which option controls where recipients are redirected after signing?

options.text: Branding Resource File
Brand Destination URLs
Custom Landing pages
In-Session Landing pages

answerText: Brand Destination URLs
explanation: For remote signing, the redirect after completion is configured with brand destination URLs.

optionExplanations.A: Resource files customize the signing and email experience (text and appearance); they do not define the redirect destination.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Brand destination URLs configure where remote-signing recipients are redirected after they finish.
optionExplanations.C: This is not the brand setting Docusign uses for post-signing redirects; the documented control is destination URLs.
optionExplanations.D: In-session (embedded) signing redirects are set with returnUrl, and this is not the remote-signing redirect setting.

whyNotOthers: B is right because destination URLs are the brand setting that controls redirects after remote signing. The trap is A: it is a real brand component that customizes the signing experience, but it does not set where the recipient goes. C and D fail because they are not the documented remote-signing redirect setting.

stem: After the Send Documents for Signature step, the agreement must be stored in Google Drive only if the envelope is completed; otherwise the HR representative must be notified. Which design fits?

options.text: A Store Files step directly after signing, with no condition
A Connect webhook that calls custom code to decide
A Multi Branch Rule step on the Job Location field
A Branching Rule on envelope status = completed: true stores the file, false sends an email

answerText: A Branching Rule on envelope status = completed: true stores the file, false sends an email
explanation: A Branching Rule on the envelope status routes completed envelopes to a Store Files step and others to a Send an Email step, as in the course onboarding example.

optionExplanations.A: Stores unconditionally and never notifies HR when signing is not completed.
optionExplanations.B: Custom code is unnecessary; the branching rule handles the condition natively.
optionExplanations.C: Job Location is not the condition; envelope status is.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Branch on envelope status: completed goes to storage, otherwise HR is emailed.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the condition is the envelope status, with two outcomes. The trap is A: it uses the right storage step, but without a condition it never notifies HR when the envelope is not completed. B moves the logic into custom code, and C branches on the wrong field.

stem: After a developer submits an extension app for review from the Developer Console, what does Docusign's review evaluate?

options.text: Whether the app has made at least 20 successful API calls
The business, technical, security and functional aspects of the app
The developer's envelope usage fees
Whether the app uses the most recent SDK version

answerText: The business, technical, security and functional aspects of the app
explanation: The extension app review evaluates the business, technical, security and functional aspects of the app.

optionExplanations.A: The 20 API call threshold is an eSignature go-live requirement, not extension app review.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Review covers business, technical, security and functional aspects.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope fees are billing matters, not part of app review.
optionExplanations.D: SDK version is not a review criterion for extension apps.

whyNotOthers: B is right because those are the review areas. The trap is A: the 20-call requirement belongs to eSignature integration key go-live, not extension app review. C and D are not review criteria.

stem: In a pull request review, the code hard-codes https://demo.docusign.net/restapi as the API base path. The reviewer asks the developer to look up the base URI and account ID after getting the token instead. Which endpoint should the code call?

options.text: /oauth/token
/oauth/auth
/oauth/userinfo
Use account-d.docusign.com as the REST API base URI

answerText: /oauth/userinfo
explanation: The code should call /oauth/userinfo and use the default account's base_uri and account_id, because accounts can live on different base URIs.

optionExplanations.A: /oauth/token issues tokens; it does not report which base URI the account uses.
optionExplanations.B: /oauth/auth is the sign-in and consent URL, not an account lookup.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. /oauth/userinfo returns base_uri and account_id for the user's accounts.
optionExplanations.D: account-d.docusign.com hosts the demo OAuth service, not eSignature REST API calls.

whyNotOthers: C is right because userinfo returns the correct base URI per account. The trap is D: account-d.docusign.com is the demo authentication server where userinfo lives, but it is not the REST API base URI. A and B are earlier steps of the OAuth flow.

stem: Which sequence matches the main steps of the Docusign Go-Live process described in the course?

options.text: Make 20 API calls, request review, wait for the approval email
Request a production account, open a support case, copy the key manually
Submit to Go Live, create the key in production, then request a production account
Create your integration, request a production account, submit your integration to Go Live

answerText: Create your integration, request a production account, submit your integration to Go Live
explanation: The course lists three main steps: create your integration, request a production account, and submit your integration to Go Live.

optionExplanations.A: The 20 API call step was removed from the Go-Live process.
optionExplanations.B: eSignature Go-Live uses Start Go live in Apps and Keys, and the key is duplicated for you.
optionExplanations.C: You need the integration and a production account before you submit to Go Live.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Create the integration, request a production account, then submit to Go Live.

whyNotOthers: D is right because it lists the three steps in the course order. The trap is A: it reflects the old process, but the 20 API call requirement no longer exists. B adds a support case and manual copy that eSignature Go-Live does not use, and C reverses the order, since you need a production account before submitting.

stem: A support team needs a clear rule: what should a Connect listener do when it receives a duplicate webhook message?

options.text: Treat every message as new and create a new record
Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
Ask Docusign to turn off retries for the account
Republish all events daily to resynchronize

answerText: Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
explanation: Webhook listeners must tolerate retries and duplicate delivery by processing idempotently.

optionExplanations.A: Treating repeats as new events creates duplicate records.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Skip or safely reapply events already processed.
optionExplanations.C: Retries protect against lost events; disabling them is not the fix for duplicates.
optionExplanations.D: Daily republishing creates more duplicate deliveries, not fewer.

whyNotOthers: B is right because idempotency turns duplicates into no-ops. The trap is C: removing retries would stop duplicates but would also lose events whenever the listener fails, which is why retries exist. A creates duplicate records, and D generates even more duplicates.

stem: A createRecipient request for an embedded signer is being written. Which set of values does it require?

options.text: recipientId and routingOrder only
envelopeId in the body and the signer's email only
email, userName and clientUserId plus frameAncestors for every view
email, userName and clientUserId matching the envelope, plus returnUrl and authenticationMethod

answerText: email, userName and clientUserId matching the envelope, plus returnUrl and authenticationMethod
explanation: The recipient view request needs email, userName and clientUserId that match the signer, plus returnUrl and authenticationMethod.

optionExplanations.A: recipientId and routingOrder are not the values the recipient view request matches on.
optionExplanations.B: envelopeId goes in the URL path, and email alone does not identify the embedded signer.
optionExplanations.C: frameAncestors (with messageOrigins) is needed only for focused view, not for every recipient view.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Matching email, userName and clientUserId plus returnUrl and authenticationMethod are required.

whyNotOthers: D is right because those are the required parameters for a recipient view. The trap is C: frameAncestors is required only for focused view, not for every view. A and B omit the matching recipient details the endpoint relies on.

stem: Daniel's compliance system needs the personal information and document details captured during signers' ID Verification. The account admin has enabled retention of this data. Which API should the integration call?

options.text: IdentityVerifications:list
The Connect envelope-completed payload
Envelopes:get on the completed envelope
ID Evidence API

answerText: ID Evidence API
explanation: Admin-enabled retention plus retrieving captured IDV data points to the ID Evidence API.

optionExplanations.A: This returns IDV workflow configurations for sending, not the data captured during verification.
optionExplanations.B: The envelope event does not include retained ID verification data.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope details show status and recipients, not the retained ID evidence.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Once the admin configures retention, the ID Evidence API returns the selected data from ID verification events.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the ID Evidence API retrieves the IDV data the admin chose to retain. The trap is A: it is the IDV call developers already know, but it lists workflows, not results. B and C fail because neither the Connect envelope payload nor envelope details contain ID evidence.

stem: Leasing agents inside the company start a rental application workflow for an approved tenant from the Docusign web app, entering the tenant's name and email when they start it. Which start method fits?

options.text: From a link
From an API call
Manually in Docusign (Run Workflow)
Started by a Connect event

answerText: Manually in Docusign (Run Workflow)
explanation: Manually in Docusign is for workflows started by someone in the organization, who uses Run Workflow and fills in participant details, similar to sending from a template. Users need Workflows: Prepare permission.

optionExplanations.A: Links suit self-service starts by participants, not internal agents entering tenant details.
optionExplanations.B: No custom integration is involved; agents work in the Docusign web app.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Internal users with Workflows: Prepare permission use Run Workflow and enter participant details.
optionExplanations.D: A Connect event is a notification, not how agents start this workflow.

whyNotOthers: C is right because internal staff start it from Docusign and enter participant details. The trap is A: From a link also starts workflows without code, but it is for participants who start the workflow themselves, such as self-service forms. B needs an integration calling the API, and D is not how this process starts.

stem: An extension app manifest will call a CRM API that requires OAuth. The developer wants authentication defined once and reused by several actions. Which manifest object owns those reusable auth settings?

options.text: connections
connectionsReference
actions
extensions

answerText: connections
explanation: The connections object defines reusable authentication settings; actions point to it.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. connections defines reusable authentication for actions.
optionExplanations.B: connectionsReference only points to a connection; it does not own the auth settings.
optionExplanations.C: actions describe operations and reference a connection; they do not own reusable auth.
optionExplanations.D: extensions declare extension types and their actionReferences, not auth.

whyNotOthers: A is right because connections own the auth configuration. The trap is B: connectionsReference is the pointer on each action, not the place where credentials are defined. C defines operations and D groups actions by extension type.

stem: A partner's native app cannot store a client secret securely, and each user signs in. Which OAuth configuration is correct?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant without PKCE
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: Public clients use the Authorization Code Grant with PKCE; the code_challenge and code_verifier prove that the app finishing the flow is the one that started it.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant needs a client secret that a native app cannot keep.
optionExplanations.B: Right grant family, but Docusign requires code_challenge and code_verifier for all Public Auth Code Grant implementations.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE is the configuration for a native app without a secret.
optionExplanations.D: JWT Grant is for unattended services, not a native app where users sign in.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a native app is a public client and PKCE is required for every Public Auth Code Grant implementation. The trap is B: it is the right grant family, but without PKCE nothing replaces the missing secret to protect the code exchange. A needs a secret, and D is for services with no user present.

stem: A company builds an integration only for its own HR and legal staff. A separate vendor builds an app that many Docusign customers install and connect to their own Docusign accounts. Which detail decides that the vendor app is a Public integration?

options.text: It is used by many Docusign customers through their own Docusign accounts
It authenticates with JWT Grant instead of Authorization Code Grant
It sends envelopes created from server templates
It makes more than 3,000 API calls per hour

answerText: It is used by many Docusign customers through their own Docusign accounts
explanation: Classification is determined by the business model; an app used by many Docusign customers who authorize it against their own accounts is a Public integration.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Use by many customers through their own Docusign accounts makes it a Public integration.
optionExplanations.B: The OAuth grant type does not determine the integration type.
optionExplanations.C: Using templates says nothing about who uses the app or through which accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Call volume affects API limits, not the classification.

whyNotOthers: A is right because classification follows who uses the app and through which accounts. The trap is B: the OAuth flow is an important design choice, but it does not determine the classification. C and D describe technical behavior that both apps could share.

stem: A webhook listener only needs envelopeId, status and event timing. The team will call the API later if it needs documents or detailed metadata. Which Connect payload choice best supports that design?

options.text: Include every available document and recipient field
Configure the event payload to include only needed data
Switch to polling every minute
Use legacy XML aggregate mode to shrink each message

answerText: Configure the event payload to include only needed data
explanation: Connect payloads should be minimized to the data the listener needs, especially when the app can query details later.

optionExplanations.A: Including all fields and documents makes payloads large and slow to process.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Include only the data the listener needs and query the rest later.
optionExplanations.C: Polling every minute violates the once-per-15-minutes-per-envelope limit and loses event-driven delivery.
optionExplanations.D: Aggregate mode reduces message count, not message size, and is a legacy XML option.

whyNotOthers: B is right because a minimal event payload matches what the listener uses. The trap is D: aggregate mode reduces how many messages arrive, but each legacy XML message is envelope-focused and not smaller. A inflates every message, and C abandons Connect and breaks the polling limit.

stem: Users report expired-link errors because the app creates embedded signing URLs long before they are ready. What is the right fix?

options.text: Cache the URL and reuse it for later sessions
Increase the envelope expiration setting
Request the recipient view URL only when the user is ready to sign
Create the envelope with status created instead of sent

answerText: Request the recipient view URL only when the user is ready to sign
explanation: Signing URLs are short-lived and single-use, so the app should call createRecipient at the moment the user is ready, and request a new URL for each session.

optionExplanations.A: Signing URLs are single-use and short-lived, so reusing a cached URL fails.
optionExplanations.B: Envelope expiration controls how long the envelope stays open, not the signing URL lifetime.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Generate the recipient view URL only when the user is ready to sign.
optionExplanations.D: A draft envelope cannot be signed; embedded signing needs a sent envelope.

whyNotOthers: C is right because generating the URL on demand avoids its short lifetime. The trap is B: envelope expiration is a real setting, but it controls the envelope, not the minutes-long signing URL. A fails because the URL is single-use and D would leave a draft that cannot be signed.

stem: Grace reviews an integration that embeds a Docusign web form in a records portal. Which pairing of URL source and client-side tool is correct?

options.text: Docusign JS with a signing URL from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
A URL from Configurations:getForm
Docusign JS with the instance URL from Instances:createInstance
The formValues returned by Instances:getInstance

answerText: Docusign JS with the instance URL from Instances:createInstance
explanation: Embedded web forms are rendered by passing the createInstance instance URL to Docusign JS.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign JS is right, but the URL is wrong: a recipient view URL is for an envelope, while an embedded web form uses the instance URL (its envelope is only created when the first user submits).
optionExplanations.B: Configurations:getForm returns the form configuration, including field names for prefill; it does not return a URL to render for a participant.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The instance URL from createInstance is what Docusign JS renders for an embedded web form.
optionExplanations.D: formValues are the submitted or prefilled data; they are read after the fact and are not a rendering URL.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the instance URL from createInstance is the URL that Docusign JS renders. The trap is A: it pairs the right SDK with the envelope signing URL, which belongs to embedded signing, not to a web form instance. B and D fail because getForm and getInstance return configuration details and form data, not a URL to display.

stem: A backend calls TriggerWorkflow successfully. What does the response give the app?

options.text: The envelope ID of the first signing step
The new instance ID and a workflow instance URL
The workflow's trigger_input_schema
A consentUrl for the participant

answerText: The new instance ID and a workflow instance URL
explanation: A successful TriggerWorkflow response returns the new instance's ID and a URL for the running instance, which the app can redirect to or embed.

optionExplanations.A: The response identifies the workflow instance, not an eSignature envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Use the instance ID with getWorkflowInstance and the URL to embed or redirect.
optionExplanations.C: The input schema comes from GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements, before triggering.
optionExplanations.D: consentUrl appears in publish errors for missing consent, not in a trigger response.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the app needs the instance ID to track status and the URL to show the workflow. The trap is A: workflows often send envelopes, but the trigger response identifies the workflow instance, not an envelope. C comes from GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements before the trigger, and D relates to consent errors when publishing.

stem: What value must an action's connectionsReference contain?

options.text: The name of the extension in the extensions object
The external provider's OAuth client ID
The name of a connection defined in the connections object
The action's own endpoint URL

answerText: The name of a connection defined in the connections object
explanation: connectionsReference names a connection defined in the connections object, so its value must match that connection's name.

optionExplanations.A: Extension names are used with actionReferences on the extension side, not in connectionsReference.
optionExplanations.B: The client ID is stored inside the connection, not in the reference.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. It must match the name of a connection in the connections object.
optionExplanations.D: The endpoint is part of the action definition, not the connection reference.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the reference resolves to a named connection. The trap is A: extensions are linked to actions through actionReferences, not through connectionsReference. B is a credential stored in the connection, and D is defined by the action itself.

stem: A sales contracting app gets an access token, but REST calls return 401 Unauthorized. Where should the access token be supplied?

options.text: In the Authorization header as a Bearer token
In the Authorization header as Bearer <authorization code>
In the state parameter of the request
In a browser cookie set by the app

answerText: In the Authorization header as a Bearer token
explanation: Docusign REST calls use Authorization: Bearer <access_token>.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Supply the access token as Authorization: Bearer <access_token>.
optionExplanations.B: The authorization code must be exchanged at /oauth/token for an access token; it cannot call APIs.
optionExplanations.C: state protects the sign-in redirect against CSRF; it does not carry API credentials.
optionExplanations.D: Docusign REST APIs do not read the token from cookies; use the Authorization header.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the access token goes in a Bearer Authorization header. The trap is B: it uses the right header format, but the authorization code is only exchanged at /oauth/token and expires after 120 seconds. C is a CSRF value used during sign-in, and D is not read by the API.

stem: A production app calls userinfo before every single API request to look up the account's base URI. What does Docusign recommend instead?

options.text: Call userinfo for every request, because base URIs change often
Get base_uri once when the user first authenticates and cache it
Read the base URI from the developer account's Apps and Keys page
Skip userinfo and derive the base URI from the integration key

answerText: Get base_uri once when the user first authenticates and cache it
explanation: Docusign recommends getting base_uri from userinfo once when the user first authenticates and caching it, because accounts move between base URIs infrequently.

optionExplanations.A: Base URIs change infrequently, so calling userinfo for every request wastes calls.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Retrieve base_uri once at first authentication and cache it.
optionExplanations.C: The developer account shows the demo base URI, not the production account's base URI.
optionExplanations.D: The integration key does not identify the account's server; userinfo does.

whyNotOthers: B is right because base URIs rarely change and can be cached for a day or more. The trap is A: calling userinfo is correct, but doing it on every request is wasteful since base URIs change infrequently. C gives the demo value, and D is wrong because the integration key does not encode the account's server.

stem: A sender needs webhook events for a single API-sent envelope only, and the setting must not carry over to the next envelope the app sends. Which approach matches Docusign platform behavior?

options.text: An account-level Connect configuration for the sending user
An organization-level Connect configuration
A scheduled Envelopes:get call for that envelope
Add an eventNotification object to the Envelopes:create request

answerText: Add an eventNotification object to the Envelopes:create request
explanation: Envelope-level Connect is configured per envelope and must be set again on the next envelope, which matches the requirement that the setting not carry over.

optionExplanations.A: Account-level configurations are configured once and used until disabled, so they would also cover later envelopes.
optionExplanations.B: Organization-level configurations persist and cover all or selected accounts in the org.
optionExplanations.C: Scheduled Envelopes:get calls are polling; they add API traffic and are limited to once per 15 minutes per envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. eventNotification applies only to the envelope created with it and must be reconfigured for the next envelope.

whyNotOthers: D is right because eventNotification lives on one envelope and does not persist. The trap is A: account-level configurations are configured once and stay active until disabled, so they would apply to the next envelope too. B also persists and spans accounts, and C is polling rather than a webhook.

stem: Guidance for an embedded sending feature must say what state the envelope needs before the app requests the sender view. What should it recommend?

options.text: Status sent, so recipients are already notified
Status created (draft)
Status delivered
Status completed

answerText: Status created (draft)
explanation: EnvelopeViews:createSender is used on a draft envelope, created with status created, so the user can tag and send it in the app.

optionExplanations.A: A sent envelope has already gone to recipients, so there is nothing left to prepare and send.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Embedded sending starts from a draft envelope created with status created.
optionExplanations.C: delivered is set by Docusign when a recipient opens the envelope; it is not a preparation state.
optionExplanations.D: completed is a terminal status after all recipients finish.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the sender view prepares an envelope that has not been sent. The trap is A: sent is the usual create value, but a sent envelope is already out and cannot go through embedded preparation. C and D are statuses Docusign sets after recipients act.

stem: An API-driven intake flow creates one embedded web form instance per customer record. Which value should be supplied so that instances can be correlated back to the app's records?

options.text: The web form configuration formId
clientUserId
A brandId
The returnUrl

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: The value that ties each instance to one record in your app is clientUserId.

optionExplanations.A: formId identifies the configuration all instances are created from, so it is shared across customers.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. clientUserId is the developer-supplied identifier of the user in your system, required for embedded instances.
optionExplanations.C: brandId only selects branding for the envelope; it does not identify a customer.
optionExplanations.D: returnUrl controls where the user goes after the session; it is not an identifier.

whyNotOthers: B is right because clientUserId is the per-user identifier supplied on createInstance. The trap is A: a configuration ID sounds like a tracking key, but it is the same for every instance of the form. C and D fail because they control branding and redirect, not identity.

stem: A workflow with a Google Drive Store Files step runs in a new Docusign account. Instances fail at that step with an error that the app is unavailable, while all earlier steps succeed. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Google Drive extension app is not installed and authorized in that account
The Branching Rule before signing is in the wrong order
The integration's token lacks the aow_manage scope
Connect is not configured for JSON SIM

answerText: The Google Drive extension app is not installed and authorized in that account
explanation: Extension app steps rely on apps that an administrator has installed and authorized in the account. Runtime errors at an app step often trace to an uninstalled or unauthorized extension.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Install and authorize the Google Drive extension app in this account.
optionExplanations.B: Step order affects routing; it does not make an app unavailable.
optionExplanations.C: aow_manage governs Maestro API calls, and earlier steps already run fine.
optionExplanations.D: Connect settings affect event delivery, not step execution.

whyNotOthers: A is right because only the app step fails, and the error names the app. The trap is C: missing aow_manage is a common error, but it blocks API calls to the Maestro API, not the execution of one step inside a running instance. B would change routing, not cause an app error, and D only affects notifications.

stem: A government agency must confirm the validity of a U.S. Social Security Number entered in an envelope, using a standard verification type at the eSignature Add Fields view and signing. Which extension type fits?

options.text: Data IO
File IO
Data Verification (SSN verification)
Connected Fields

answerText: Data Verification (SSN verification)
explanation: SSN verification is one of the Data Verification extensions, which verify specific standard data types at the Add Fields view and signing.

optionExplanations.A: Data IO reads and writes records in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.B: File IO stores documents.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. SSN verification is a Data Verification extension for a standard data type.
optionExplanations.D: Connected fields verify custom values against your system of record, not a standard SSN check.

whyNotOthers: C is right because SSN is a predefined standard type covered by Data Verification. The trap is D: connected fields use the same extension point but are for custom data verified against your own system of record. A runs in Maestro workflows, and B stores files.

stem: A portal team still uses a legacy flow that returns the access token directly in the browser redirect. Their app has a web server that can store a client secret, and users sign in interactively. Which flow should they move to?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant
Implicit Grant
Confidential Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Because the app has a server that can protect a secret and users sign in interactively, the recommended replacement is Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE replaces Implicit for SPAs that have no server; this app does have one that can keep a secret.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is for service integrations with no user present, while these users sign in interactively.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant is the legacy flow described in the stem and is not recommended.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Server that can store a secret plus interactive users means Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the deciding clue is the web server that can store a secret. The trap is A: Public Auth Code with PKCE is the usual replacement for Implicit in browser-only apps, but this app is not browser-only. B has no user sign-in, and C is the legacy flow they are leaving.

topic: In the Apps and Keys section of Docusign eSignature Adm
stem: Where do you specify allowed origins for an eSignature integration that implements CORS?

options.text: In the Apps and Keys section of Docusign eSignature Admin
In a separate CORS section of Docusign eSignature Admin
In the list of scopes requested when obtaining an access token
In the request headers of each API request

answerText: In the Apps and Keys section of Docusign eSignature Admin
explanation: Allowed CORS origins are part of the integration key's settings, configured in Apps and Keys together with authentication and redirect URIs.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. CORS origins are configured on the integration key in Apps and Keys.
optionExplanations.B: There is no standalone CORS section; origins are set on the integration key.
optionExplanations.C: Scopes control what the token may do, not which browser origins are allowed.
optionExplanations.D: The client cannot declare its own allowed origins; Docusign checks the configured allowlist.

whyNotOthers: A is right because CORS configuration is set on the integration key in Apps and Keys. The trap is B: it names the right product area, but there is no standalone CORS section; origins are configured under the key. C controls permissions, not origins, and D is wrong because Docusign enforces the configured allowlist, not values the client sends.

stem: An implementation note must tell developers how a contract system should track envelope status in production. Which design is preferred?

options.text: Poll Envelopes:get every few minutes for every open envelope
Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges continuously as the only status mechanism
Subscribe to Connect events; use listStatusChanges only for catch-up
Have users click a Refresh button that calls Envelopes:get

answerText: Subscribe to Connect events; use listStatusChanges only for catch-up
explanation: Docusign recommends Connect for status tracking, with Envelopes:listStatusChanges using overlapping time spans only to catch up on anything missed.

optionExplanations.A: Polling every few minutes per envelope exceeds the once-per-15-minutes limit.
optionExplanations.B: listStatusChanges is meant for catch-up; using it continuously is still a polling design.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect for real-time events, plus listStatusChanges with overlapping windows for catch-up.
optionExplanations.D: Manual refresh still polls the API and does not give timely status.

whyNotOthers: C is right because events arrive as they happen and polling is reserved for recovery. The trap is B: listStatusChanges is the right call for catch-up, but calling it continuously as the main mechanism is still polling. A breaks the 15-minute per-envelope polling limit, and D depends on manual refreshes that still poll.

stem: A developer is planning a bulk send with the eSignature API v2.1. Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Create a draft envelope, create a bulk send list, optionally test, then initiate the bulk send
Create a bulk send list, send the envelope with status sent, then attach the list
Initiate the bulk send, then create the bulk send list from the results
Create one envelope per recipient, then group them into a bulk send list

answerText: Create a draft envelope, create a bulk send list, optionally test, then initiate the bulk send
explanation: The bulk send process is: create a draft envelope, create a bulk send list, test the bulk send (optional), initiate the bulk send, and optionally check its status.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Draft envelope, bulk send list, optional test, then initiate the bulk send.
optionExplanations.B: Sending the envelope first delivers it to its own recipients; bulk send needs a draft source.
optionExplanations.C: The list must exist before the bulk send is initiated, since it supplies the recipients.
optionExplanations.D: Bulk Send creates the per-recipient envelopes itself; creating them manually defeats the purpose.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the list is applied to a draft envelope when the bulk send is initiated. The trap is B: it has the right building blocks, but sending the envelope with status sent delivers it instead of using it as the bulk send source. C reverses the order and D creates individual envelopes, which is what Bulk Send does for you.

stem: An envelope sent with eSignature REST API v2.1 must make the signer scan a passport before signing. What should the recipient configuration include?

options.text: identityVerification.workflowId of the ID verification workflow
identityVerification.workflowId of the phone authentication workflow
authenticationMethod on the createRecipient request
A clientUserId for embedded signing

answerText: identityVerification.workflowId of the ID verification workflow
explanation: A passport scan is ID verification, so the recipient needs the IDV workflow's workflowId.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The IDV workflow ID (from IdentityVerifications:list) in the recipient's identityVerification object enforces the document check.
optionExplanations.B: The mechanism is right, but the phone authentication workflow sends a code by call or SMS; it does not check a passport.
optionExplanations.C: This only records your app's authentication on the certificate; it does not enforce a passport check.
optionExplanations.D: clientUserId only makes the recipient embedded; it adds no identity check.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the IDV workflow is the one that verifies identity documents such as passports. The trap is B: phone authentication uses the same identityVerification.workflowId field, so the shape is right but the workflow is the wrong one. C and D fail because recording authenticationMethod enforces nothing and clientUserId only controls embedded signing.

stem: An app will embed workflow instances and pass starting variable values in the trigger_inputs object of TriggerWorkflow. Which start method does Docusign recommend for the workflow?

options.text: From a link
Manually in Docusign
Triggered from a CLM workflow
From an API call

answerText: From an API call
explanation: For integrations that pass starting variable values in trigger_inputs, Docusign recommends setting the start method to From an API call.

optionExplanations.A: Supported for embedding, but not the recommended method when passing trigger_inputs.
optionExplanations.B: Manual start is done by internal users in Docusign, not by an app.
optionExplanations.C: A CLM-triggered start runs from within Docusign CLM.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. From an API call is recommended when the app passes starting variables.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the app supplies starting variables through the API. The trap is A: From a link is also supported for embedded instances, but Docusign recommends From an API call when trigger_inputs carry starting values. B and C are designed to be started from within Docusign, not by an external app.

stem: A team's existing backend API works but does not match the format Docusign sends for extension actions. Why would they put an API proxy in front of it?

options.text: To let Docusign call the API without OAuth
To translate Docusign's request and response format without changing the backend
To let the app skip the App Center review
To cache completed envelope documents for Connect

answerText: To translate Docusign's request and response format without changing the backend
explanation: An API proxy transforms Docusign's request and response format to match the existing API, so the backend does not need to change.

optionExplanations.A: Authorization is still required; the extension app must be authorized with the platform or proxy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The proxy adapts formats so the existing backend can stay unchanged.
optionExplanations.C: A proxy has no effect on the review requirement.
optionExplanations.D: Connect and document caching are unrelated to an API proxy for extension actions.

whyNotOthers: B is right because translation without backend changes is the proxy's purpose. The trap is A: the app still authenticates through its connection (the proxy itself needs authorization). C is wrong because every app goes through review, and D confuses the proxy with Connect.

stem: A browser-only SPA cannot protect a client secret, and each user must authenticate individually. A developer proposes JWT Grant so users never see a login page. Which flow should the developer choose?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: Each user must authenticate individually in a client that cannot keep a secret, which is Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant needs a client secret that a browser-only app cannot protect.
optionExplanations.B: JWT would put the RSA private key in the browser and would skip individual user authentication, which the requirement forbids.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Individual sign-in in a client without a secret is Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is legacy and not recommended for new or updated Docusign integrations.

whyNotOthers: C is right because users must sign in themselves and the SPA cannot hold a secret. The trap is B: JWT avoids a login page, but it needs a protected RSA private key (impossible in a browser) and does not authenticate the person at the keyboard. A needs a client secret, and D is legacy.

stem: After Go-Live, how can a team add its templates to the production account?

options.text: Create them in production with the eSignature web app or the eSignature REST API
They are added automatically when the integration key goes live
Attach them to the Go-Live request so the review copies them
Point the production app at the developer account's templates

answerText: Create them in production with the eSignature web app or the eSignature REST API
explanation: Users, templates and settings are added to the production account with Docusign Admin, the web app, or the eSignature REST API; Go-Live does not copy them.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Recreate or upload the templates in the production account by UI or API.
optionExplanations.B: Only the integration key is duplicated; templates are not.
optionExplanations.C: The Go-Live request selects a production account; it does not carry templates.
optionExplanations.D: Production calls work against production accounts; developer account templates are not reachable.

whyNotOthers: A is right because production data must be created in the production account. The trap is B: the key is duplicated automatically, which makes it easy to assume templates follow, but they do not. C is not part of the Go-Live request, and D fails because production calls cannot use developer account data.

stem: Which statement about Docusign Connect configuration levels is correct?

options.text: Account-level Connect is the only level that supports JSON SIM
Organization-level Connect always uses the JSON SIM format
Envelope-level Connect can be created from the eSignature Send page
Organization-level Connect supports legacy XML aggregate messages

answerText: Organization-level Connect always uses the JSON SIM format
explanation: Organization-level configurations always use the JSON SIM model; legacy XML and aggregate options exist only at account and envelope level.

optionExplanations.A: JSON SIM is supported at organization, account and envelope level.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. All organization-level configurations use JSON SIM.
optionExplanations.C: Envelope-level webhooks are API only; the Send page cannot create them.
optionExplanations.D: Legacy XML and aggregate mode are available only at account and envelope level.

whyNotOthers: B is right because org-level Connect is JSON SIM only. The trap is D: aggregate mode is a real legacy option, but only for account- and envelope-level configurations using XML. A is false because JSON SIM is supported at all three levels, and C is false because eventNotification can be set only through the API.

stem: A records office reviews a create-envelope request built with the template reference model (templateId plus templateRoles). The envelope must reach signers immediately. Which status should the request set?

options.text: created
voided
completed
sent

answerText: sent
explanation: Whatever the envelope model, status sent in the create request sends the envelope immediately. The clue is that it must reach signers immediately.

optionExplanations.A: created saves the envelope as a draft; nothing is delivered until the status is later changed to sent.
optionExplanations.B: voided is used to cancel an envelope that is already in process; it cannot be used to deliver a new one.
optionExplanations.C: completed is reached by Docusign after every recipient finishes; an integration does not set it on create.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. status sent tells Envelopes:create to send the envelope to recipients immediately.

whyNotOthers: D is right because sent is the status that delivers the envelope on creation, including with templateId and templateRoles. The trap is A: created is valid in the same request but only saves a draft. B cancels an in-process envelope and C is a terminal status Docusign sets after all recipients finish.

stem: A real-estate team's ticket says: before opening the envelope, the signer must type a code that Docusign texts to them. Which option implements this?

options.text: An access code on the recipient
The email verification extension (Verify.Version1.Email)
Docusign JS focused view
Phone authentication on the recipient

answerText: Phone authentication on the recipient
explanation: The clue is a code texted by Docusign before the envelope opens, which is phone authentication.

optionExplanations.A: An access code is a sender-defined secret shared out of band; Docusign does not text it.
optionExplanations.B: This extension verifies an email address value in a field or web form; it does not gate envelope access with a texted code.
optionExplanations.C: Focused view changes the embedded signing display and adds no authentication.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Phone authentication sends the code by SMS (or voice) and blocks access until it is entered.

whyNotOthers: D is right because phone authentication texts the code and requires it before access. The trap is A: it is the closest code-based method, but the sender chooses the code and delivers it separately. B and C fail because email verification validates field data and focused view only affects the signing UI.

stem: A customer wants its Maestro workflows to use a partner's Docusign extension app listed in the App Center. Who makes the app available to workflow designers, and where?

options.text: The developer registers it in the Developer Console under their own integration key
A designer uploads the app manifest into Workflow Builder
An account administrator installs it from Docusign App Center
A developer adds the partner's URL to a Connect configuration

answerText: An account administrator installs it from Docusign App Center
explanation: Administrators install extension apps from Docusign App Center and authorize them for the account. The app's steps then become available in Workflow Builder.

optionExplanations.A: The Developer Console is for building and registering extension apps, not installing partner apps.
optionExplanations.B: Designers do not upload manifests; they use apps already installed in the account.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An administrator installs and authorizes it from App Center.
optionExplanations.D: Connect delivers event notifications; it does not install apps.

whyNotOthers: C is right because installation is an admin action in App Center. The trap is A: the Developer Console is where extension apps are registered and tested by the app's builder, not where a customer installs a partner app. B is not how apps are added, and D configures event notifications.

stem: During testing, Docusign cannot reach an action endpoint running at http://localhost:3000 on the developer's laptop. What is the underlying problem?

options.text: Docusign's servers need a publicly reachable HTTPS endpoint
The action's connectionsReference is misspelled
The app must be published to the App Center before it can be tested
The laptop needs a CNAME DNS entry for apps.docusign.com

answerText: Docusign's servers need a publicly reachable HTTPS endpoint
explanation: Docusign calls extension endpoints from its own servers, so the endpoint must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS (directly, through a firewall allow-list, or via a proxy).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Docusign can only call an endpoint it can reach publicly over HTTPS.
optionExplanations.B: A misspelled reference would fail manifest validation, not network reachability.
optionExplanations.C: Apps are tested in the Developer Console before review and publishing.
optionExplanations.D: No DNS entry for Docusign domains is needed; the endpoint must be reachable.

whyNotOthers: A is right because localhost is not reachable from Docusign. The trap is B: a bad connectionsReference is a manifest validation problem, not a reachability one. C is false because apps are tested in the developer account before publishing, and D is not a requirement.

stem: A nightly service has an RSA key pair on its integration key. It signs an assertion containing iss (integration key), sub (user ID), and aud (account-d.docusign.com), and no person signs in. Which authentication model is appropriate?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: JSON Web Token Grant
explanation: Signing an assertion with an RSA private key using iss, sub, and aud claims is the JWT Grant flow for unattended services.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant uses a secret key and an authorization code from an interactive sign-in, not an RSA-signed assertion.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. An RSA-signed assertion with iss, sub, and aud claims is JWT Grant.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE uses a code_verifier and an interactive user, not an RSA assertion.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a legacy browser flow with no assertion and no server-side signing.

whyNotOthers: B is right because an RSA-signed assertion with iss, sub, and aud is how JWT Grant requests a token. The trap is A: Confidential Auth Code also runs on a server and uses integration key credentials, but it authenticates with a secret key and an authorization code from a user sign-in. C and D need a user in a browser.

stem: A business user asks whether the envelopes signed during development testing are legally binding. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Yes, all signed envelopes are legally binding in either environment
Yes, if a real person signed them with a real email address
Only after the key shows App is live do demo envelopes become binding
No; developer account envelopes are not binding, production envelopes are

answerText: No; developer account envelopes are not binding, production envelopes are
explanation: eSignature transactions captured with a developer account are not legally binding; once the integration moves to production, its transactions become legally binding.

optionExplanations.A: Developer account envelopes are never legally binding.
optionExplanations.B: Who signed does not matter; the developer environment is not legally binding.
optionExplanations.C: Going live affects production transactions only; earlier demo envelopes stay non-binding.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Developer envelopes are not legally binding; production envelopes are.

whyNotOthers: D is right because legal effect depends on the environment. The trap is C: Go-Live does make the integration's transactions binding, but only new production transactions, not the envelopes sent earlier in demo. A and B ignore that the developer environment never produces binding agreements.

topic: Connect subscription to the recipient-completed event
stem: A company's internal dashboard shows whether each individual recipient has signed an envelope. What is the most efficient way to obtain this status?

options.text: Connect subscription to the recipient-completed event
Polling request to the Envelopes: listStatus endpoint
Polling request to the EnvelopeRecipients: list endpoint
Connect subscription to the envelope-completed event

answerText: Connect subscription to the recipient-completed event
explanation: A Connect subscription to recipient-completed pushes a message as each recipient finishes, giving per-recipient status without polling.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. recipient-completed fires for each recipient who finishes, pushed by Connect.
optionExplanations.B: Polling Envelopes:listStatus wastes calls and gives envelope-level, not per-recipient, status.
optionExplanations.C: EnvelopeRecipients:list gives recipient status but only by polling, which is inefficient.
optionExplanations.D: envelope-completed fires only when every recipient is done, too coarse for per-recipient status.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the requirement is per-recipient status, delivered by webhook. The trap is D: envelope-completed is also a Connect event, but it fires only once the whole envelope is done, so it cannot show individual recipients' progress. B and C are polling calls that waste API calls, and B returns envelope-level status only.

stem: Signatures must be captured from within your application. What should be added to the eSignature REST API payload so recipients sign inside the application?

options.text: email property set to null
clientUserId property
emailSubject property
emailNotification property set to false

answerText: clientUserId property
explanation: Adding clientUserId marks the recipient as embedded, so they sign inside your app instead of through emailed remote signing.

optionExplanations.A: The recipient's email is still needed; it must match in the createRecipient request.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. clientUserId marks the recipient as embedded so signing happens in your app.
optionExplanations.C: emailSubject sets the subject line of the envelope email; it has nothing to do with embedding.
optionExplanations.D: emailNotification customizes recipient email settings; it does not make a recipient embedded.

whyNotOthers: B is right because clientUserId is the documented way to make a recipient embedded. The trap is D: it sounds like turning off email makes signing embedded, but emailNotification customizes email settings and does not make the signer embedded. A breaks the recipient (email is still required for createRecipient) and C is only the email subject line.

stem: A bank lets customers start account opening from its online banking portal: a Docusign web form collects information, some fields are pre-filled with known customer data, the experience stays inside the portal, and it ends in signing. Which approach fits?

options.text: Start the workflow 'From a link', pass data through the trigger URL to populate starting variables, and embed the workflow in the portal
Use 'From an API call', share a public Web Form URL, and pre-fill with query parameters built in the Web Forms builder
Use the 'Manually by someone in your organization' start method and step variables to pre-fill
Trigger by API, set signing to remote signing, and rely on Docusign Connect to pre-fill data

answerText: Start the workflow 'From a link', pass data through the trigger URL to populate starting variables, and embed the workflow in the portal
explanation: A link-started workflow lets the portal start it and pass starting-variable data for pre-fill, and embedding keeps the experience inside the portal.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The portal launches the workflow from a link, the starting variables carry the pre-fill data, and embedding keeps the customer in the portal.
optionExplanations.B: It mixes an API-triggered start with a shared public form link, which takes the customer out of the integrated experience and is not how start-variable pre-fill works.
optionExplanations.C: A manual start is run by someone in your organization, not by the customer from the portal.
optionExplanations.D: Remote signing sends the customer to email, and Connect only sends event notifications; it cannot pre-fill data.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it covers customer-initiated start, pre-fill through starting variables, and an embedded experience. The trap is B: it names real start methods and Web Forms features but sends the customer to a public form instead of pre-filling through starting variables. C fails because a manual start is internal, and D fails because remote signing leaves the portal and Connect does not pre-fill.

stem: A webhook listener must track Maestro workflow instances through events such as workflow-completed. Which Connect message format must be configured?

options.text: JSON SIM
JSON aggregated
XML SIM
XML aggregated

answerText: JSON SIM
explanation: Maestro workflow events (workflow-started, workflow-failed, workflow-completed) are only available with the JSON SIM event message format.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Maestro events are only available in JSON SIM.
optionExplanations.B: Aggregate JSON is a legacy envelope-focused format without workflow events.
optionExplanations.C: Individual XML messages are legacy and do not carry workflow events.
optionExplanations.D: Legacy aggregate XML does not deliver Maestro events.

whyNotOthers: A is right because workflow events are delivered only as JSON SIM. The trap is C: XML SIM also sends individual messages, but it is a legacy format and does not carry Maestro workflow events. B and D are aggregate formats, which are legacy and envelope-focused.

stem: In the extension app JSON manifest, which core object defines the authentication mechanism the app uses to access the external platform?

options.text: publisher
actions
connections
extensions

answerText: connections
explanation: The connections object defines the authentication (for example OAuth parameters) used to reach the external platform.

optionExplanations.A: publisher holds organization and contact details.
optionExplanations.B: Actions use a connection through connectionsReference; they do not define auth.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. connections defines how the app authenticates to the external platform.
optionExplanations.D: extensions declare extension types and actionReferences, not authentication.

whyNotOthers: C is right because connections hold the auth configuration. The trap is B: actions call the platform but only reference a connection for auth. A is publisher contact information and D lists extension types and their actions.

stem: A company built its own internal JWT integration (the integration key is owned by its organization). It has Access Management and a claimed domain and wants one action to consent for all users in that domain. What should it do?

options.text: Grant admin consent in Docusign Admin > Connected Apps > Authorize Application
Use admin consent for external applications (scope=openid plus admin_consent_scope)
Have each user grant individual consent through /oauth/auth
Mark the integration key as internal during Go-Live review

answerText: Grant admin consent in Docusign Admin > Connected Apps > Authorize Application
explanation: For an internal app whose key belongs to the organization, an admin grants consent for all reserved-domain users from Docusign Admin > Connected Apps > Authorize Application.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Internal apps get admin consent from Docusign Admin > Connected Apps > Authorize Application.
optionExplanations.B: This is admin consent for external apps owned by another organization, not an internal integration key.
optionExplanations.C: Individual consent works, but it needs each user to act instead of one admin action.
optionExplanations.D: Go-Live review promotes a key to production; it does not grant consent to anyone.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the app is internal and the org has Access Management and a claimed domain. The trap is B: it is also admin consent, but the openid plus admin_consent_scope URL flow is for external (ISV) apps owned by another organization. C works but requires every user to act, and D is not a consent mechanism.

stem: A batch job sends a sudden spike of API calls. What is the default burst limit in production?

options.text: 3,000 calls per 30 seconds
200 calls per 30 seconds
500 calls per 30 seconds
1,000 calls per minute

answerText: 500 calls per 30 seconds
explanation: The burst limit is 500 calls per 30 seconds in production (200 in the developer environment), in addition to the 3,000 per hour account limit.

optionExplanations.A: 3,000 is the hourly account limit, not the 30-second burst limit.
optionExplanations.B: 200 per 30 seconds is the developer environment burst limit.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Production allows 500 calls per 30 seconds.
optionExplanations.D: This is not the documented burst limit.

whyNotOthers: C is right because production allows 500 calls per 30 seconds. The trap is B: 200 per 30 seconds is the developer environment's burst limit, not production's. A borrows the hourly number, and D is not a Docusign limit.

stem: When the last signer completes an envelope, a listener must receive one message for recipient-completed and a separate message for envelope-completed. Which Connect setting fits?

options.text: JSON SIM format (one message per event)
XML aggregate mode
Organization-level Connect with legacy XML
Polling listStatusChanges for both statuses

answerText: JSON SIM format (one message per event)
explanation: SIM (send individual messages) delivers a message for each triggering event, so recipient-completed and envelope-completed arrive separately.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. SIM sends one message per event, so both events arrive separately.
optionExplanations.B: Aggregate mode combines recipient-completed and envelope-completed into one message.
optionExplanations.C: Organization-level configurations cannot use legacy XML.
optionExplanations.D: Polling is not a webhook and adds API calls.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the listener needs each event as its own message. The trap is B: aggregate mode would combine recipient-completed and envelope-completed into a single message, the exact opposite of the requirement. C is impossible because org-level is JSON SIM only, and D is polling, not event delivery.

stem: A document generation flow must create the envelope, fill the docGen form fields, and only then send it. Which status should the initial Envelopes:create request use?

options.text: sent
draft
created
completed

answerText: created
explanation: Document generation needs a draft envelope: create it with status created, update the docGen fields, then send it. The clue is that fields are filled before sending.

optionExplanations.A: sent would deliver the envelope before the docGen fields are populated.
optionExplanations.B: draft is the concept, not the value; the status property must be created.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. status created keeps the envelope as a draft while the docGen form fields are updated.
optionExplanations.D: completed is set by Docusign after all recipients finish; it cannot start a flow.
