whyNotOthers: C is right because created is the API value that builds the envelope without sending it. The trap is B: the envelope is a draft, but draft is not a valid status value. A would send before the fields are filled and D is set only by Docusign at the end of the process.

stem: Remote signers should be redirected to a custom page after finishing. Which branding feature is relevant?

options.text: Branding email resource file
A brand logo
Brand destination URLs
Docusign JS sessionEnd event handler

answerText: Brand destination URLs
explanation: Post-signing redirects for remote signers are controlled by brand destination URLs.

optionExplanations.A: Email resource files customize notification email content; they do not redirect signers after signing.
optionExplanations.B: A logo only changes appearance.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A brand's destination URLs redirect remote signers after events such as signing complete or decline.
optionExplanations.D: This handler runs in your own page during embedded signing and does not apply to remote signers.

whyNotOthers: C is right because destination URLs are the brand setting for remote signer redirects. The trap is A: it is part of the same brand, but it changes email content rather than browser navigation. B and D fail because a logo is visual only and sessionEnd belongs to embedded signing.

stem: After a participant submits the web form and signs, the workflow should display a thank-you message in the participant's browser before ending. Which step should be added?

options.text: Send an Email
Show a Confirmation Screen
Set Up Invite
Branching Rule

answerText: Show a Confirmation Screen
explanation: Show a Confirmation Screen is the utility step that displays a message to the participant in the browser.

optionExplanations.A: Sends a message to an inbox, not to the participant's screen.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Displays a message to the participant in the browser.
optionExplanations.C: Invites a participant to act; it does not display a closing message.
optionExplanations.D: Routes the workflow; it displays nothing.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the message must appear on screen at the end. The trap is A: Send an Email is the other notification step, but it sends to an inbox rather than showing the message in the browser. C invites a participant to a step, and D routes the process.

stem: Which set of actions belongs to the Data IO extension?

options.text: GetTypeNames, GetTypeDefinitions and Verify
Verify.Version1.Email and Verify.Version1.PhoneNumber
TabInfo:GetConnectedFieldsTabGroups and Envelopes:create
GetTypeNames, GetTypeDefinitions, CreateRecord, PatchRecord, SearchRecords

answerText: GetTypeNames, GetTypeDefinitions, CreateRecord, PatchRecord, SearchRecords
explanation: Data IO actions describe the data model (GetTypeNames, GetTypeDefinitions) and read/write records (CreateRecord, PatchRecord, SearchRecords). There is no UpdateRecord action.

optionExplanations.A: This is the connected fields set (type discovery plus Verify), not Data IO.
optionExplanations.B: These are data verification extension identifiers.
optionExplanations.C: These are API endpoints your integration calls, not actions Docusign calls on your app.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. These are the Data IO actions for type discovery and record read/write.

whyNotOthers: D is right because it lists the Data IO record actions. The trap is A: GetTypeNames and GetTypeDefinitions plus Verify is the connected fields set. B are data verification extensions, and C are eSignature/Connected Fields API endpoints, not extension actions.

stem: An organization has 4,000 agents who use a client-server portal to send Docusign quotes. Each agent signs in and must track their own envelopes. What is the recommended OAuth model?

options.text: Implicit Grant
JSON Web Token (JWT) Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant
Confidential Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Each agent signs in individually and the server can store a secret, so Confidential Authorization Code Grant keeps a per-agent identity for tracking their own envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: Implicit Grant is a legacy browser flow and is not used for a secure client-server portal.
optionExplanations.B: JWT through one system user removes individual identity, so agents could not see their own envelopes as distinct senders.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant is for clients that cannot store a secret; a client-server portal can.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Interactive agents on a server that can keep a secret is Confidential Authorization Code Grant.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the agents are present and need their own identity on a server that can hold a secret. The trap is B: the large user count makes a single service integration tempting, but JWT through one system user would merge all agents into one sender, so they could not track their own envelopes. A is legacy, and C is for clients that cannot keep a secret.

stem: A support agent who has no access to the account's API integrations needs to capture the API requests a user's session makes. Which tool should the agent use?

options.text: API Dashboard under Admin > Apps and Keys
API request logging under My Preferences
API Usage Center efficiency scores
The Connect failure log

answerText: API request logging under My Preferences
explanation: API request logging (My Preferences) is available to all users, is off by default, and keeps up to 50 logs that can be downloaded or cleared.

optionExplanations.A: The API Dashboard is only for users with access to the API integrations.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Request logging is available to all users; enable it in My Preferences (up to 50 logs).
optionExplanations.C: The API Usage Center shows efficiency scores and call volume, not individual request logs.
optionExplanations.D: The Connect failure log lists failed webhook deliveries, not API requests.

whyNotOthers: B is right because request logging is available to every user, which suits a support agent without integration access. The trap is A: the API Dashboard shows request logs and failures, but it is available only to users with access to the API integrations. C shows app efficiency rather than individual requests, and D covers webhook deliveries, not API requests.

stem: A listener has HMAC security enabled. How should it validate that a Connect message is authentic?

options.text: Decrypt the payload with the account's RSA private key
Compare X-DocuSign-Signature-1 directly to the stored secret key
Recompute the HMAC over the parsed and re-serialized JSON
Compute HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the secret, Base64-encode, compare to X-DocuSign-Signature-1

answerText: Compute HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the secret, Base64-encode, compare to X-DocuSign-Signature-1
explanation: Docusign hashes the entire request body with the HMAC key using HMAC-SHA256; the listener recomputes the Base64 hash over the raw bytes and compares it to the signature header.

optionExplanations.A: HMAC payloads are not encrypted with an RSA key; the body is plain JSON with a hash header.
optionExplanations.B: The header holds a hash of the body, not the secret key itself.
optionExplanations.C: Re-serialized JSON may differ from the raw bytes Docusign hashed, so validation fails.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, Base64-encoded, compared to X-DocuSign-Signature-1.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the hash must be computed over the exact raw body bytes and compared to the header. The trap is C: it uses the right algorithm, but re-serializing JSON changes whitespace or ordering, so the hash will not match. A confuses HMAC with RSA encryption, and B compares the header to the key instead of to a hash of the body.

stem: A sent envelope has a fatal error. The developer must stop it for good, not just pause it while someone edits it. Which action fits?

options.text: Set status completed to close the envelope
Update the envelope to status voided with a voidedReason
Lock the envelope with an envelope lock
Change the envelope back to status created

answerText: Update the envelope to status voided with a voidedReason
explanation: Voiding is permanent cancellation, which is what 'stop it for good' requires.

optionExplanations.A: completed is set by Docusign after all recipients finish; an integration cannot close an envelope this way.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Voiding is the permanent cancel action for an in-process envelope.
optionExplanations.C: An envelope lock is temporary, used while an envelope is being edited; it does not cancel it.
optionExplanations.D: Returning to created is not the documented way to cancel; recipients would not be notified of a cancellation.

whyNotOthers: B is right because voiding with a voidedReason permanently cancels the in-process envelope. The trap is C: locking is a real envelope operation, but it is temporary and meant for editing, not cancelling. A is a status only Docusign sets and D does not cancel the envelope for its recipients.

stem: During a demo test, a team notices that a signer-entered account number is not checked against their core system during signing. Which feature closes this gap?

options.text: The Connect extension-executed event
Connected Fields (data verification extension)
A Data IO extension
A public App Center listing

answerText: Connected Fields (data verification extension)
explanation: The gap is real-time checking of a signer-entered value, which is the Connected Fields capability.

optionExplanations.A: This event delivers verification results (JSON SIM only) after a verification runs; on its own it does not check anything.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connected Fields verify the signer's entries against an external system while they sign.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO reads and writes system-of-record data from Maestro workflows, not during eSignature signing.
optionExplanations.D: Publishing publicly only changes who can install an extension app; it is not the verification feature.

whyNotOthers: B is right because Connected Fields perform the check against the external system during signing. The trap is A: it is part of the same verification story, but it only reports results. C and D fail because Data IO targets Maestro and a public listing is a distribution choice.

stem: After a Verify Someone's Identity step, only verified participants may go on to sign their contract. If verification fails, the HR representative must be notified. Which design fits?

options.text: A Branching Rule on the verification result: true goes to the signing steps, false to a Send an Email step
Rely on the identity step alone, assuming it notifies HR automatically on failure
A Multi Branch Rule on Job Location after the identity step
An app that calls cancelWorkflowInstance whenever verification fails

answerText: A Branching Rule on the verification result: true goes to the signing steps, false to a Send an Email step
explanation: The course example uses a Branching Rule on Validated = True after the identity step: verified participants proceed to the contract, and failures go to a Send an Email step for the HR representative.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Branch on the verification result; the false path emails HR.
optionExplanations.B: HR notification must be added as its own step; it is not implied by the identity step.
optionExplanations.C: Job Location does not tell you whether identity was verified.
optionExplanations.D: Canceling from custom code is unnecessary and still does not notify HR.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the routing on the result and the notification must be modelled explicitly. The trap is B: the identity step performs verification, but notifying HR is a separate action the designer must add. C branches on the wrong field, and D moves logic into custom code and never notifies HR.

stem: Where is a File IO extension (file output cloud storage) invoked?

options.text: In the eSignature Add Fields view and during signing
In Web Forms
In Maestro workflows
From the App Center listing page

answerText: In Maestro workflows
explanation: File output cloud storage runs in Maestro workflows, for example to write a file generated during a workflow to cloud storage.

optionExplanations.A: Add Fields and signing are for connected fields and data verification.
optionExplanations.B: Web Forms supports only email and phone verification extensions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. File IO is invoked from Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.D: The App Center is where admins install apps, not where extensions run.

whyNotOthers: C is right because File IO's extension point is Maestro workflows. The trap is A: Add Fields and signing are the extension points for connected fields and data verification. B applies only to email and phone verification, and D is where apps are installed, not invoked.

stem: A support ticket says users are alarmed by a long list of permissions on the consent screen, and some decline. The app only sends envelopes and reads user account information. Which response best matches Docusign behavior?

options.text: Switch to JWT Grant so users never see a consent screen
Ask Docusign to hide the consent screen for the integration key
Add the extended scope so consent is shown only once
Request only the minimum scopes required for those operations

answerText: Request only the minimum scopes required for those operations
explanation: The consent screen lists the requested scopes, so trimming them to what the app needs fixes the root cause.

optionExplanations.A: JWT still needs consent and is designed for services without users, so it does not fit or fix the issue.
optionExplanations.B: Docusign does not hide the consent screen; consent is how users approve requested scopes.
optionExplanations.C: extended makes the refresh token roll forward 30 days from the last refresh; it does not shorten the consent list.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Requesting fewer scopes shortens the consent screen and follows least privilege.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the long list comes from over-requesting scopes. The trap is A: JWT runs without per-call prompts, but it still requires consent and is meant for services, not interactive users. B is not something Docusign offers, and C changes the refresh-token lifecycle, not what consent asks for.

stem: An app relies on Basic Data Verification in the developer account. What must the team confirm before going live?

options.text: That the production plan includes every feature the app used, such as Basic Data Verification
Nothing, because developer account features carry over to the production key
That the Go-Live review will enable any missing features at no cost
That the key uses the Embedded integration type, which unlocks all features

answerText: That the production plan includes every feature the app used, such as Basic Data Verification
explanation: Developer accounts can include features that production plans lack; the production plan must include every feature the app relied on, for example Basic Data Verification, which is only in certain plans.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Verify the production plan includes every feature the app used, such as Basic Data Verification.
optionExplanations.B: Features belong to the account plan, not to the key, so they do not carry over.
optionExplanations.C: Go-Live review does not add features; production plan features may need to be purchased.
optionExplanations.D: Integration type reflects the business model and does not unlock plan features.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the app will not work as expected if the production plan lacks a feature it used. The trap is B: everything works in the developer account, but features belong to the account plan, not the integration key. C is wrong because Go-Live submission is free but production plans may cost money, and D misuses the integration type, which reflects the business model.

stem: After fixing a listener bug, the team sees several events marked as failed in the Connect logs. What should they do so the downstream system gets those events?

options.text: Delete and recreate the Connect configuration
Resend the affected envelopes to the signers
Republish the failed events from the Connect failure list
Do nothing; failed events are retried forever

answerText: Republish the failed events from the Connect failure list
explanation: Connect logs and the failure list are the troubleshooting tools; once the listener is fixed, failed events can be republished.

optionExplanations.A: Recreating the configuration does not resend past events.
optionExplanations.B: Resending envelopes bothers signers and creates new activity instead of delivering the missed events.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Republish failed events from the Connect logs and failure list after fixing the listener.
optionExplanations.D: Retries use exponential back-off over a limited period, not forever.

whyNotOthers: C is right because republishing delivers the recorded events again without touching the envelopes. The trap is D: Connect does retry automatically, but retries follow a back-off schedule that ends after a set period, so they are not indefinite. Recreating the configuration (A) does not resend past events, and B would make signers repeat work.

stem: A stakeholder challenges the design for handling a create-envelope request that may be submitted twice after a network failure. Which envelope field should the team keep in the request?

options.text: transactionId
clientUserId
batchId
envelopeId

answerText: transactionId
explanation: A sender-generated transactionId on the envelope lets the app determine whether the first attempt already created the envelope, avoiding duplicates.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. transactionId identifies the create transaction so a resubmission does not create a duplicate.
optionExplanations.B: clientUserId marks a recipient as embedded; it has no role in duplicate detection.
optionExplanations.C: batchId is returned by a bulk send request; it does not apply to single envelope creation.
optionExplanations.D: envelopeId is created by Docusign on success, so it cannot be supplied in the original request.

whyNotOthers: A is right because transactionId is the client-supplied identifier for the create transaction. The trap is D: envelopeId is generated by Docusign after creation, so the client cannot send it on the first attempt. B marks an embedded recipient and C tracks a bulk send batch.

stem: In a pull request, code assumes the integration can fetch retained data about a completed ID Verification event. Which API should that code call?

options.text: ID Evidence API
The certificate of completion download
IdentityVerifications:list
The Agreement Manager API

answerText: ID Evidence API
explanation: Retained ID verification data is fetched with the ID Evidence API.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The ID Evidence API is the API for retrieving evidence from Docusign ID Verification events.
optionExplanations.B: The certificate lists envelope events and authentication used, not the retained ID images and document details.
optionExplanations.C: This lists IDV workflow configurations for use when sending, not evidence from completed verifications.
optionExplanations.D: This returns agreements and AI-extracted agreement data, not identity evidence.

whyNotOthers: A is right because ID evidence is retrieved through the ID Evidence API. The trap is B: it is an audit document that mentions authentication, but it does not hold the retained ID data. C and D fail because IdentityVerifications:list returns configurations and Agreement Manager handles agreement data.

stem: After signing completes, the workflow must update the related opportunity in the company's CRM to Closed Won. The CRM extension app is installed. Which step fits?

options.text: A Read step from the CRM extension app
A Store Files step to the CRM
A Send an Email step to sales operations
A Writeback step with the CRM extension app, after Send Documents for Signature

answerText: A Writeback step with the CRM extension app, after Send Documents for Signature
explanation: Writeback steps automate updating information in external systems such as Salesforce, HubSpot or Dynamics 365. Placing it after signing ensures the update reflects the completed agreement.

optionExplanations.A: Read steps pull data into the workflow; they do not update the CRM.
optionExplanations.B: Store Files saves documents; it does not change the opportunity status.
optionExplanations.C: An email relies on a manual update.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A Writeback step after signing updates the CRM record.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the requirement is to update a record in the CRM after signing. The trap is A: it uses the same CRM app, but a Read step imports data into the workflow rather than updating the CRM. B saves documents, not field values, and C depends on a person doing the update manually.

stem: A real estate firm must verify that a postal address entered by a client is valid and deliverable, and have the signer correct it before signing proceeds. Which extension type addresses this real-time validation?

options.text: File IO
Data IO
Connected Fields
Data Verification

answerText: Data Verification
explanation: Postal address verification is a Data Verification extension that checks existence and deliverability in real time at signing.

optionExplanations.A: File IO stores documents.
optionExplanations.B: Data IO reads and writes records in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields are for custom values against your own system, not standard address checks.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Postal address verification is a Data Verification extension.

whyNotOthers: D is right because address deliverability is a standard data verification type. The trap is C: connected fields also verify in real time at signing, but they are for custom data against your own system of record. A stores files and B reads/writes records in Maestro.

stem: After exchanging an authorization code for an access token, a user who belongs to more than one Docusign account signs in. The app must discover the correct accountId and API base URI before making REST calls. Which endpoint provides that context?

options.text: /oauth/token
/oauth/userinfo
eSignature Accounts:get
The coid claim of the ID token

answerText: /oauth/userinfo
explanation: /oauth/userinfo returns every account available to the user with its account_id, base_uri, and is_default flag.

optionExplanations.A: /oauth/token issues tokens; its response has no account list or base URIs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. /oauth/userinfo returns account_id and base_uri for each account the user can access.
optionExplanations.C: Accounts:get needs an account ID and base URI in its URL, so it cannot discover them.
optionExplanations.D: coid lists organizations that granted admin consent, not the user's accounts or base URIs.

whyNotOthers: B is right because userinfo lists all of the user's accounts and their base URIs. The trap is C: Accounts:get is an account endpoint, but it requires the account ID and base URI you are trying to discover. A returns tokens only, and D lists organizations that granted admin consent.

stem: A vendor embeds Docusign features into its own product. Its customers do not have Docusign accounts; they use the features through the vendor's own Docusign account. Which integration type applies?

options.text: Public integration
Embedded integration
Private custom integration
Third-party integration key

answerText: Embedded integration
explanation: When customers use Docusign features through the vendor's account and do not need their own Docusign accounts, the classification is Embedded integration (it requires an ISV Embed partner license).

optionExplanations.A: Public integration connects to customers' own Docusign accounts; here customers have none.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Customers using Docusign through the vendor's account is an Embedded integration.
optionExplanations.C: Private custom integration covers direct use by employees, not a resold Docusign-powered service.
optionExplanations.D: Third-party integration key is chosen by a customer using a partner product, not by the vendor.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the clue is that customers have no Docusign accounts of their own. The trap is A: it also serves many customers, but a Public integration connects to each customer's own Docusign account. C is for apps used directly by your employees or your customers' employees, and D is for a customer supplying its own key to a partner product.

stem: The team reviews Docusign guidance after a listener receives duplicate webhook messages. What design practice should the integration use?

options.text: Enable Connect logging so duplicate deliveries are suppressed
Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
Republish the failed events from the Connect failure list
Change the listener URL from HTTPS to HTTP

answerText: Idempotent processing based on event identifiers or envelope state
explanation: Duplicate deliveries are normal with retries, so the listener must process events idempotently.

optionExplanations.A: Logs help diagnose delivery issues but do not stop duplicates.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Idempotent processing makes repeated deliveries harmless.
optionExplanations.C: Republishing resends failed events; it does not address duplicates and can create more.
optionExplanations.D: HTTP weakens security and does not change duplicate delivery.

whyNotOthers: B is right because idempotent processing is the design fix for duplicates. The trap is A: Connect logs are the right tool for troubleshooting, but logging records deliveries; it does not suppress duplicates. C is for events that failed, and republishing them can add duplicates, and D weakens security without affecting delivery.

stem: Two envelope designs are compared: one uses a single saved template unchanged, the other must combine a saved template with runtime recipients and a directly supplied document. Which model does the second design require?

options.text: templateId reference with templateRoles
Composite templates using serverTemplates and inlineTemplates
Direct documents with fixed-position tabs
One envelope per document sent in sequence

answerText: Composite templates using serverTemplates and inlineTemplates
explanation: Composite templates are used when an envelope must combine saved server templates, inline runtime data and documents.

optionExplanations.A: templateId with templateRoles suits the first design only; it cannot combine a template with another document.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Composite templates combine a server template, inline runtime recipients and a supplied document.
optionExplanations.C: Direct documents do not apply the saved template, and fixed positions are unrelated to the requirement.
optionExplanations.D: Sending several envelopes splits the agreement instead of building one combined envelope.

whyNotOthers: B is right because composite templates combine serverTemplates, inlineTemplates and a document. The trap is A: templateId fits the first design, but it cannot add a separate document or combine templates. C drops the saved template and D splits the agreement into several envelopes.

stem: Sofia's team must embed a Docusign web form inline in a partner's site. Which createInstance setup and client-side step is correct?

options.text: Omit clientUserId and render the instance URL with Docusign JS
Use sendOption 'now' with recipients[] by roleName
Add an identityVerification workflowId to the instance
Set clientUserId on createInstance, then render the instance URL with Docusign JS

answerText: Set clientUserId on createInstance, then render the instance URL with Docusign JS
explanation: An embedded web form needs clientUserId on createInstance and Docusign JS to render the instance URL.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign JS is right, but clientUserId is required to create an embedded instance; without it the instance is not set up for embedding.
optionExplanations.B: This creates a remote instance that emails participants; it is not displayed inline on the site.
optionExplanations.C: ID verification settings control identity checks; they do not make a form render inline.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. clientUserId is required for an embedded instance (max 100 characters), and Docusign JS renders the returned URL.

whyNotOthers: D is right because embedded instances require clientUserId and are rendered with Docusign JS. The trap is A: it has the right renderer but drops the required clientUserId, which is exactly what makes the instance embedded. B and C fail because sendOption with recipients is the remote email mode and identity verification is unrelated to rendering.

stem: A designer placed a Branching Rule on the loanAmount variable before the Collect Data with Web Forms step that captures loanAmount. Applicants are not routed as intended. What is the fix?

options.text: Replace the Branching Rule with a Multi Branch Rule step
Change the start method to From an API call
Move the branching step after the Collect Data with Web Forms step
Republish the workflow without changes

answerText: Move the branching step after the Collect Data with Web Forms step
explanation: A branch can only evaluate a variable after the step that produces it has run. Step order must match the data flow: collect the value, then branch on it.

optionExplanations.A: More branches do not help when the variable has not been collected yet.
optionExplanations.B: The start method does not reorder steps inside the workflow.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Branch after the form so loanAmount has a value.
optionExplanations.D: Republishing the same design keeps the same faulty order.

whyNotOthers: C is right because loanAmount does not exist yet when the branch runs. The trap is A: a Multi Branch Rule adds more paths, but it has the same problem because it still runs before the data exists. B changes how the workflow starts, not the order of steps, and D does not change the design.

stem: A team wants to use connected fields inside a Maestro workflow. What is true?

options.text: They run automatically in Maestro as a Data IO step
Connected fields are not currently supported in Maestro
Only private connected fields apps work in Maestro
They must be added through a Store Files step

answerText: Connected fields are not currently supported in Maestro
explanation: Connected fields are not currently supported in Docusign Maestro; they work in eSignature envelopes (Add Fields view and signing).

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields do not turn into Data IO steps; Data IO is a separate extension.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connected fields are not currently supported in Maestro.
optionExplanations.C: Distribution type does not change Maestro support.
optionExplanations.D: Store Files steps save documents; they have nothing to do with connected fields.

whyNotOthers: B is right because Maestro does not currently support connected fields. The trap is A: Data IO is the Maestro extension for system-of-record data, but connected fields do not become Data IO steps. C invents a distribution exception, and D is a file storage step.

stem: A native app uses Public Authorization Code Grant and has no client secret. Which mechanism lets Docusign verify that the app redeeming the authorization code is the same app that started the flow?

options.text: The client secret in an Authorization: Basic header
A PKCE code verifier and code challenge
An exactly matching registered redirect URI
The 120-second authorization code lifetime

answerText: A PKCE code verifier and code challenge
explanation: PKCE sends a code_challenge (S256 hash of a random code_verifier) on /oauth/auth and the code_verifier on /oauth/token, which verifies that the app that started the flow is the one finishing it.

optionExplanations.A: A native public client has no secret, so it cannot send a Basic header with one.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The code_challenge on /oauth/auth and the matching code_verifier on /oauth/token prove the same app finished the flow.
optionExplanations.C: An exactly matching redirect URI is required, but it controls where the code goes and does not prove who redeems it.
optionExplanations.D: The 120-second lifetime narrows the window for misuse but does not bind the code to the app that requested it.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the code_verifier and code_challenge pair proves the token request comes from the app that began the flow. The trap is C: the redirect URI must match exactly, but it only controls where the code is sent and does not prove who redeems it. A needs a secret the app does not have, and D only limits how long a stolen code stays usable.

stem: Which pair of hosts should an eSignature app use in production?

options.text: Auth: account-d.docusign.com; API: demo.docusign.net/restapi
Auth: account.docusign.com; API: demo.docusign.net/restapi
Auth: account.docusign.com; API: the account's base URI plus /restapi
Auth: account-d.docusign.com; API: the account's base URI plus /restapi

answerText: Auth: account.docusign.com; API: the account's base URI plus /restapi
explanation: In production, OAuth uses https://account.docusign.com and API calls use the account's base URI (https://{server}.docusign.net/restapi).

optionExplanations.A: This is the developer environment pair.
optionExplanations.B: The authentication host is right, but the API host is still the demo host.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Production uses account.docusign.com for OAuth and the account's base URI for API calls.
optionExplanations.D: account-d.docusign.com is the developer authentication host.

whyNotOthers: C is right because both hosts are the production values. The trap is B: the authentication host is correctly switched, but API calls still go to the demo host. A is the full developer pair, and D switches the API host but keeps the developer authentication host.

stem: A team wants event messages that carry only the triggering event's data, adding the envelope summary only for the event types where it is useful. Which Connect design choice is relevant?

options.text: Configure the JSON SIM event payload to include only needed data
Use legacy XML so every message has a consistent envelope summary
Poll Envelopes:get after each event instead
Enable aggregate mode for smaller messages

answerText: Configure the JSON SIM event payload to include only needed data
explanation: JSON SIM messages contain data about the triggering event by default, and you can choose to include the envelope summary depending on the event type.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. JSON SIM is event-focused and lets you add the envelope summary only where needed.
optionExplanations.B: Legacy XML is envelope-focused, so every message includes the envelope summary.
optionExplanations.C: Polling after each event adds API calls and defeats the purpose of Connect.
optionExplanations.D: Aggregate mode combines events into fewer messages; it does not trim message content.

whyNotOthers: A is right because JSON SIM makes the payload event-focused and customizable. The trap is B: legacy XML does give a consistent payload, but it is envelope-focused, so every message carries the summary the team wants to avoid. C adds API calls, and D reduces message count rather than message content.

stem: In a composite template object, the app must supply the PDF at runtime even though the server template also has a document. Which location takes precedence for that object's document?

options.text: The inlineTemplate's documents property
The server template, because it has the lowest sequence
The composite template object's document property
The template with the highest sequence value

answerText: The composite template object's document property
explanation: If the composite template object includes a document element, that document is used and all template documents are ignored. It is also the recommended place to supply a runtime document.

optionExplanations.A: An inline template can carry documents, but Docusign recommends the document property, which takes precedence.
optionExplanations.B: The lowest-sequence template supplies the document only when no document property is present.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The composite object's document property takes precedence over server and inline template documents.
optionExplanations.D: For documents the lowest sequence wins (first in wins); highest sequence wins only for attributes.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the composite object's document property always wins for document contribution. The trap is A: an inline template can contribute documents, but the best practice is the document property, and the inline document does not override it. B applies only when there is no document property, and D reverses the rule: for documents the lowest sequence wins, not the highest.

stem: Robin's app embeds a web form for each sales customer and stores the customer's internal ID with each instance. Which statement about the value used for this is correct?

options.text: The signer's email address is the unique key Docusign uses for each instance
The API account ID distinguishes each customer's instance
clientUserId identifies the user in your system and is limited to 100 characters
The web form configuration formId is unique per customer

answerText: clientUserId identifies the user in your system and is limited to 100 characters
explanation: The stem's clue is an internal ID stored per embedded instance, which is clientUserId (max 100 characters).

optionExplanations.A: Email is not the key that identifies an embedded web form user; clientUserId is.
optionExplanations.B: The account ID is the same for all instances in the account.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. clientUserId is required for embedded instances, is chosen by your app, and has a 100-character maximum.
optionExplanations.D: formId identifies the configuration, which all customers' instances share.

whyNotOthers: C is right because clientUserId carries your internal user ID and is capped at 100 characters. The trap is A: email identifies recipients in many eSignature flows, but it is not the embedded web form correlation key. B and D fail because the account ID and the configuration ID are shared across all customers.

stem: A workflow was set to start From a link, and the link was placed on a website. Later the designer changes the start method to From an API call. What happens to the existing link?

options.text: The link stops working immediately
The link can still start the workflow, because the start method does not block other ways of starting it
The link now requires an OAuth access token
The link starts only instances that the API already created

answerText: The link can still start the workflow, because the start method does not block other ways of starting it
explanation: Docusign documents that the selected start method does not prevent starting the workflow in other ways; an existing link still works after the start method is changed to API.

optionExplanations.A: Changing the start method does not disable an existing link.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The link still triggers the workflow after the start method changes.
optionExplanations.C: The link endpoint is unauthenticated; it does not start requiring a token.
optionExplanations.D: Opening the link creates a new instance; it does not depend on API-created instances.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the start method mainly sets up shortcuts and prompts; it is not an access restriction. The trap is A: it seems logical that changing the method disables the link, but the documentation says the existing link can still be used. C and D describe behavior that does not exist.

stem: A signer enters their company's federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN), which must be checked against government records at signing. Which extension fits?

options.text: Business FEIN verification (Verify.Version1.BusinessEntity)
Connected Fields with a custom FEIN type
Bank account owner verification
SSN verification

answerText: Business FEIN verification (Verify.Version1.BusinessEntity)
explanation: Business FEIN verification is the Data Verification extension for confirming a business identifier, used at the Add Fields view and signing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Business FEIN verification checks business identifiers at signing.
optionExplanations.B: Connected fields are for custom data against your own system, not a standard FEIN check.
optionExplanations.C: Bank account owner verification checks ownership of a US bank account.
optionExplanations.D: SSN verification validates an individual's social security number, not a business FEIN.

whyNotOthers: A is right because a standard business entity check is exactly what FEIN verification does. The trap is B: connected fields could verify custom data against your own database, but a standard FEIN check against government records is a predefined Data Verification type. C and D verify different data.

stem: Guidance for maintainers of a JWT integration: REST calls return 401 Unauthorized even though the token endpoint returned an access token. What should the guidance recommend?

options.text: Send the access token in the Authorization header as a Bearer token
Send the signed JWT assertion itself as the Bearer value
Send the token in a JSON field named token in the request body
Add the impersonation scope to every API request

answerText: Send the access token in the Authorization header as a Bearer token
explanation: The signed JWT assertion is only exchanged at /oauth/token; the access token it returns goes in Authorization: Bearer on API calls.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Use Authorization: Bearer <access_token> on API calls.
optionExplanations.B: The JWT assertion is exchanged at /oauth/token; APIs only accept the access token it returns.
optionExplanations.C: Docusign reads credentials from the Authorization header, not the request body.
optionExplanations.D: Scopes are set at consent and in the token request, not on each API call.

whyNotOthers: A is right because API calls need the access token in a Bearer header. The trap is B: the signed JWT looks like a token, but it is only the assertion posted to /oauth/token. C is not where Docusign reads credentials, and D confuses scopes, which are requested at consent and token time, with per-request headers.

stem: After Go-Live, should the team keep using the developer environment version of the integration key?

options.text: No; Go-Live moves the key to production, so demo calls stop working
Yes; the key is duplicated, so the developer version stays available for testing
No; the developer version expires 90 days after Go-Live
Yes, but only after generating a new GUID for the developer version

answerText: Yes; the key is duplicated, so the developer version stays available for testing
explanation: Go-Live duplicates the integration key into production rather than moving it, so the developer version keeps working and is recommended for ongoing regression testing.

optionExplanations.A: Go-Live duplicates the key; the developer version keeps working.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The developer version remains available and is useful for regression testing.
optionExplanations.C: The developer version does not expire after Go-Live.
optionExplanations.D: Both versions keep the same key value; no new GUID is needed.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the key is copied, not moved. The trap is A: the word promote suggests the key leaves the developer environment, but Docusign duplicates it. C invents an expiry, and D is wrong because both versions share the same key value.

stem: A stakeholder suggests setting a special callback URL for one API-sent envelope from the eSignature web app instead of in code. Which option should the team keep?

options.text: Configure it on the account's Connect page in eSignature Admin
Configure it in the Organization Admin Connect settings
Set it as the envelope's brand destination URL
Add an eventNotification object to the Envelopes:create request

answerText: Add an eventNotification object to the Envelopes:create request
explanation: eventNotification must be set through the API (Envelopes:create); an envelope-level webhook cannot be created from the Send page or admin UI.

optionExplanations.A: The eSignature Admin Connect page creates account-level configurations, not a webhook for one envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Organization Admin creates organization-level configurations spanning accounts.
optionExplanations.C: A brand destination URL redirects the signer's browser after signing; it does not deliver webhook events.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Envelope-level Connect is configured only through the API with eventNotification on Envelopes:create.

whyNotOthers: D is right because envelope-level webhooks are API only. The trap is A: the eSignature Admin Connect page is real, but it creates an account-level configuration that applies to many envelopes. B is an org-level setting, and C changes where the signer is redirected after signing, not where events are posted.

stem: An API call to create an envelope failed and the app wants to retry. Which parameter lets the retry avoid creating a duplicate envelope?

options.text: envelopeId
recipientId
transactionId
documentId

answerText: transactionId
explanation: Supplying the same sender-generated transactionId on the retry identifies it as the same envelope transaction, so a retry does not create a second envelope.

optionExplanations.A: envelopeId is assigned by Docusign only when the create succeeds; the client cannot set it on a retry.
optionExplanations.B: recipientId identifies a recipient within the envelope, not the create transaction.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Reusing the same transactionId lets Docusign and the app treat the retry as the same transaction.
optionExplanations.D: documentId identifies a document within the envelope; it does not prevent duplicate envelopes.

whyNotOthers: C is right because transactionId is the sender-generated identifier for the create attempt. The trap is A: envelopeId identifies an envelope, but Docusign generates it and a failed call does not return one. B and D identify a recipient and a document inside the envelope.

stem: Elena troubleshoots an integration: the developer set authenticationMethod on EnvelopeViews:createRecipient expecting Docusign to verify signers' photo IDs, but signers are never challenged. What should be used instead?

options.text: Also send authenticationInstant and assertionId so the record is complete
Add identityVerification with the account's IDV workflowId to the recipient
Render signing with Docusign JS focused view
Set clientUserId on the recipient

answerText: Add identityVerification with the account's IDV workflowId to the recipient
explanation: authenticationMethod only records authentication; enforcing a photo ID check requires identityVerification.workflowId.

optionExplanations.A: These fields complete the authentication record on the certificate, but they still only record your app's check and never challenge the signer.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. identityVerification.workflowId is what makes Docusign enforce ID verification for the recipient.
optionExplanations.C: Focused view changes how the signing session is displayed; it adds no identity verification.
optionExplanations.D: clientUserId is already required for embedded signing and has no identity-checking effect.

whyNotOthers: B is right because IDV is enforced by the identityVerification workflowId, not by authentication record fields. The trap is A: adding the other record fields looks like fixing an incomplete setup, but those fields are also record-only. C and D fail because focused view and clientUserId control the embedded experience, not identity.

stem: A backend knows only the display name of a Maestro workflow. Before triggering it, the backend needs the workflow ID. Which call should it make?

options.text: GetWorkflowsList (GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows)
getWorkflowInstancesList
eSignature Templates:list
GetWorkflowTriggerRequirements

answerText: GetWorkflowsList (GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/workflows)
explanation: GetWorkflowsList returns the available workflows with their IDs, names and trigger input schema, so the app can find the ID by name.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Lists the account's workflows with IDs and names.
optionExplanations.B: Needs a workflowId already and returns instances, not workflows.
optionExplanations.C: Templates are eSignature resources, not Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.D: Requires the workflowId in its path, so it cannot be used to find it.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it is the only call that lists workflows without already knowing an ID. The trap is D: trigger requirements are the next call in the flow, but they need the workflowId in the path. B also needs a workflowId and lists instances, and C lists eSignature templates, not workflows.

stem: A financial institution builds an extension app that verifies client data against its proprietary internal system. Only administrators of its designated corporate Docusign accounts may install it. Which distribution must be chosen?

options.text: Public extension app
Private extension app
Public app with publicationRegions set to the bank's region
Keep the app in Draft in the developer account

answerText: Private extension app
explanation: Private distribution restricts installation to a predefined list of production accounts, matching an app tied to an internal system.

optionExplanations.A: Public apps are available to all App Center customers, which violates the requirement.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Private distribution limits installation to the bank's designated production accounts.
optionExplanations.C: Regions restrict geography, not organizations, so other customers in that region could install it.
optionExplanations.D: A Draft app exists only in the developer account (demo) and cannot be installed in production.

whyNotOthers: B is right because private apps are installable only by the listed production accounts. The trap is C: publicationRegions narrows a public app by region, but every customer in that region could still install it. A exposes the app to all customers, and D never reaches production.

stem: A contracting web app's server can store a client secret. Users sign in once, then the server should keep calling Docusign for them for weeks using refresh tokens. Which flow fits?

options.text: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
JSON Web Token Grant
Implicit Grant
Confidential Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Confidential Authorization Code Grant returns a refresh token valid for up to 30 days (rolling with the extended scope), and the server can protect the secret it needs.

optionExplanations.A: Public Auth Code Grant refresh tokens last only 24 hours, and the flow is for clients without a safe place for a secret.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant returns no refresh token; its 1-hour access token is renewed by signing a new assertion, and it has no user sign-in.
optionExplanations.C: Implicit Grant is a legacy browser flow and does not provide the refresh-token lifecycle described.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Confidential Auth Code Grant gives a refresh token valid up to 30 days to a server that can protect the secret.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the server can hold a secret and needs long-lived refresh tokens after one interactive sign-in. The trap is A: Public Auth Code also returns a refresh token, but it lasts only 24 hours and the flow is meant for clients that cannot store a secret. B never returns a refresh token, and C is legacy.

stem: A developer worries that promoting a key will change its value and break existing configuration files. What actually happens to the integration key value?

options.text: The production key has the same value as the developer key
Production assigns a new key value that must replace the old one everywhere
The key value is kept, but it stops working in the developer environment
The key value changes only for Authorization Code Grant apps

answerText: The production key has the same value as the developer key
explanation: When you go live, a production version of the integration key with the same value is created in the production environment; it is a separate key with its own settings.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The production key has the same value but is configured separately.
optionExplanations.B: No new value is issued; only its settings must be re-added in production.
optionExplanations.C: The developer version keeps working because the key is duplicated, not moved.
optionExplanations.D: The key value is the same for every OAuth flow.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the production copy keeps the same key value. The trap is C: the value is indeed kept, but the developer version also keeps working, since the key is duplicated rather than moved. B and D are wrong because the value never changes, whatever the OAuth flow.

stem: Which statement correctly describes an advantage of Docusign Connect over polling?

options.text: Polling gives real-time data with fewer API calls
Connect requires a confirming status call for each event
Connect sends a message only when something changes
Connect works only for envelopes sent through the API

answerText: Connect sends a message only when something changes
explanation: Connect messages arrive only when an event occurs, which removes the polling logic and the wasted calls on unchanged envelopes.

optionExplanations.A: Polling is slower and uses more calls, the opposite of this statement.
optionExplanations.B: Connect messages carry the event data; no confirming call is required.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connect pushes a message only when a subscribed event occurs.
optionExplanations.D: Only envelope-level Connect is API only; account- and org-level configurations cover envelopes however they were sent.

whyNotOthers: C is right because event-driven delivery is the core advantage. The trap is D: it mixes Connect in general with envelope-level Connect, which is API only; account- and org-level configurations also cover envelopes sent from the web app. A reverses the comparison, and B invents a confirmation call that Connect does not require.

stem: Contracts are generated with different clause lengths, so the signature line lands on different pages. The signature tab must always sit beside the text 'Customer Signature'. Which option is correct?

options.text: Fixed-position tabs with pageNumber set to the last page
Anchor tagging with anchorString and offsets
A composite template with a second inline template
templateRoles mapping the signer to a role

answerText: Anchor tagging with anchorString and offsets
explanation: Anchor tagging searches the document for the text and places the tab beside it on whatever page it appears.

optionExplanations.A: Fixed positions with a page number break when the signature line moves to another page or spot.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Anchor tagging places the tab relative to 'Customer Signature' wherever it appears.
optionExplanations.C: An extra inline template adds recipients or tabs but does not by itself make a tab follow text.
optionExplanations.D: templateRoles assign a recipient to a role; they do not position tabs.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the anchor finds the text wherever it lands. The trap is A: putting the tab on the last page sounds reasonable, but the signature line is not always there and fixed coordinates do not follow the text. C and D change envelope structure or recipient mapping, not tab position.

stem: A signer must receive a one-time code by phone before accessing the envelope. Which method should the developer configure on the recipient?

options.text: Phone authentication (SMS or voice code)
Access code
Knowledge-based authentication (KBA)
authenticationMethod on createRecipient

answerText: Phone authentication (SMS or voice code)
explanation: A one-time code delivered by phone is phone authentication.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Phone authentication is configured with an identityVerification workflowId (from IdentityVerifications:list) and sends the code by SMS or call.
optionExplanations.B: An access code is a fixed code set by the sender and shared out of band, not a one-time code delivered by Docusign.
optionExplanations.C: KBA uses public-record questions (US only), not a code.
optionExplanations.D: This only records authentication your app performed; it sends nothing to the signer.

whyNotOthers: A is right because phone authentication delivers a code by SMS or voice call. The trap is B: it also requires the signer to type a code, but the sender sets and shares it. C and D fail because KBA asks questions and authenticationMethod is record-only.

stem: A designer corrected a step in a published workflow and published the change. Instances that were already running still behave the old way. What explains this?

options.text: The browser cached the old workflow definition
The change was published to the demo account only
The workflow must be paused, and changes published while it is paused
Edits apply to new instances only; instances already running are not modified

answerText: Edits apply to new instances only; instances already running are not modified
explanation: When you edit participants or steps, current active instances are not modified, but new instances reflect the changes.

optionExplanations.A: Caching does not explain the behavior; running instances simply keep their version.
optionExplanations.B: Nothing in the scenario suggests the wrong environment.
optionExplanations.C: Changes to a paused workflow cannot be published, and running instances are still not updated.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Only new instances pick up the edited steps.

whyNotOthers: D is right because running instances keep the version they started with. The trap is C: pausing sounds like a safe way to change a workflow, but changes made to a paused workflow cannot be published, and pausing still does not change running instances. A and B invent causes not supported by the scenario.

stem: A developer has registered, tested and published an extension app. Where do customer account administrators discover and install it?

options.text: In the Developer Console, where the app was registered and tested
On the Apps and Keys page of eSignature Admin settings
In a Connect configuration under eSignature Settings
In the Docusign App Center

answerText: In the Docusign App Center
explanation: Published extension apps are listed in the Docusign App Center, where admins discover and install them. The Developer Console is the developer-side tool.

optionExplanations.A: The Developer Console is the developer's tool for registering, testing and publishing; customers do not install apps there.
optionExplanations.B: Apps and Keys manages integration keys for API integrations, not extension app installation.
optionExplanations.C: Connect configurations define event webhooks; they do not install extension apps.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Admins discover and install published extension apps from the Docusign App Center.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the App Center is the central place where customers find and install extension apps. The trap is A: the Developer Console is where developers register, test and submit the app, not where customers install it. B manages integration keys for API apps, and C configures webhooks.

stem: A security architect reviews a browser-only SPA that cannot protect a client secret but must authenticate each individual user. The design will be rejected if the flow does not match the client type. Which flow should the developer choose?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
explanation: A public client (browser-only, no secret) with interactive users matches Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant matches a confidential client that can hold a secret, not a browser-only SPA.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant matches a service integration with no user present, not a per-user SPA.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Public client plus interactive user equals Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant fits the client type historically but is legacy; Docusign recommends the PKCE code flow instead.

whyNotOthers: C is right because it matches a public client with an interactive user. The trap is D: Implicit Grant also targets browser apps without a secret, but it is the legacy flow and does not match current Docusign guidance. A requires a confidential client, and B is for services without a user.

stem: The operations team wants a single Connect configuration, set up once in Docusign Organization Admin, that applies to all of the organization's accounts until disabled. Which Connect level is most appropriate?

options.text: Account-level Connect created with the ConnectConfigurations API
Organization-level Connect
eventNotification added to each envelope
The pre-built Connect for Salesforce integration

answerText: Organization-level Connect
explanation: Organization-level Connect is configured in Organization Admin or by API, spans accounts, and stays active until disabled.

optionExplanations.A: ConnectConfigurations creates an account-level configuration that covers one account.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Org-level Connect is set up in Organization Admin and covers all or selected accounts.
optionExplanations.C: eventNotification is per envelope and must be reconfigured on each new envelope.
optionExplanations.D: Connect for Salesforce is a pre-built integration that updates the Docusign for Salesforce app, not a custom org-wide webhook.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the clues are Organization Admin and all accounts. The trap is A: ConnectConfigurations does create persistent configurations, but at account level, so it would cover one account only. C must be repeated on every envelope, and D pushes data to the Docusign for Salesforce app rather than to a custom listener.

stem: An app calls EnvelopeViews:createRecipient and gets an error that the recipient is not found. email and userName match the signer exactly. Which value most likely does not match the envelope?

options.text: clientUserId
recipientId
returnUrl
frameAncestors

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: createRecipient requires email, userName and clientUserId that match the values used when the envelope was created. With email and name matching, the mismatch is clientUserId.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. clientUserId must match the value set on the signer when the envelope was created.
optionExplanations.B: recipientId is not one of the matching values that the recipient view request depends on.
optionExplanations.C: returnUrl is where Docusign redirects after signing; a wrong value does not cause a recipient-not-found error.
optionExplanations.D: frameAncestors is used for focused view embedding; it does not identify the recipient.

whyNotOthers: A is right because clientUserId is the remaining recipient-matching value. The trap is B: recipientId identifies the recipient inside the envelope, but the view request matches on email, userName and clientUserId. C and D are request settings for redirect and focused view, not recipient-matching values.

stem: Amir is comparing options for a sales team whose customers sign remotely from email. After signing, customers must be sent to the team's thank-you page. Which branding feature is relevant?

options.text: returnUrl in EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
Branding signing resource file
A Connect webhook
Brand destination URLs

answerText: Brand destination URLs
explanation: Remote signing plus a post-signing redirect points to brand destination URLs.

optionExplanations.A: returnUrl only applies to embedded signing; these customers sign remotely from email.
optionExplanations.B: Signing resource files change the text and look of the signing pages, not the redirect target.
optionExplanations.C: Connect posts events to a server; it does not control the signer's browser.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Destination URLs on the brand (applied with brandId) control where remote signers are redirected.

whyNotOthers: D is right because destination URLs are how a brand redirects remote signers. The trap is A: it is the redirect parameter for embedded signing and does not apply here. B and C fail because resource files are cosmetic and Connect is server-side.

stem: A team plans to embed workflow instances in its web app. Which step type is NOT supported in embedded workflow instances?

options.text: Collect Data with Web Forms
Send Documents for Signature
Collect Data from an ID
Branching Rule

answerText: Collect Data from an ID
explanation: All step types are supported in embedded instances except Collect Data from an ID.

optionExplanations.A: Web form steps are supported in embedded instances.
optionExplanations.B: Supported; only the focused view display is unavailable when embedded.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Collect Data from an ID is not supported in embedded instances.
optionExplanations.D: Branching runs without a UI and is supported.

whyNotOthers: C is right because it is the one documented exception. The trap is B: signing in an embedded instance has a restriction (focused view is not supported), but the step itself is supported. A and D are supported normally.

stem: A developer shares a private extension app with a customer's production account. In the Developer Console the account shows status Pending. What does this mean?

options.text: Docusign's app review is still in progress
The account ID entered is invalid and must be corrected
The account's administrator has not yet accepted the app in the App Center
The app must be republished as public before the account can use it

answerText: The account's administrator has not yet accepted the app in the App Center
explanation: A shared account stays Pending until its administrator accepts the private app in the App Center; it then changes to Accepted.

optionExplanations.A: Review status is shown on the app itself (In Review); sharing with accounts happens after approval.
optionExplanations.B: Pending does not indicate a bad account ID; it indicates the admin has not accepted yet.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The account remains Pending until its administrator accepts the app, then becomes Accepted.
optionExplanations.D: Private apps are used by the listed accounts as private apps; no public republishing is needed.

whyNotOthers: C is right because Pending refers to the account administrator's acceptance of the shared app. The trap is A: review status (In Review) applies to the app as a whole and is finished before private sharing. B and D are not what Pending means, and private apps never need to become public to be used.

stem: Guidance for a partner vendor: a scheduled service runs nightly using a dedicated system sender account, no person is present, and it must authenticate in both demo and production. What should the guidance recommend?

options.text: Confidential Authorization Code Grant
JSON Web Token Grant
Public Authorization Code Grant with PKCE
Implicit Grant

answerText: JSON Web Token Grant
explanation: An unattended service acting as a system user uses JWT Grant in both environments; only the aud value and auth server change (account-d.docusign.com in demo, account.docusign.com in production).

optionExplanations.A: Confidential Auth Code Grant still needs a user to sign in through a browser, which this nightly service cannot do.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. JWT Grant fits an unattended system-user service in both demo and production.
optionExplanations.C: Public Auth Code Grant with PKCE requires an interactive user on a client without a secret.
optionExplanations.D: Implicit Grant is a legacy interactive browser flow.

whyNotOthers: B is right because no person is present. The trap is A: it is the right choice for server apps that can store a secret, but only when users sign in. C needs an interactive user, and D is legacy; none of those depend on the environment.

stem: Which Connect message format is supported at all three custom configuration levels: organization, account and envelope?

options.text: JSON SIM format
Legacy XML format
XML aggregate mode
SOAP messages based on the eSignature SOAP API

answerText: JSON SIM format
explanation: JSON SIM is supported for organization-level, account-level and envelope-level Connect; legacy options are available only at account and envelope level.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. JSON SIM works at organization, account and envelope level.
optionExplanations.B: Legacy XML is limited to account- and envelope-level configurations.
optionExplanations.C: Aggregate mode is an XML-only legacy option, not available at org level.
optionExplanations.D: SOAP-style messages are the legacy XML format, not available at org level.

whyNotOthers: A is right because JSON SIM is the only format available at every level. The trap is B: legacy XML is still supported, but only at account and envelope level, never for organization-level configurations. C and D are legacy XML variants with the same restriction.

stem: Which request path does an app call to get the embedded signing URL for a recipient?

options.text: POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender
POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/recipients
GET /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}
POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient

answerText: POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient
explanation: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient is a POST to .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient, using the accountId and envelopeId of the envelope just created.

optionExplanations.A: views/sender returns an embedded sending view, not a signing view.
optionExplanations.B: The recipients endpoint lists or modifies recipients; it does not return a signing URL.
optionExplanations.C: GET on the envelope returns envelope information, not a signing session.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. POST .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient is EnvelopeViews:createRecipient.

whyNotOthers: D is right because views/recipient returns the signing URL. The trap is A: views/sender is the neighbouring view endpoint, but it is for embedded sending. B manages the envelope's recipient list and C reads the envelope's details.

stem: An ISV wants Maestro workflows to read records from and write records to its system of record. Which extension type should it build?

options.text: A connected fields extension
A Data IO extension
A Connect webhook listener
A bank account verification extension

answerText: A Data IO extension
explanation: Data IO extensions are used in Maestro workflows to read from and write to a system of record.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Data IO reads and writes system-of-record data in workflows.
optionExplanations.C: Connect pushes events out; it does not provide workflow read or write steps.
optionExplanations.D: Verifies bank data only; it does not read or write records.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the requirement is read and write access from workflows. The trap is A: connected fields also link Docusign to external data, but they work in eSignature and are not supported in Maestro. C only receives events, and D verifies bank details.

stem: A PUBLIC extension app passes review and shows Approved in the Developer Console. What must the developer do next so administrators can find and install it in production?

options.text: Run an additional functional test with a production envelope
Publish the app to the Docusign App Center
Submit a go-live request for an integration key
Start calling the production eSignature endpoint

answerText: Publish the app to the Docusign App Center
explanation: After approval, the developer clicks Publish to App Center; for a public app this makes it available to all customers in the App Center.

optionExplanations.A: Testing happens before review; it is not the step that lists an approved app.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Publishing to the App Center makes the approved public app installable.
optionExplanations.C: Go-live applies to integration keys for API integrations, not to extension apps.
optionExplanations.D: Calling production APIs does not make an extension app discoverable.

whyNotOthers: B is right because approval is followed by the publish step. The trap is C: go-live requests promote eSignature API integration keys and are not part of extension app publishing. A is not a required post-approval step, and D has nothing to do with listing the app.

stem: A background JWT integration gets an error during token exchange. Logs show the integration key and RSA key are correct, but the impersonated user has never approved the requested scopes. What must be completed before the request can succeed?

options.text: Individual or admin consent for the integration key and requested scopes
Adding impersonation to the scope claim of the JWT assertion
Requesting a refresh token with the extended scope
Changing aud to account.docusign.com

answerText: Individual or admin consent for the integration key and requested scopes
explanation: JWT tokens are only issued after the impersonated user, or an admin, has consented to the integration key and its scopes.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Consent for the integration key and scopes must exist before any JWT token is issued.
optionExplanations.B: Listing impersonation in the assertion does not replace consent by the user or an admin.
optionExplanations.C: extended is for Auth Code refresh tokens; JWT Grant never returns a refresh token.
optionExplanations.D: account.docusign.com is the production aud; changing it does not create consent and breaks a demo integration.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the logs rule out key problems and point to missing consent. The trap is B: impersonation must be part of the consent, but putting it in the assertion does not grant consent. C does not apply because JWT never returns a refresh token, and D would point a demo integration at the production auth server.

stem: An implementation note must state how long an embedded signing URL from EnvelopeViews:createRecipient can be used. What should it say?

options.text: 2 minutes, then it must be exchanged for a token
8 hours, like an access token
About 5 minutes, and it can be used only once
Until the envelope expires

answerText: About 5 minutes, and it can be used only once
explanation: The recipient view URL expires in about 5 minutes and is single-use, so it should be requested when the user is ready.

optionExplanations.A: 2 minutes is the authorization code lifetime in Authorization Code Grant, not the signing URL.
optionExplanations.B: 8 hours is the access token lifetime, not the recipient view URL.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The signing URL expires in about 5 minutes and is single-use.
optionExplanations.D: The envelope can stay open much longer, but each signing URL expires within minutes.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the signing URL is short-lived and single-use. The trap is A: 2 minutes is the lifetime of an OAuth authorization code, which is a different value. B is the access token lifetime and D confuses the URL with the envelope.

stem: A custom sales dashboard has a button that starts a Docusign workflow to send account-opening documents to a prospect. The dashboard's backend passes the prospect's name and email as starting values. Which start method should the workflow use?

options.text: From an API call
From an event
Manually in Docusign (Run Workflow)
From a link

answerText: From an API call
explanation: A custom app that starts the workflow programmatically and passes starting values uses the From an API call start method.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The dashboard backend triggers the workflow through the API with the prospect's values.
optionExplanations.B: The workflow is started by a user action in the dashboard, not by an event.
optionExplanations.C: Run Workflow is done inside Docusign, not from a custom dashboard.
optionExplanations.D: A link suits participant self-service; passing starting values calls for API start.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the backend triggers the workflow and supplies the starting values. The trap is D: a button could open a link, but links are for participants starting a workflow themselves, and Docusign recommends API start when passing starting values. B does not fit a button click, and C requires a user to work inside Docusign.

stem: A storage vendor wants Docusign customers to find its extension in the App Center, install it, and use it in their own agreement workflows. Which distribution model matches?

options.text: Private extension app limited to one organization's accounts
Public extension app published to the Docusign App Center
Keep the app in the developer account so customers use it in demo
Private app whose only allowed account is the vendor's own

answerText: Public extension app published to the Docusign App Center
explanation: Public App Center distribution is used when customers broadly need to discover and install an extension app.

optionExplanations.A: Private apps are limited to listed accounts, so customers could not find it in the App Center.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A public app in the App Center is discoverable and installable by customers.
optionExplanations.C: An unpublished app is only usable in the developer account in demo.
optionExplanations.D: Sharing only with the vendor's own account keeps customers from installing it.

whyNotOthers: B is right because public distribution is how many customers find and install an app. The trap is A: private distribution is for one organization's accounts, not a marketplace audience. C never reaches customers' production accounts, and D shares the app only with the vendor.

stem: An app requests consent to send envelopes and read basic user and account context. A developer suggests requesting every available scope now to avoid future changes. What is the better OAuth practice?

options.text: Request only the minimum scopes required for the current operations
Request every scope now, as the developer suggests
Omit scopes and let Docusign infer permissions
Add impersonation now so the app can switch to JWT later

answerText: Request only the minimum scopes required for the current operations
explanation: OAuth consent should follow least privilege: request only the scopes the app's current operations need.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Request only the scopes needed for the app's current operations.
optionExplanations.B: Requesting every scope grants access the app does not use and broadens the consent request.
