optionExplanations.C: Scopes must be requested explicitly; Docusign does not infer them from later API calls.
optionExplanations.D: impersonation lets the app act as the user through JWT; requesting it without a current need breaks least privilege.

whyNotOthers: A is right because least privilege limits risk and keeps consent focused. The trap is D: adding impersonation for a possible JWT move sounds forward-looking, but it grants the ability to act as the user without any current need. B is the over-requesting the question warns against, and C fails because scopes must be requested explicitly.

stem: Which request returns the embedded sending (sender view) URL for an existing draft envelope?

options.text: POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/recipient
POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender
POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes
PUT /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId} with status sent

answerText: POST /restapi/v2.1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender
explanation: EnvelopeViews:createSender is a POST to .../envelopes/{envelopeId}/views/sender for a draft envelope.

optionExplanations.A: views/recipient returns the embedded signing view for a recipient.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. POST .../views/sender is EnvelopeViews:createSender, the embedded sending view.
optionExplanations.C: POST .../envelopes creates an envelope; it does not return a view URL.
optionExplanations.D: PUT with status sent sends the draft immediately, skipping the in-app preparation.

whyNotOthers: B is right because views/sender is the sender view endpoint. The trap is A: views/recipient has the same shape, but it returns a signing URL for a recipient. C creates a new envelope and D sends an existing draft without any preparation view.

stem: In a loan workflow, the applicant, a loan officer and a branch manager each complete actions. How should the designer handle these people?

options.text: Define all three as participants with roles, ideally at the start of workflow creation
Give a role only to the person who starts the workflow
Skip participants; they are created automatically from the templates
Add participants only after the workflow is published

answerText: Define all three as participants with roles, ideally at the start of workflow creation
explanation: Anyone who takes action in a workflow is a participant and needs a defined role. Adding participants at the beginning is the recommended practice, although they can be added at any point while building.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Every person who acts is a participant; define them early.
optionExplanations.B: The officer and manager also act, so they need participant roles too.
optionExplanations.C: Participants are defined in the workflow; they are not created automatically from templates.
optionExplanations.D: Participants are configured while building the workflow, before publishing.

whyNotOthers: A is right because each person who acts needs a participant role. The trap is B: the person who starts the workflow is often a participant, but the officer and manager also act and need roles. C and D are wrong: participants are defined in the workflow, during design and not after publishing.

stem: Which two registration paths does the Developer Console offer for a new extension app?

options.text: A form-based experience, or uploading or editing a JSON manifest
Uploading a manifest through the eSignature REST API, or the App Center
The Apps and Keys page in eSignature Admin, or a support ticket
A Maestro workflow template, or a Web Forms configuration

answerText: A form-based experience, or uploading or editing a JSON manifest
explanation: In the Developer Console, Create App offers a form-based experience or editing/uploading a manifest file (with a built-in editor that validates in real time).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Register using the form-based experience or by uploading/editing a JSON manifest.
optionExplanations.B: Manifests are uploaded in the Developer Console; the App Center is where customers install published apps.
optionExplanations.C: Apps and Keys manages integration keys, and support tickets are not a registration path.
optionExplanations.D: Maestro and Web Forms consume extension apps; they do not register them.

whyNotOthers: A is right because those are the two Developer Console options. The trap is B: manifests are uploaded in the Developer Console, not through the eSignature API, and the App Center is for customers installing apps. C is for integration keys, and D are agreement process features, not registration methods.

stem: The /oauth/userinfo response lists several accounts for the user. Which account context should the app use by default for API calls?

options.text: The first account in the accounts array
Any account, because all accounts share one base URI
The account with is_default set to true, using its account_id and base_uri
The account whose ID matches the integration key

answerText: The account with is_default set to true, using its account_id and base_uri
explanation: The app typically uses the account with is_default=true and takes its account_id and base_uri for all later API requests.

optionExplanations.A: Array order does not mark the default account; use the is_default flag.
optionExplanations.B: Accounts can sit on different base URIs, which is why base_uri is returned per account.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Use the account with is_default=true and its account_id and base_uri.
optionExplanations.D: The integration key identifies the app, not a Docusign account.

whyNotOthers: C is right because is_default marks the account to use. The trap is A: taking the first array entry often works in testing, but the order is not a guarantee of the default account. B is wrong because accounts can have different base URIs, and D confuses the app's integration key with an account ID.

stem: An HR department implements embedded signing with its HR system. Users report a timeout expiration error when trying to sign. Which practice could cause this error?

options.text: Creating the envelope and signing URL before the user indicates they are ready to sign
Creating the envelope for remote signing instead of embedded signing
Creating the envelope in draft status
Creating the envelope using a composite template

answerText: Creating the envelope and signing URL before the user indicates they are ready to sign
explanation: Embedded signing URLs are short-lived. If the app creates the envelope and signing URL before the user is ready, the URL can expire before they use it, causing the timeout.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Generating the signing URL too early lets it expire before the user opens it.
optionExplanations.B: A remote signer would get an email instead; it would not produce a timeout in the embedded session.
optionExplanations.C: A draft envelope cannot be signed, but that is a status problem, not a timeout expiration.
optionExplanations.D: Composite templates are a way to build envelope content and do not affect URL expiration.

whyNotOthers: A is right because early URL generation is the classic cause of expiration errors. The trap is C: a draft envelope does cause embedded signing problems, but it produces a status error, not a timeout. B would produce an email invitation instead of an embedded session and D is just an envelope structure.

stem: After a Verify Someone's Identity step, compliance wants the ID evidence saved automatically to the company's SharePoint. The SharePoint extension app is installed. Which step fits?

options.text: A Writeback step to SharePoint
A Send an Email step with the evidence attached
A Connect configuration that forwards events to SharePoint
A Store Files step with the SharePoint app, after the identity step

answerText: A Store Files step with the SharePoint app, after the identity step
explanation: Store Files app steps automate storage of completed agreements and ID evidence data in services such as SharePoint, Box or Google Drive.

optionExplanations.A: Writeback updates data in external systems; it is not used to store evidence files.
optionExplanations.B: Emailing evidence is not automated storage and raises data-handling concerns.
optionExplanations.C: Connect sends events; it does not save ID evidence to SharePoint.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Store Files saves ID evidence data to SharePoint after verification.

whyNotOthers: D is right because Store Files covers ID evidence as well as agreements. The trap is A: Writeback also sends data to an external system, but it updates record fields, not stored files. B relies on email, and C only delivers event notifications.

stem: Where is the call to an external API defined within an extension app's structure?

options.text: In a Maestro workflow variable definition
In an extension's actionReferences list
In a connection that references the Docusign API gateway
In an action that references an external platform endpoint

answerText: In an action that references an external platform endpoint
explanation: An action defines the call to the external platform endpoint; extensions only reference actions, and connections supply authentication.

optionExplanations.A: Workflow variables hold data inside Maestro; they do not define extension app calls.
optionExplanations.B: actionReferences only names the actions; the call itself is defined in the action.
optionExplanations.C: Connections authenticate to the external platform, not to a Docusign API gateway.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. An action references the external platform endpoint that Docusign calls.

whyNotOthers: D is right because actions describe the external endpoint calls. The trap is B: actionReferences names the actions an extension uses but does not define the call. A is a workflow concept, and C wrongly points the connection at Docusign instead of the external platform.

stem: Inside a native app's Public Authorization Code Grant flow, which mechanism prevents an intercepted authorization code from being redeemed by another app?

options.text: The client secret in an Authorization: Basic header
A PKCE code verifier and code challenge
The state parameter echoed to the redirect URI
A JWT assertion signed with the app's RSA private key

answerText: A PKCE code verifier and code challenge
explanation: With PKCE, the code_challenge is sent on /oauth/auth and only the holder of the original code_verifier can redeem the code at /oauth/token, so an intercepted code is useless.

optionExplanations.A: A native app is a public client with no secret, so a Basic secret header is not available.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The code_verifier and code_challenge bind the code to the app that requested it.
optionExplanations.C: state protects the redirect against CSRF; it does not prevent an intercepted code from being redeemed.
optionExplanations.D: A signed JWT assertion is part of JWT Grant, not the Public Auth Code flow, and needs a protected private key.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the stem asks for the mechanism inside the flow, and PKCE binds the code to the original code_verifier. The trap is C: state is also sent through the redirect, but it protects against CSRF and does not stop someone else from redeeming the code. A needs a secret a native app cannot keep, and D belongs to JWT Grant.

stem: After initiating a bulk send, the app must report how many envelopes were sent, queued or failed. What should it use?

options.text: The batchId with BulkSend:getBulkSendBatchStatus, or Connect notifications
Poll each envelope with Envelopes:get every minute
The bulkListId with BulkSend:createBulkSendList
The canBeSent value from the test request

answerText: The batchId with BulkSend:getBulkSendBatchStatus, or Connect notifications
explanation: Initiating a bulk send returns a batchId; checking the batch status returns sent, queued and failed counts, and Connect can push status without polling.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. batchId with getBulkSendBatchStatus (or Connect) gives sent, queued and failed counts.
optionExplanations.B: Polling each envelope every minute exceeds polling guidance; Connect is the recommended alternative.
optionExplanations.C: bulkListId identifies the list, and createBulkSendList creates lists; neither reports batch results.
optionExplanations.D: canBeSent is returned by the test step and says only whether the bulk send can be sent.

whyNotOthers: A is right because batch status reports per-batch counts. The trap is C: bulkListId is a real bulk send identifier, but it identifies the list and createBulkSendList creates lists rather than reporting results. B breaks polling guidance and D only says whether the request could be sent.

stem: Agreements saved to Box by a workflow are missing signatures. The Box app is installed, and its Store Files step runs without errors. What should be fixed?

options.text: Reinstall the Box extension app
Change the start method to From an API call
Move the Store Files step after the Send Documents for Signature step
Switch Connect to JSON SIM

answerText: Move the Store Files step after the Send Documents for Signature step
explanation: The step runs successfully but stores an unsigned file, so it runs too early. Placing it after the signing step stores the completed agreement.

optionExplanations.A: The app already works; reinstalling does not change when the file is stored.
optionExplanations.B: The start method does not change step order.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Store the file after signing so the completed agreement is saved.
optionExplanations.D: Connect format affects notifications only.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the clue is that the app works but the document is unsigned. The trap is A: reinstalling is the usual fix for app failures, but the step already runs without errors. B and D change how the workflow starts or reports events, not when the file is saved.

stem: A partner is building a PUBLIC extension app that connects Docusign to its external SaaS platform. Which OAuth 2.0 grant should the app's connection use?

options.text: Implicit Grant
JWT Grant with an RSA key pair
Client Credentials Grant
Authorization Code Grant

answerText: Authorization Code Grant
explanation: Extension app connections support Authorization Code Grant or Client Credentials Grant; public apps connecting to external systems use Authorization Code Grant.

optionExplanations.A: Implicit Grant is not a supported extension app connection grant.
optionExplanations.B: JWT Grant is how your app calls Docusign APIs; extension connections use Authorization Code or Client Credentials.
optionExplanations.C: Client Credentials is allowed only for private apps connecting to internal systems, not public apps.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Public extension apps use Authorization Code Grant for their connection.

whyNotOthers: D is right because public extension apps use Authorization Code Grant. The trap is C: Client Credentials is an option only for private apps connecting to internal systems (and only for US clients). A and B are Docusign eSignature auth flows for your app calling Docusign, not grants for extension app connections.

stem: Envelopes:create calls return 201 Created, but no recipient gets an email and the envelopes sit in the sender's Drafts folder. Which status value should the request use so envelopes go out immediately?

options.text: created
voided
completed
sent

answerText: sent
explanation: Envelopes appearing as drafts means the request used status created. Changing the request to status sent delivers them immediately.

optionExplanations.A: created is the cause of the symptom: it saves the envelope as a draft, so no email is sent.
optionExplanations.B: voided cancels an in-process envelope; it would stop the envelope rather than deliver it.
optionExplanations.C: completed is a terminal status set by Docusign when all recipients finish; it cannot be used to send.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. status sent sends the envelope as part of the create call, so recipients are notified.

whyNotOthers: D is right because sent is the value that sends the envelope on creation. The trap is A: created is exactly what produces the draft symptom described. B would cancel the envelope and C is set by Docusign only after every recipient finishes.

stem: In Workflow Builder, which category contains branching rules, along with steps such as Send an Email and Show a Confirmation Screen?

options.text: Docusign steps
Utility steps
Apps steps
Start methods

answerText: Utility steps
explanation: Utility steps cover notification actions such as sending an email and workflow control actions such as branching rules.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign steps cover features like Web Forms, eSignature and ID verification, not branching.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Utility steps include branching rules, Send an Email and confirmation screens.
optionExplanations.C: Apps steps call third-party extension apps.
optionExplanations.D: Start methods decide how a workflow begins; they are not steps.

whyNotOthers: B is right because branching is a workflow control action, which is a utility step. The trap is A: Docusign steps are the built-in Docusign feature steps (Web Forms, eSignature, identity verification), not control logic. C is for extension apps, and D decides how a workflow starts.

stem: Which statement correctly describes cross-references in an extension app manifest?

options.text: Actions reference extensions, and connections reference actions
Connections reference extensions through actionReferences
Extensions reference actions (actionReferences); actions reference connections (connectionsReference)
Extensions reference connections directly through connectionsReference

answerText: Extensions reference actions (actionReferences); actions reference connections (connectionsReference)
explanation: The chain is extension to action (actionReferences) and action to connection (connectionsReference).

optionExplanations.A: This reverses both links; extensions point to actions, and actions point to connections.
optionExplanations.B: actionReferences belongs to extensions, and connections do not reference anything.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Extensions point to actions, and actions point to connections.
optionExplanations.D: connectionsReference is on actions, not extensions.

whyNotOthers: C is right because it gives both links in the correct direction. The trap is D: extensions do not reference connections directly; the connection link sits on each action. A and B reverse the direction of the references.

stem: A bulk send flow starts by creating the envelope that a bulk send list will later be applied to. Which status should that envelope be created with?

options.text: sent
voided
created
completed

answerText: created
explanation: The bulk send process begins with a draft envelope (status created), whose envelopeId is then used with the bulk send list. The clue is that the list is applied later.

optionExplanations.A: sent would deliver this single envelope immediately instead of keeping it as the bulk send source.
optionExplanations.B: voided cancels an in-process envelope; it is never used to create one.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The bulk send flow starts with a draft envelope created with status created.
optionExplanations.D: completed is set by Docusign after all recipients finish; it is not a create value.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the bulk send envelope is created as a draft with status created. The trap is A: sent is the normal create value, but sending would deliver the envelope to its own recipients instead of serving as the bulk send source. B and D are not create values: voided cancels and completed is set by Docusign.

stem: Customers without Docusign accounts must be able to submit an account change request at any time via a link in an automatic email reply. Which start method should the workflow use?

options.text: From a link
Manually in Docusign (Run Workflow)
From an API call
Triggered from a CLM workflow

answerText: From a link
explanation: From a link is recommended for self-service forms such as account change requests; the link can be placed in a website or an automatic email reply.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The link in the auto-reply lets customers start the workflow themselves.
optionExplanations.B: Requires an internal user with Workflows: Prepare permission.
optionExplanations.C: Needs custom code with an access token; nothing here calls the API.
optionExplanations.D: Started from within Docusign CLM, not by customers.

whyNotOthers: A is right because customers start the workflow themselves from a link. The trap is B: Run Workflow is also a no-code start, but only internal users with Workflows: Prepare permission can use it. C needs an integration with an access token, and D runs from inside Docusign CLM.

stem: A retailer must check a customer's custom loyalty ID against its own system of record while the customer enters details during signing. Which extension type and extension point should be used?

options.text: Data Verification at eSignature signing
File archive through a Maestro workflow
Connected Fields through the eSignature Add Fields view and signing
Data IO through a Maestro workflow

answerText: Connected Fields through the eSignature Add Fields view and signing
explanation: Connected fields verify custom values against your own system of record at the Add Fields view and during signing.

optionExplanations.A: Data Verification handles standard types, not a custom loyalty ID.
optionExplanations.B: File archive stores documents and is legacy.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Connected fields verify custom data at Add Fields and signing.
optionExplanations.D: Data IO runs in Maestro workflows, not during the signing ceremony.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a custom loyalty ID checked against the retailer's system is connected fields territory. The trap is A: Data Verification runs at the same point but only covers standard types like bank account, address or SSN. B and D run in Maestro, not during signing.

stem: One of two signers has already signed a sent envelope when a fatal error is found. The envelope must be canceled so the second signer cannot sign. Which status should be set?

options.text: created
voided
sent
completed

answerText: voided
explanation: An envelope can be voided while it is still in process, even after some recipients have signed. The clue is that it is not yet completed.

optionExplanations.A: created is the draft status; it does not cancel a sent, partially signed envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Voiding cancels the in-process envelope so the remaining signer cannot sign.
optionExplanations.C: sent is the current status; setting it again would not stop the second signer.
optionExplanations.D: completed is set by Docusign only when all recipients finish; it does not cancel the envelope.

whyNotOthers: B is right because voided cancels an in-process envelope, including a partially signed one. The trap is D: one signer finished, but completed is only reached when all recipients finish and is not set by the sender. A is a draft status and C is the status it already has.

stem: Which data does the body of a TriggerWorkflow request contain?

options.text: An envelope definition with documents and recipients
The workflowId and an envelope status of 'sent'
Only the mtid and mtsec values
An instance_name and trigger_inputs matching the workflow's trigger_input_schema

answerText: An instance_name and trigger_inputs matching the workflow's trigger_input_schema
explanation: TriggerWorkflow requires an instance_name and the input data described by the workflow's trigger_input_schema, passed in trigger_inputs.

optionExplanations.A: An envelope definition belongs to Envelopes:create, not to a workflow trigger.
optionExplanations.B: Envelope status is an eSignature concept; it is not part of a trigger body.
optionExplanations.C: mtid and mtsec are query parameters on the trigger URL, not the body.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. instance_name plus trigger_inputs that match the input schema.

whyNotOthers: D is right because those are the documented body fields. The trap is C: mtid and mtsec are required to identify and authenticate the trigger, but they are query parameters on the trigger URL, not the body. A and B describe eSignature envelope requests.

stem: Before configuring an extension app manifest, which information should the developer gather from the external service, identity provider and any API proxy?

options.text: The Docusign integration key, secret and redirect URI of an eSignature app
Endpoint URLs, authorization details, and required request and response parameters
The Connect HMAC secret for the customer's account
Recipient email addresses for the test envelopes

answerText: Endpoint URLs, authorization details, and required request and response parameters
explanation: The developer needs endpoint URLs, authorization details, and the required parameters in requests and responses from the external service, identity provider and proxy.

optionExplanations.A: These identify an app calling Docusign; the manifest needs the external platform's details.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Endpoints, auth details and request/response parameters are needed to configure the app.
optionExplanations.C: The Connect HMAC secret secures webhooks, not extension app calls.
optionExplanations.D: Recipient emails are envelope data, not extension app configuration.

whyNotOthers: B is right because those values configure the connections and actions. The trap is A: those are Docusign credentials for calling Docusign, not what the manifest needs to call the external service. C belongs to Connect, and D is test data.

stem: An architect asks which platform-native field addresses duplicate envelopes when a create request is retried after a dropped connection. Which option is correct?

options.text: transactionId
bulkListId
batchId
envelopeId

answerText: transactionId
explanation: transactionId is a sender-generated value on the envelope definition used to tell whether an envelope from an earlier attempt was already created.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. transactionId is supplied by the sender and identifies the create attempt across retries.
optionExplanations.B: bulkListId identifies a bulk send list; it is unrelated to single envelope retries.
optionExplanations.C: batchId identifies a bulk send batch; it does not cover single Envelopes:create calls.
optionExplanations.D: envelopeId is generated by Docusign, so after a dropped connection the client does not have it.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the client supplies transactionId with the create request. The trap is D: envelopeId identifies envelopes, but it is generated by Docusign and unknown to the client after a dropped connection. B and C are bulk send identifiers for a list and a batch.

stem: A trigger call works with a token from API Explorer, but the app's JWT token, requested with only the 'signature impersonation' scopes, gets an authorization error. What should the developer change?

options.text: Use the eSignature base path /restapi/v2.1
Republish the workflow
Request the aow_manage scope as well and have consent granted for it
Add more fields to trigger_inputs

answerText: Request the aow_manage scope as well and have consent granted for it
explanation: Maestro API calls need the signature scope plus Maestro scopes such as aow_manage. A newly requested scope also needs consent before JWT can use it.

optionExplanations.A: Maestro uses api-d.docusign.com/v1 or api.docusign.com/v1, not /restapi/v2.1.
optionExplanations.B: Republishing does not change the scopes in the app's token.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Add aow_manage to the requested scopes and grant consent for it.
optionExplanations.D: Input problems cause validation errors, not authorization errors.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the app's token lacks the Maestro scope. The trap is D: missing inputs are another common trigger error, but they cause input validation failures, not an authorization error. A uses the wrong base path for Maestro, and B does not change the token.

stem: Security rules forbid exposing an internal system of record directly to the internet, but an extension action must reach it. Which approach fits?

options.text: Expose a publicly reachable API proxy in front of it and allow Docusign traffic
Have the internal system poll Docusign for pending actions
Use Connect to push action requests into the private network
Distribute the app privately, which runs actions inside Docusign's network

answerText: Expose a publicly reachable API proxy in front of it and allow Docusign traffic
explanation: Docusign must be able to call the endpoint, so a reachable API proxy (with Docusign traffic allowed) can front the internal system without exposing it directly.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A reachable API proxy lets Docusign call in while the backend stays internal.
optionExplanations.B: Extension actions are called by Docusign; the service does not poll for work.
optionExplanations.C: Connect sends event notifications; it does not deliver extension action calls.
optionExplanations.D: Private distribution controls installation, not network location; Docusign still calls your endpoint.

whyNotOthers: A is right because a proxy gives Docusign a reachable endpoint while shielding the internal system. The trap is D: private distribution limits who can install the app, but Docusign still calls your endpoint over the network. B and C are not how extension actions are invoked.

topic: Make an API call to request the signing URL
stem: An embedded signing flow has created and sent the envelope with clientUserId on the signer. The app now needs the browser URL for that recipient's signing ceremony. Which step starts the ceremony?

options.text: Call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient to request the recipient view URL
Wait for Docusign to email the embedded signer
Call EnvelopeViews:createSender for the signer
Set the envelope status back to created

answerText: Call EnvelopeViews:createRecipient to request the recipient view URL
explanation: For embedded signing, the app calls EnvelopeViews:createRecipient to get a short-lived recipient view URL and redirects the signer to it.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. createRecipient returns the URL for the embedded signer's ceremony.
optionExplanations.B: Embedded signers with clientUserId are not emailed a signing invitation.
optionExplanations.C: createSender opens the sending and tagging view for the sender, not the signing ceremony.
optionExplanations.D: Reverting to created is not part of embedded signing; the envelope must stay sent.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the recipient view is the signing ceremony. The trap is C: createSender is another view endpoint, but it opens the sender's preparation view, not the signer's ceremony. B fails because embedded signers are not emailed and D would turn the envelope back into a draft workflow.

stem: An app redirects users to the workflow instance URL from TriggerWorkflow instead of embedding it. Where are users when they finish the workflow?

options.text: Redirected automatically to the app's returnUrl
They remain on the Docusign platform
Signed out and sent to the Docusign login page
Shown a download prompt for the agreement

answerText: They remain on the Docusign platform
explanation: With the redirect option, users are routed to the Docusign platform and remain there when they complete the workflow. To keep them in the app, embed the instance URL in an iframe.

optionExplanations.A: returnUrl belongs to eSignature recipient views, not to workflow instance redirects.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Users stay on Docusign; use an iframe to keep them in the app.
optionExplanations.C: Nothing signs the user out at the end of the workflow.
optionExplanations.D: No download prompt is part of this behavior.

whyNotOthers: B is right because a redirect does not return users to the app. The trap is A: returnUrl comes from eSignature embedded signing, but workflow instance URLs do not send the user back to the app. C and D are not documented behavior.

stem: A financial institution needs real-time validation of a customer's bank account details, using a standard bank verification service, while the customer signs a loan agreement. Which extension type and extension point apply?

options.text: Connected Fields, triggered in a Maestro workflow
Data IO, triggered at the eSignature Add Fields view
Data Verification, triggered at eSignature signing
File archive, triggered at eSignature signing

answerText: Data Verification, triggered at eSignature signing
explanation: Data Verification at eSignature signing validates the bank account details in real time as the customer signs.

optionExplanations.A: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro and target custom data.
optionExplanations.B: Data IO runs in Maestro workflows and does not verify fields at Add Fields.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Data Verification runs at signing to validate the bank account.
optionExplanations.D: File archive stores documents and is a legacy workflow extension.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a standard bank account check during signing is Data Verification. The trap is A: connected fields are not supported in Maestro and are for custom data. B places Data IO at the wrong extension point, and D stores files.

stem: A template-reference request worked in the demo environment and is moving to production at Go-Live. Which value in the request references the stored template and must be updated for production?

options.text: roleName in templateRoles
sequence
The template's display name
templateId

answerText: templateId
explanation: Requests reference stored templates by templateId, and template IDs differ between demo and production, so they must be updated during Go-Live.

optionExplanations.A: roleName maps recipients to template roles; it is defined by the template, not an environment-specific ID.
optionExplanations.B: sequence orders server and inline templates inside composite templates; it does not identify a template.
optionExplanations.C: The display name is not how the API references a template; requests use templateId.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. templateId references the stored template and differs between demo and production.

whyNotOthers: D is right because templateId is the reference, and it changes between environments. The trap is C: the template's name may be the same in both environments, but requests do not reference templates by name. A maps recipients to roles and B applies to server and inline templates in composite templates.

stem: A team wants its Maestro workflow to use connected fields to verify data. What must they know?

options.text: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows; use an extension app step such as Data IO instead
Connected fields can be added to the Prepare eSignature Template step
Connected fields are enabled through the Connect configuration
Connected fields are installed from the Developer Console

answerText: Connected fields are not supported in Maestro workflows; use an extension app step such as Data IO instead
explanation: Connected fields are not currently supported in Maestro workflows. Workflows use extension app steps, such as Data IO, to work with external data.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Connected fields are not supported in Maestro; use extension app steps such as Data IO.
optionExplanations.B: Connected fields remain unsupported in Maestro, even through a template step.
optionExplanations.C: Connect is the webhook service and has nothing to do with connected fields.
optionExplanations.D: The Developer Console is for building apps; admins install apps from App Center.

whyNotOthers: A is right because Maestro does not support connected fields. The trap is B: templates used by workflows can contain tabs, so it seems possible, but connected fields are still not supported in Maestro. C confuses Connect with connected fields, and D confuses building an app with installing one.

stem: Where is a Data IO extension invoked?

options.text: In the eSignature Add Fields view and during signing
Only in Web Forms
Through Connect envelope events
In Maestro workflows

answerText: In Maestro workflows
explanation: The extension point for Data IO is Maestro workflows.

optionExplanations.A: Add Fields and signing are the extension points for connected fields and data verification.
optionExplanations.B: Web Forms is an extension point only for email and phone verification.
optionExplanations.C: Connect sends event notifications; it is not where Data IO runs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Data IO's extension point is Maestro workflows.

whyNotOthers: D is right because Data IO runs as part of Maestro workflows. The trap is A: Add Fields and signing are the extension points for connected fields and data verification. B applies only to email and phone verification, and C is a notification mechanism, not an extension point.

stem: A composite template object has a server template that defines the role 'customer' and an inline template that maps a recipient to that role. How should their sequence values be set?

options.text: Inline template lower, so its recipient is applied first
Both templates use the same sequence value
Server template lower than the inline template
Omit sequence on the inline template

answerText: Server template lower than the inline template
explanation: Attributes are applied in sequence order and later ones overwrite earlier ones, so the server template must have the lower sequence to establish the role before the inline template maps a recipient to it.

optionExplanations.A: If the inline template runs first, the role it maps to does not exist yet.
optionExplanations.B: Sequence values must be unique within a composite template object.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Server template first (lower sequence) establishes the role; the inline template then maps the recipient.
optionExplanations.D: Every serverTemplate and inlineTemplate object must have a sequence property.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the role must exist before a recipient is mapped to it. The trap is A: it sounds like the recipient should be applied first, but then the role 'customer' would not exist yet. B fails because sequence values must be unique within a composite template object, and D fails because every serverTemplate and inlineTemplate needs a sequence.

stem: In Workflow Builder, which step category uses installed extension apps such as Box, Google Drive or SharePoint to save completed agreements?

options.text: Writeback steps
Read steps
Store Files steps
ID Verification steps

answerText: Store Files steps
explanation: Store Files steps automate storing completed agreements and ID Evidence data with apps such as Google Drive, Box, Dropbox, OneDrive and SharePoint.

optionExplanations.A: Writeback steps update data in external systems, not store files.
optionExplanations.B: Read steps import data into the workflow.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Store Files steps save agreements to storage apps.
optionExplanations.D: ID Verification verifies the signer's identity, not file storage.

whyNotOthers: C is right because saving agreements to storage is a Store Files step. The trap is A: Writeback steps update data in external systems such as Salesforce or ServiceNow, not files. B imports data, and D verifies the signer's identity.

stem: A team converts a manual process to the API. The document's length varies, but the signature should appear near a specific text string. Which tab placement method is best?

options.text: Copy the coordinates from a sample document into xPosition/yPosition
Anchor tagging with anchorString and offsets
Reference the document by templateId
Use one tab per page and let the signer choose

answerText: Anchor tagging with anchorString and offsets
explanation: Anchor tagging places tabs relative to document text, so placement survives changes in length. The clue is 'near a specific text string'.

optionExplanations.A: Coordinates from one sample document are fixed and break when the next document's length differs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. anchorString with offsets puts the tab next to the text regardless of length.
optionExplanations.C: templateId references a saved template; it does not place tabs on a variable document.
optionExplanations.D: Extra tabs on every page create unwanted fields and do not place the signature correctly.

whyNotOthers: B is right because anchor tabs follow the text. The trap is A: coordinates from a sample work for that sample, but fixed positions do not move when another document is longer or shorter. C references a template rather than positioning tabs and D creates extra fields instead of placing one correctly.

stem: A connected fields extension app connects to a system of record that uses its own proprietary schema. Which data model must the app expose to Docusign?

options.text: JSON Schema types declared in the manifest's actions
The Concerto data model
The legacy XML Connect format
Only standard eSignature tab types

answerText: The Concerto data model
explanation: Docusign models data input and output definitions with Concerto; if your system does not already use it, you implement logic to map to it.

optionExplanations.A: Type definitions use the Concerto model, not JSON Schema in the actions object.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Connected fields (and Data IO) type definitions use the Concerto data model.
optionExplanations.C: XML Connect is a webhook payload format, not a data model for extensions.
optionExplanations.D: Custom data types are defined by your Concerto models, not limited to standard tabs.

whyNotOthers: B is right because type definitions returned to Docusign use Concerto. The trap is A: actions describe endpoints, but the type definitions are Concerto models. C is an event notification format, and D would not describe custom data types.

stem: A pull request adds embedded signing. The reviewer checks the envelope JSON for the recipient property that marks the signer as embedded. Which property should be present?

options.text: clientUserId
recipientId
returnUrl
EnvelopeViews:createRecipient

answerText: clientUserId
explanation: clientUserId on the signer marks embedded (captive) signing. The clue is a recipient property in the envelope JSON.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Setting clientUserId on the signer marks the recipient as embedded (captive).
optionExplanations.B: recipientId identifies the recipient within the envelope; every recipient has one, embedded or not.
optionExplanations.C: returnUrl is sent in the createRecipient request to say where to redirect after signing; it is not a recipient property.
optionExplanations.D: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient is the endpoint that returns the signing URL, not a recipient property.

whyNotOthers: A is right because clientUserId is the recipient property for embedded signing. The trap is D: createRecipient is part of the same feature, but it is an endpoint called afterwards, not a property in the envelope JSON. B identifies any recipient and C is set in the createRecipient request.

stem: Which extension point does a postal address verification extension use?

options.text: eSignature Add Fields view and signing
eSignature and Web Forms
Maestro workflows
The App Center listing

answerText: eSignature Add Fields view and signing
explanation: Postal address verification runs at the eSignature Add Fields view and during signing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Postal address verification runs at Add Fields and signing.
optionExplanations.B: Only email and phone verification are also available in Web Forms.
optionExplanations.C: Maestro workflows are the extension point for Data IO and File IO.
optionExplanations.D: The App Center is for installing apps, not an extension point.

whyNotOthers: A is right because that is the extension point for postal address verification. The trap is B: Web Forms support applies only to email and phone verification. C is the extension point for Data IO and File IO, and D is where apps are installed.

stem: An app will show the embedded signing session in focused view. Which two additional parameters must the createRecipient request include beyond the standard ones?

options.text: clientUserId and recipientId
returnUrl and authenticationMethod
identityVerification and returnUrl
frameAncestors and messageOrigins

answerText: frameAncestors and messageOrigins
explanation: Focused view requires frameAncestors (your site plus the Docusign apps domain) and messageOrigins in addition to the standard recipient view parameters.

optionExplanations.A: clientUserId is a standard matching value and recipientId is not a focused view parameter.
optionExplanations.B: returnUrl and authenticationMethod are required for all recipient views, not the focused view additions.
optionExplanations.C: identityVerification cannot be used with focused view; ID verification requires classic view.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Focused view needs frameAncestors and messageOrigins in the createRecipient request.

whyNotOthers: D is right because frameAncestors and messageOrigins are the focused view additions. The trap is B: returnUrl and authenticationMethod are required, but for every recipient view, not specifically for focused view. A mixes a matching value with an envelope identifier and C fails because identityVerification cannot be used with focused view.

stem: When registering an extension app with the form-based experience, the developer must choose at least one extension type. Which list matches the available types?

options.text: Connect, PowerForms, Web Forms and Bulk Send
Read, Store Files, Writeback and Sign steps
Data IO, File IO, Connected Fields and ID Verification
File IO, Data IO, Data Verification and Connected Fields

answerText: File IO, Data IO, Data Verification and Connected Fields
explanation: The registration form offers File Input Output, Data Input Output, Data Verification and Connected Fields as extension types.

optionExplanations.A: These are eSignature sending and notification features, not extension types.
optionExplanations.B: These are Workflow Builder step categories that use installed apps, not the extension types chosen at registration.
optionExplanations.C: ID Verification is a separate identity product; the fourth extension type is Data Verification.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. File IO, Data IO, Data Verification and Connected Fields are the extension types offered at registration.

whyNotOthers: D is right because those four are the extension types offered at registration. The trap is C: it swaps Data Verification for ID Verification, which is a separate Docusign identity product, not an extension type. B lists Workflow Builder step categories, and A lists eSignature features.

stem: A design must avoid expired embedded signing sessions. Which pattern should the team choose?

options.text: Generate each signing URL at envelope creation and store it in the database
Generate signing URLs in a nightly batch
Create the envelope ahead of time and request the signing URL when the user clicks Sign
Email the signing URL to the user as a backup

answerText: Create the envelope ahead of time and request the signing URL when the user clicks Sign
explanation: The envelope can be created in advance, but the short-lived signing URL should be requested only when the user is ready, such as on the Sign click.

optionExplanations.A: A stored URL will usually have expired by the time the user opens it.
optionExplanations.B: Nightly batch generation creates URLs hours before use, so they expire.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Requesting the URL when the user clicks Sign avoids its short lifetime.
optionExplanations.D: Emailing an embedded signing URL does not help; it expires quickly and bypasses the app.

whyNotOthers: C is right because it requests the URL just before use. The trap is A: storing the URL at creation looks efficient, but the URL expires within minutes and is single-use. B generates URLs even earlier and D sends a short-lived embedded URL by email, outside the app.

stem: A company that is not a Docusign partner builds an extension app only for its own accounts. Which distribution plan is correct?

options.text: Public, because any developer account can list an app publicly
Public, then restrict it with publicationRegions
Private, limited to the company's listed production accounts
Private for now, then switch the same published app to public later

answerText: Private, limited to the company's listed production accounts
explanation: Private distribution suits an app for the company's own accounts and does not require Docusign Partner Program membership, which public publishing does.

optionExplanations.A: Only Docusign partners may publish public extension apps, and the app is meant for one company anyway.
optionExplanations.B: publicationRegions limits regions for public apps; it does not restrict installation to one company.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Private distribution limits installation to listed production accounts and fits a non-partner's internal app.
optionExplanations.D: The distribution type cannot be changed after the app is published, so this plan does not work.

whyNotOthers: C is right because the app serves only the company's accounts and private distribution needs no partner membership. The trap is D: the distribution type cannot be changed after an app is published. A is wrong because only Docusign partners may publish public apps, and B uses a region setting that does not restrict to one organization.

stem: A sender must prepare or edit an envelope from inside a custom app. Which endpoint is relevant?

options.text: EnvelopeViews:createRecipient
EnvelopeViews:createSender
Envelopes:create with status sent
Templates:create

answerText: EnvelopeViews:createSender
explanation: Embedded sending uses EnvelopeViews:createSender to get a sender view URL for a draft envelope.

optionExplanations.A: createRecipient is for embedded signing by a recipient, not for preparing an envelope.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. createSender opens the sending view where the user tags and sends the envelope.
optionExplanations.C: status sent sends the envelope at once; the user cannot prepare it first.
optionExplanations.D: Templates:create saves a template; it does not let a sender edit this envelope in the app.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the sender view lets the user prepare and send inside the app. The trap is A: createRecipient is the other embedded view, but it serves signers. C sends immediately without preparation and D creates a reusable template, not an in-app sending experience for this envelope.

stem: A partner's public extension app must be installable only by customers in selected geographic regions. Which manifest property controls this?

options.text: distribution set to PRIVATE
publicationRegions
connections
actions

answerText: publicationRegions
explanation: publicationRegions (public apps only) chooses the regions from which the app can be installed.

optionExplanations.A: PRIVATE restricts installation to listed accounts, not regions, and removes broad availability.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. publicationRegions sets the regions from which a public app can be installed.
optionExplanations.C: connections defines authentication to the external platform, not installation regions.
optionExplanations.D: actions describes the external operations Docusign calls, not where the app is available.

whyNotOthers: B is right because publicationRegions limits a public app by region. The trap is A: PRIVATE limits installation to specific listed accounts, not to regions, and it would stop broad availability. C holds authentication settings and D holds the external operations.

stem: In the bulk send process, which step returns the batchId used to track the envelopes in the batch?

options.text: Initiating the bulk send (BulkSend:createBulkSendRequest)
Creating the bulk send list (BulkSend:createBulkSendList)
Testing the bulk send (BulkSend:createBulkSendTestRequest)
Creating the draft envelope (Envelopes:create)

answerText: Initiating the bulk send (BulkSend:createBulkSendRequest)
explanation: Initiating the bulk send returns a batchId, which is then used to check the status of envelopes in that batch.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Initiating the bulk send returns the batchId for status tracking.
optionExplanations.B: Creating the bulk send list returns a bulkListId, not a batchId.
optionExplanations.C: The test request returns canBeSent, a Boolean saying whether the bulk send can go ahead.
optionExplanations.D: Creating the draft envelope returns its envelopeId for use in the bulk send request.

whyNotOthers: A is right because the batch exists only once the bulk send is initiated. The trap is B: creating the list is a bulk send step, but it returns a bulkListId, not a batchId. C returns a canBeSent Boolean and D returns the draft's envelopeId.

stem: A manifest review finds an extension app must invoke a customer-hosted pricing API from a workflow step. The connection exists, but the callable operation itself is not yet described. Where should it be defined?

options.text: In an action definition inside the extension app manifest
In the connections object, next to the token URL
In the App Center listing description
In the publisher object

answerText: In an action definition inside the extension app manifest
explanation: The callable operation belongs in an action definition; the existing connection handles authentication separately.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The action definition describes the external operation Docusign can invoke.
optionExplanations.B: Connections hold authentication details such as the token URL, not the operation.
optionExplanations.C: The App Center listing description is customer-facing text, not call configuration.
optionExplanations.D: publisher holds the publisher's name and contact details only.

whyNotOthers: A is right because actions describe what Docusign calls. The trap is B: the connection already exists and only covers authentication, so adding the operation there is wrong. C is listing text and D is publisher contact information.

stem: Why must each connection in an extension app manifest have a unique name?

options.text: Docusign uses the name as the OAuth client ID
The name becomes the redirect URI for the authorization flow
The App Center shows it as the app's listing title
Actions refer to the connection by name through connectionsReference

answerText: Actions refer to the connection by name through connectionsReference
explanation: Connection names are referenced again by actions through connectionsReference, so each must be unique.

optionExplanations.A: The client ID is a separate auth parameter from the external provider.
optionExplanations.B: The redirect URI is not derived from the connection name.
optionExplanations.C: The listing title comes from the app's name property, not a connection name.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Actions use connectionsReference to point to a connection by its unique name.

whyNotOthers: D is right because the name is the key that actions use to find the connection. The trap is C: the App Center title comes from the app's name property, which also must be unique, but that is a different field. A and B confuse the connection name with OAuth parameters.

stem: Two actions in one extension app call the same CRM with the same OAuth credentials. How should the manifest express this?

options.text: Copy the client ID and secret into each action definition
Create a separate extension app for each action
Define one connection and set both actions' connectionsReference to its name
List both actions in one extension's actionReferences

answerText: Define one connection and set both actions' connectionsReference to its name
explanation: One connection can be shared: each action points to it by name with connectionsReference.

optionExplanations.A: Actions do not store credentials; they reference a connection.
optionExplanations.B: Separate apps are unnecessary; one app can share a connection across actions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Both actions reference the same connection via connectionsReference.
optionExplanations.D: actionReferences ties actions to an extension but does not supply auth.

whyNotOthers: C is right because a single named connection can be reused by many actions. The trap is D: actionReferences groups the actions under an extension but provides no authentication. A duplicates credentials in the wrong place, and B adds needless apps.

stem: In an extension app architecture, where does an API proxy sit?

options.text: Between the signer's browser and the Docusign signing page
Between Docusign and the third-party API, translating requests and responses
Inside the customer's Docusign account as an installed app
Between the Connect service and the developer's webhook listener

answerText: Between Docusign and the third-party API, translating requests and responses
explanation: The proxy sits between Docusign and the external API, converting calls into the format each side expects.

optionExplanations.A: The signer's browser is not part of the extension action call path.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The proxy mediates and translates between Docusign and the external API.
optionExplanations.C: The installed app is configuration in the account; the proxy is infrastructure you host.
optionExplanations.D: Connect listeners receive events; they do not sit in the extension action path.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the proxy mediates Docusign's calls to the third-party API. The trap is D: Connect delivers events to a listener and is not part of extension action calls. A concerns the signing UI, and C confuses the proxy with the installed app.

stem: Which statement about extension app infrastructure is correct?

options.text: You host the action endpoints and must let Docusign's calls through your firewall
Docusign hosts your action code once the manifest is uploaded
Endpoints only need to be reachable from the developer's network
The firewall must be opened only for Connect event delivery

answerText: You host the action endpoints and must let Docusign's calls through your firewall
explanation: The developer hosts the service behind the actions; Docusign calls it, so the firewall must allow Docusign's requests.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Your service hosts the endpoints, and Docusign's calls must get through.
optionExplanations.B: The manifest only describes endpoints; your service still runs on your infrastructure.
optionExplanations.C: Docusign's servers, not the developer's network, make the calls.
optionExplanations.D: Connect is separate; extension action calls also need to reach your endpoint.

whyNotOthers: A is right because you host the endpoints and they must be reachable by Docusign. The trap is D: Connect is a separate webhook feature; extension actions are a different set of calls that also need firewall access. B is wrong because Docusign does not host your code, and C ignores that Docusign is the caller.

stem: A Maestro workflow step must look up a customer's current account tier in an external system, then write the signed-agreement reference back after completion. Which extension type is designed for this structured record exchange?

options.text: File IO extension
Data IO extension
Connected Fields extension
Data Verification extension

answerText: Data IO extension
explanation: Data IO extensions read and write structured records in external systems from Maestro workflows.

optionExplanations.A: File IO writes files, not structured record values.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Data IO reads and writes structured records from a workflow.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields verify eSignature field values and are not supported in Maestro.
optionExplanations.D: Data Verification validates values such as addresses; it does not read/write records.

whyNotOthers: B is right because the step reads and writes records. The trap is A: File IO writes documents to storage, not structured fields back to a record. C is not supported in Maestro and verifies eSignature fields, and D checks standard data types.

stem: What is Docusign's guidance on the file archive extension?

options.text: It is the recommended extension for all new File IO apps
It has been removed, and existing apps stopped working
Existing apps stay supported, but new apps should use file output cloud storage
It is available only to private extension apps

answerText: Existing apps stay supported, but new apps should use file output cloud storage
explanation: Docusign continues to support existing apps that use file archive, but new apps should use the file output cloud storage extension.

optionExplanations.A: New apps should use file output cloud storage, not file archive.
optionExplanations.B: Existing file archive apps remain supported.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. File archive is legacy; use file output cloud storage for new apps.
optionExplanations.D: Distribution type does not determine whether file archive is available.

whyNotOthers: C is right because file archive is legacy and file output cloud storage is for new apps. The trap is A: it reverses the recommendation. B overstates the change, since existing apps remain supported, and D invents a distribution restriction.

stem: Besides a pass or fail result, what can a connected fields extension return to Docusign when a signer enters a value?

options.text: A new signing URL that redirects the signer
Custom guidance messages and autofill values for envelope fields
An instruction to void the envelope
A new routing order for the remaining recipients

answerText: Custom guidance messages and autofill values for envelope fields
explanation: In its verification response, the system can supply custom messages guiding the user and autofill values based on known information.

optionExplanations.A: Signing URLs are created through the eSignature API, not returned by a verify action.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The response can include custom messages and autofill values.
optionExplanations.C: Voiding is an eSignature operation, not part of the verification response.
optionExplanations.D: Routing order is envelope configuration, not a connected fields result.

whyNotOthers: B is right because connected fields support custom messages and autofill. The trap is A: signing URLs come from the eSignature API for embedded signing, not from a verification response. C and D are envelope management actions the extension cannot perform.

stem: What distinguishes Data Verification extensions from Connected Fields extensions?

options.text: Data Verification verifies specific standard types; Connected Fields verifies custom data against your system
Data Verification verifies custom data; Connected Fields verifies only standard types
Data Verification runs only in Maestro; Connected Fields runs only in Web Forms
Data Verification is only for private apps; Connected Fields is only for public apps

answerText: Data Verification verifies specific standard types; Connected Fields verifies custom data against your system
explanation: Data verification extensions verify specific types (bank account, address, SSN, email, phone, FEIN); connected fields perform custom verification of any type against your system of record.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Standard types for Data Verification; custom data against your system for Connected Fields.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses the roles of the two extension types.
optionExplanations.C: Both run at the eSignature Add Fields view and signing; connected fields are not in Maestro or Web Forms.
optionExplanations.D: Distribution type does not determine which extension type you can build.

whyNotOthers: A is right because it states the standard-versus-custom split. The trap is B, which reverses the two. C misstates the extension points (both run at Add Fields and signing), and D invents a distribution rule.

stem: A user revokes consent for a JWT-based integration through Manage Profile > Connected Apps. The integration still holds an access token issued 20 minutes ago. What happens?

options.text: The token keeps working, and the integration can keep minting new JWT tokens because JWT does not use consent
Docusign automatically re-prompts the user for consent on the next API call
The existing access token works until it expires; the next JWT exchange fails until consent is granted again
The existing access token is invalidated immediately and the next API call returns 401

answerText: The existing access token works until it expires; the next JWT exchange fails until consent is granted again
explanation: Revoking consent invalidates refresh tokens and blocks new tokens, but live access tokens, including JWT ones, keep working until they expire.

optionExplanations.A: JWT requires consent; after revocation, new JWT token requests fail until consent is granted again.
optionExplanations.B: API calls never show a consent prompt; the user must be sent to /oauth/auth again.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Live access tokens stay valid until they expire, but new tokens cannot be issued without consent.
optionExplanations.D: Revocation does not end live access tokens; they stay valid until they expire.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: C is right because revocation stops new tokens but does not kill live ones. The trap is D: it sounds like the secure outcome, but Docusign does not invalidate existing access tokens on revocation. A is wrong because JWT requires consent, and B is wrong because API calls never trigger a consent prompt.

stem: Consent for an internal JWT integration was granted by an organization administrator for all users in the claimed domain. A user in that domain wants to revoke the app's access to their account. What is true?

options.text: The user must open a support case with Docusign
The integration key must be deleted to remove consent
The user can revoke it from Manage Profile > Connected Apps like any other app
An administrator must revoke it in Docusign Admin; reserved-domain users cannot revoke it individually

answerText: An administrator must revoke it in Docusign Admin; reserved-domain users cannot revoke it individually
explanation: Admin-granted consent is revoked in Docusign Admin, and users in the organization's reserved domains cannot revoke it themselves.

optionExplanations.A: Revoking admin consent is self-service for the organization admin in Docusign Admin; no support case is needed.
optionExplanations.B: Deleting the key is unnecessary and affects every user; consent is revoked in Docusign Admin.
optionExplanations.C: Connected Apps revocation applies to individual consent; reserved-domain users cannot revoke admin-granted consent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Admin-granted consent is revoked in Docusign Admin, not by individual reserved-domain users.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: D is right because the consent was granted by an admin for the reserved domain. The trap is C: Connected Apps is where users revoke individual consent, but not consent that an admin granted for their domain. A is unnecessary because revocation is self-service for the admin, and B removes the app for everyone.

stem: An ISV sells a JWT-based integration to many customers. Some have Docusign Access Management with claimed domains; others do not. Which two design choices follow Docusign best practice? (Select two)

options.text: Always build an individual consent fallback for users or customers who cannot use admin consent
Ask each customer's admin to authorize the app from Docusign Admin > Connected Apps > Authorize Application
Offer admin consent for external applications (scope=openid plus admin_consent_scope) to customers with claimed domains
Skip consent by requesting the impersonation scope in the JWT assertion

answerText: Always build an individual consent fallback for users or customers who cannot use admin consent; Offer admin consent for external applications (scope=openid plus admin_consent_scope) to customers with claimed domains
explanation: JWT best practice is to offer admin consent where possible (the external-app flow for ISV apps) and always fall back to individual consent, because admin consent needs Access Management and a claimed domain.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Not every customer has Access Management and a claimed domain, so an individual consent path is required.
optionExplanations.B: Authorize Application in Docusign Admin is for internal apps; an ISV's key is external to the customer's organization.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. ISV apps used by other organizations get admin consent through scope=openid with admin_consent_scope.
optionExplanations.D: Impersonation must itself be consented to; listing it in the assertion does not replace consent.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because ISV apps use the external admin consent flow and still need an individual consent fallback. The trap is B: Authorize Application in Docusign Admin is real admin consent, but only for internal apps whose key the organization owns. D fails because impersonation itself must be consented to.

stem: A developer sends an org admin to /oauth/auth with scope=openid and admin_consent_scope=signature%20impersonation. After the admin consents, how does the app find out which organizations granted consent?

options.text: From the accounts list in the /oauth/userinfo response
From the coid claim in the ID token returned with the access token
From the state parameter echoed back to the redirect URI
By calling the eSignature Accounts:get endpoint

answerText: From the coid claim in the ID token returned with the access token
explanation: Requesting openid returns an ID token whose coid claim lists the consenting organization IDs; this is the only way to get that list.

optionExplanations.A: /oauth/userinfo returns the user's accounts and base URIs, not which organizations granted admin consent.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The ID token's coid claim lists the consenting organization IDs.
optionExplanations.C: state is a CSRF value the app supplies; it carries no consent information from Docusign.
optionExplanations.D: Accounts:get returns eSignature account details, not the organizations that granted admin consent.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B is right because the coid claim in the ID token records the consenting organizations. The trap is A: /oauth/userinfo lists the user's accounts and base URIs, not the organizations that granted admin consent. C is an app-supplied CSRF value, and D returns account settings.

stem: Which two statements about scopes in the admin consent for external applications flow are correct? (Select two)

options.text: The extended scope can be used with JWT Grant to get a refresh token
The scope parameter is set to openid
The Maestro aow_manage scope is implied by signature
The scopes granted for each org user go in admin_consent_scope (for example signature impersonation)

answerText: The scope parameter is set to openid; The scopes granted for each org user go in admin_consent_scope (for example signature impersonation)
explanation: External admin consent uses scope=openid plus admin_consent_scope for the per-user scopes; extended only works with Authorization Code Grant, and API scopes such as aow_manage must be requested explicitly.

optionExplanations.A: extended applies only to Authorization Code Grant; JWT Grant never returns a refresh token.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. External admin consent uses scope=openid, so the consenting organization IDs are returned in the ID token.
optionExplanations.C: Maestro scopes must be requested explicitly; signature does not imply aow_manage.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. admin_consent_scope holds the space-separated scopes granted for each user in the organization.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because the external admin consent URL uses scope=openid and lists user scopes in admin_consent_scope. The trap is A: extended is a real scope, but it applies only to Authorization Code Grant, and JWT never returns a refresh token. C fails because Maestro scopes must be requested explicitly.

stem: An account's integrations exceed the default hourly API call limit. What is the default limit, and what happens?

options.text: 3,000 calls per hour per account; further calls are blocked until the next hour
1,000 calls per hour; extra calls are queued and processed the next hour
3,000 calls per hour per integration key; the key is permanently disabled
There is no hourly limit, only a burst limit

answerText: 3,000 calls per hour per account; further calls are blocked until the next hour
explanation: The default hourly limit is 3,000 calls per account, shared by all integrations; once exceeded, calls fail with a message that the maximum number of hourly API invocations has been exceeded until the hour resets.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. 3,000 calls per hour per account; excess calls are blocked until the hour resets.
optionExplanations.B: The default is 3,000, and excess calls are rejected, not queued.
optionExplanations.C: The limit is shared per account, and exceeding it does not disable the key.
optionExplanations.D: Both an hourly limit and a burst limit apply.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: A is right because the limit is per account and calls are blocked until the next hour. The trap is C: it has the right number, but the limit is per account, not per key, and the key is not disabled. B has the wrong number and wrongly queues calls, and D ignores the hourly limit.

stem: Which two practices follow Docusign guidance for staying within API resource limits? (Select two)

options.text: Subscribe to Docusign Connect instead of polling envelope status
Split traffic across several integration keys to multiply the hourly limit
If polling is unavoidable, poll a given envelope at most once every 15 minutes
Retry failed calls immediately in a tight loop until they succeed

answerText: Subscribe to Docusign Connect instead of polling envelope status; If polling is unavoidable, poll a given envelope at most once every 15 minutes
explanation: Use Connect instead of polling and, when you must poll, respect the once-per-15-minutes rule per envelope; also read the X-RateLimit headers and back off.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Connect pushes status changes so the app does not need to poll.
optionExplanations.B: The hourly limit is per account and shared, so extra keys add no capacity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Poll a given envelope no more than once every 15 minutes.
optionExplanations.D: Tight retry loops worsen burst violations; read X-RateLimit headers and back off.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because they reduce unnecessary calls. The trap is B: it would work if limits were per key, but the hourly limit is shared by all integrations on the account. D makes burst-limit violations worse; the guidance is to back off.

stem: An app receives the error code Burst_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded. What does it indicate?

options.text: The bulk send batch is too large
The envelope has too many recipients
The account exceeded its 3,000 calls per hour
Too many calls were made against one envelope in a short burst window

answerText: Too many calls were made against one envelope in a short burst window
explanation: Docusign enforces hourly and burst limits on calls against a single envelope; exceeding the burst version returns Burst_APIInvocation_Envelope_Limit_Exceeded.

optionExplanations.A: Bulk send size is not what this rate-limit code reports.
optionExplanations.B: Recipient count is unrelated to an API invocation limit.
optionExplanations.C: The account hourly limit produces a different error about hourly API invocations.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. It signals too many calls against one envelope within the burst window.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: D is right because the code names a per-envelope burst limit. The trap is C: it is an API limit, but the account hourly limit returns a different message about hourly API invocations. A and B describe envelope content limits, not call rates.

stem: Where can an account admin see efficiency scores for each integration and the factors that lower them?

options.text: The envelope audit history
API Usage Center
The Connect failure log
The API Dashboard in Apps and Keys

answerText: API Usage Center
explanation: The API Usage Center shows each app's efficiency score, and Actions > View Efficiency Score lists the negative factors with recommendations.

optionExplanations.A: Audit history covers events on one envelope, not app-level efficiency.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The API Usage Center shows efficiency scores and the factors behind them.
optionExplanations.C: The Connect failure log lists failed webhook deliveries.
optionExplanations.D: The API Dashboard shows request history and failures (up to 90 days), not efficiency scores.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B is right because efficiency scores live in the API Usage Center. The trap is D: the API Dashboard is also a monitoring tool, but it shows request timelines and failed requests, not efficiency scores. A covers single envelopes, and C covers failed webhook deliveries.

stem: Which three are factors in the API Usage Center efficiency score? (Select three)

options.text: Number of templates in the account
Average size of the documents in each envelope
Excessive envelope status requests
Excessive document retrieval requests
Excessive requests for nonexistent envelopes

answerText: Excessive envelope status requests; Excessive document retrieval requests; Excessive requests for nonexistent envelopes
explanation: Efficiency factors include blocked calls, exceeded burst and hourly limits, excessive document retrieval, excessive envelope, status and recipient status requests, requests for nonexistent envelopes, excessive requests per envelope, and low call activity.

optionExplanations.A: Template count is not an efficiency factor.
optionExplanations.B: Document size is not scored; only excessive document retrieval requests are.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Excessive envelope status requests (polling) lower the score.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Excessive document retrieval requests lower the score.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Requests for nonexistent envelopes lower the score.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: C, D and E are right because they are listed efficiency factors about wasteful calls. The trap is B: documents matter for document retrieval requests, but their size is not scored; only excessive retrieval calls are. A is an account content metric, not a call pattern.
