stem: An admin tries to raise the account's hourly API limit in the API Usage Center, but the Update Hourly Limit option is not available. Which two conditions could explain it? (Select two)

options.text: The integration key uses JWT Grant instead of Authorization Code Grant
Some apps on the account have unresolved efficiency issues
The account has a Connect configuration
The account plan does not include the limit management feature

answerText: Some apps on the account have unresolved efficiency issues; The account plan does not include the limit management feature
explanation: Raising the limit yourself requires a plan with limit management, account admin rights, no Support-set limit, efficient apps, and enough call history.

optionExplanations.A: The OAuth grant type has no effect on limit management.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Flagged efficiency issues must be fixed before the limit can be raised.
optionExplanations.C: Using Connect is recommended and does not block limit changes.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Without limit management in the plan, the option is not available.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because both are listed prerequisites. The trap is C: Connect is part of API limit guidance, but using it is a best practice and never blocks a limit change. A is wrong because the OAuth flow is unrelated to limit management.

stem: An integration must reconcile envelope statuses after its Connect listener was down for two hours. What is the recommended way to catch up?

options.text: Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges with a from_date covering the outage, using overlapping time spans
Raise the hourly API limit and poll each envelope every minute
Delete and recreate the Connect configuration so it replays every event
Call Envelopes:get for every envelope ever sent

answerText: Call Envelopes:listStatusChanges with a from_date covering the outage, using overlapping time spans
explanation: Docusign recommends Envelopes:listStatusChanges with overlapping time spans to catch up on status changes, instead of per-envelope polling.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. listStatusChanges over the outage window, with overlapping spans, catches every change.
optionExplanations.B: Per-envelope polling is limited to once every 15 minutes regardless of the hourly limit.
optionExplanations.C: Recreating a Connect configuration does not replay historical events.
optionExplanations.D: Fetching every envelope individually wastes calls and can hit hourly and per-envelope limits.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: A is right because one listStatusChanges call returns all envelopes changed in the window. The trap is C: it stays within Connect, but recreating a configuration does not replay past events. B breaks the once-per-15-minutes polling rule, and D wastes calls and risks hourly and per-envelope limits.

stem: Which TWO mechanisms help a Connect listener verify that a webhook really came from Docusign and was not altered? (Select two)

options.text: HMAC signature validation using the X-DocuSign-Signature-1 header
Requiring the listener URL to use HTTP on port 80
Mutual TLS (client certificate) between Docusign and the listener
Checking that the envelopeId exists in the payload

answerText: HMAC signature validation using the X-DocuSign-Signature-1 header; Mutual TLS (client certificate) between Docusign and the listener
explanation: Connect listener security options include HMAC signatures, mutual TLS, Basic authentication and OAuth 2.0 for Connect; HMAC and mutual TLS are the two listed here.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Connect hashes the payload with the HMAC key; the listener recomputes and compares.
optionExplanations.B: Plain HTTP removes encryption; production Connect listeners must use HTTPS.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Mutual TLS lets the listener verify Docusign's client certificate.
optionExplanations.D: An envelope ID can be copied into a forged message; it proves nothing about the sender.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: A and C are right because each cryptographically proves Docusign is the sender. The trap is D: checking the envelope ID feels like validation, but anyone who knows an ID can include it in a forged payload. B weakens security because production listeners must use HTTPS.

stem: Which TWO listener behaviors reduce Connect failures and the impact of retries? (Select two)

options.text: Return HTTP 500 for events the app does not care about
Return HTTP 200 quickly, then process the payload asynchronously
Call Envelopes:get for every event before acknowledging
Make processing idempotent so a redelivered event does no harm

answerText: Return HTTP 200 quickly, then process the payload asynchronously; Make processing idempotent so a redelivered event does no harm
explanation: Connect retries failed deliveries, so the listener should acknowledge fast, queue the work and process idempotently.

optionExplanations.A: Any non-2xx response is a failure that triggers retries; acknowledge and ignore instead.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Slow processing causes timeouts that Connect treats as failures and retries.
optionExplanations.C: Extra synchronous API calls slow the acknowledgement and use API quota.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Retries and republishes can deliver the same event more than once.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because a fast 200 prevents timeouts and idempotency makes redelivered events harmless. The trap is A: rejecting unwanted events seems tidy, but any non-2xx is a failure that triggers retries; acknowledge and ignore instead. C slows the response and wastes API calls before acknowledging.

stem: A request uses compositeTemplates with one serverTemplate (sequence 1) and one inlineTemplate (sequence 2) that both define a signer for role 'Client'. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select two)

options.text: The server template's recipient data wins because server templates always take precedence.
Server and inline templates in the composite object are applied in order of their sequence numbers.
The inline template's recipient data overwrites the server template where they overlap.
Composite templates require envelope status created and cannot be sent directly.

answerText: Server and inline templates in the composite object are applied in order of their sequence numbers.; The inline template's recipient data overwrites the server template where they overlap.
explanation: Templates in a composite object are applied in sequence order, and for attributes such as recipients and tabs, higher sequence values overwrite lower ones. So the inline template (sequence 2) supplies the runtime recipient for 'Client'.

optionExplanations.A: Server templates do not always win; for attributes, the higher sequence (here the inline template) overwrites.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Server and inline templates are examined in order of their sequence values.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Attributes with higher sequence values overwrite lower ones, so the inline recipient data applies.
optionExplanations.D: Composite template envelopes can be sent directly with status sent; created is only needed for a draft.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B and C are right because attributes are layered by sequence and the last applied wins. The trap is A: server templates do win for documents when there is no document property (lowest sequence), but for recipient attributes the higher sequence overwrites. D is wrong because a composite template envelope can be created with status sent.

stem: Which TWO are required for embedded signing with EnvelopeViews:createRecipient? (Select two)

options.text: The signer has a clientUserId set when the envelope is created.
The signing URL is emailed to the signer.
The envelope must be in created (draft) status.
The request includes a returnUrl where Docusign redirects after the signing session.

answerText: The signer has a clientUserId set when the envelope is created.; The request includes a returnUrl where Docusign redirects after the signing session.
explanation: Embedded signing needs a signer created with clientUserId, then a createRecipient request with matching email, userName and clientUserId, an authenticationMethod and a returnUrl.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. clientUserId on the signer at creation is what makes embedded signing possible.
optionExplanations.B: The app redirects the user to the signing URL itself; Docusign does not email it.
optionExplanations.C: A draft envelope is used for embedded sending; for embedded signing the envelope is sent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. returnUrl is required in the createRecipient request so Docusign knows where to redirect.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: A and D are right because clientUserId marks the signer as embedded and returnUrl is a required part of the recipient view request. The trap is C: draft status is needed for embedded sending (createSender), but embedded signing needs a sent envelope. B is wrong because the app redirects the user to the URL itself; it is not emailed.

stem: A sender wants signers to enter a code the sender shares out of band (for example, reads out over the phone) before opening the documents. No extra cost or third-party check is wanted. Which method fits?

options.text: Phone authentication (code sent by SMS or call)
Knowledge-based authentication (KBA)
Access code authentication
Recording authenticationMethod on createRecipient

answerText: Access code authentication
explanation: The clues are a sender-defined code shared out of band and no extra cost, which is access code authentication.

optionExplanations.A: Here Docusign sends the code by call or SMS, rather than the sender sharing it, and phone authentication can incur extra cost.
optionExplanations.B: KBA uses public-record questions from a third-party service (US only) and incurs per-use fees.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. An access code is set by the sender, shared out of band, and is the lightest enforced method with no per-use fee.
optionExplanations.D: authenticationMethod only records your app's authentication on the certificate; the signer is never asked for a code.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: C is right because the access code is a sender-chosen secret shared out of band and carries no per-use fee. The trap is A: it also involves a code and a phone, but Docusign delivers that code and the method can cost extra. B fails because KBA uses third-party questions with fees, and D fails because it records rather than enforces.

stem: Which statement about ID verification (IDV) as a recipient authentication method is correct?

options.text: It needs the account's IDV workflowId, retrieved with IdentityVerifications:list (eSignature REST API v2.1)
It only records the authentication your app performed
It asks questions based on the signer's public records
It is enabled by default in every developer (demo) account

answerText: It needs the account's IDV workflowId, retrieved with IdentityVerifications:list (eSignature REST API v2.1)
explanation: IDV verifies government photo IDs or eIDs, uses the account's workflowId from IdentityVerifications:list, and is available in REST v2.1.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. IDV is applied with identityVerification.workflowId from IdentityVerifications:list in REST v2.1.
optionExplanations.B: That describes authenticationMethod on createRecipient, which is record-only; IDV actively verifies an ID.

stem: Which TWO are infrastructure considerations when hosting an extension app's backend service? (Select two)

options.text: The service must poll Docusign every minute for work
Authorization for Docusign's calls must be configured (Authorization Code or Client Credentials)
The endpoint must be reachable over HTTPS by Docusign, directly or through an API proxy
The service must run inside the customer's Docusign account

answerText: Authorization for Docusign's calls must be configured (Authorization Code or Client Credentials); The endpoint must be reachable over HTTPS by Docusign, directly or through an API proxy
explanation: Plan for reachability (HTTPS, firewall allow-listing or an API proxy) and for the OAuth 2.0 grant Docusign uses to call your service.

optionExplanations.A: Docusign calls the service when needed; polling is not part of the model.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The connection's OAuth grant must be configured for Docusign's calls.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Docusign must be able to reach the endpoint over HTTPS.
optionExplanations.D: Installing the app in an account does not run your backend inside Docusign.

source: Gap fill - official Prep Guide v.2026 objectives
whyNotOthers: B and C are right because Docusign must both reach and be authorized to call your service. The trap is D: the app is installed in the customer's account, but the service itself runs on your infrastructure. A is wrong because Docusign calls the service; the service does not poll.
